Task Detail
───────────
ID:         E-1898
Title:      Stop the dead-pane reaper from nulling live pane bindings project-wide
Project:    endless
Type:       todo
Phase:      urgent
Status:     unverified
Created:    2026-08-06 12:11 am by ES-1026 (E-1851)
Updated:    2026-08-10 7:20 am
Analysis:   11134 chars (--analysis to display)
This task:
- Relates to:     E-1900 [obsolete]
- Relates to:     E-1930 [obsolete]
- Cleaned up by:  E-1936 [unplanned]
- Cleaned up by:  E-1941 [submitted]
Touched by:
- Revisited:      ES-1034 (E-1898) [idle]
- Revisited:      ES-1054 (E-1926) [ended]
- Surfaced:       ES-1026 (E-1851) [idle]

— Description —
One root cause, one visibility gap. ROOT: `ReapDeadTmuxPanes` NULLs `process` for panes it cannot see, deciding that from an ambient $TMUX it never validates — so a caller under a foreign tmux server nulls every session row in the project, and TouchSession's COALESCE (correct, added by E-1426) is left with nothing to protect; rows then read alive with no pane, forever. Observed 2026-08-05: 27 orphaned panes, 59 of 61 status lines blank. VISIBILITY: the status line collapses every failure into one placeholder, so it ran for hours untraced, and a not-ended row with no process is incoherent and must fail loudly. Umbrella: absorbs E-1895, E-1468, E-1408 (stale) and E-1642 (idle-timeout must fill the gap that guarding the reaper opens).

— Text —
# E-1898 — liveness is observed, never inferred

## The one-sentence change

Delete the reaper. Give every pane binding an identity that is unique across
tmux server lifetimes, observe liveness into a temp table per unit of work, and
JOIN. No code path may conclude a session is dead by looking at tmux and then
writing that conclusion to the `sessions` table.

## Why the previous plan was replaced

The prior plan guarded the destructive write with an escalating series of gates
(server-uuid gate, peer-server enumeration, ordering guarantees, forced
override). Every gate was an inference about whether the pane set in front of
the process was the right one to judge by, because no row recorded which tmux
server it was bound to. Stacking gates narrows the window; it cannot close it,
and each gate added edge cases and un-mockable tmux tests.

Recording the binding's server identity removes the need for every one of those
gates. This plan is shorter than the one it replaces because the complexity was
compensation for a missing column, not essential difficulty.

## Invariants — these are the acceptance criteria

**I1 — No inferred destructive write.** No code path writes `state='ended'`, or
clears a pane binding, based on an observation of tmux. Only reported facts (a
`SessionEnd` hook) and explicit operator action close a session. There is no
sweep, no reaper, no mass UPDATE.

**I2 — Bounded blast radius.** A failed or incomplete observation may affect at
most the rows it actually observed. `unknown` is NEVER converted to `dead` by
any consumer. An unreachable server costs zero rows.

**I3 — Identity unique across server lifetimes.** A tmux pane id reused by a new
server can never match a binding made against the old one.

**I4 — Tests need no tmux server.** Liveness is a JOIN against a table; tests
seed that table directly. No private tmux servers, no socket enumeration, no
seam counters.

Verification drives each invariant explicitly. I1 and I2 are the ones this task
exists for; a change that satisfies I3 but not I1 has not fixed anything.

## Model

Multiplexer-agnostic. tmux is one populator; cmux and herdr add their own
without touching consumers.

```
process_kinds(id, slug)          -- tmux | pid | ...   (mirrors session_kinds)

processes(                       -- DURABLE identity. A fact, kept forever.
  id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  kind_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES process_kinds(id),
  server_uuid   TEXT,            -- tmux @server_uuid; NULL for kind=pid
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- tmux pane id '%414'; or the pid as text
  first_seen_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  last_seen_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE(kind_id, server_uuid, address)
)

sessions.process_id -> processes.id     -- replaces sessions.process

TEMP live_processes(kind_id, server_uuid, address, command)
TEMP observed_servers(kind_id, server_uuid)   -- which servers we actually reached
```

`processes` is append-mostly: a row is created the first time a session binds to
an address on a server, and is never deleted by observation. A tmux restart
mints a new `@server_uuid`, therefore a new `processes` row, therefore I3 holds
structurally — not by a guard that could be wrong.

## Liveness — three-valued, derived at read

```sql
CASE
  WHEN o.server_uuid IS NULL  THEN 'unknown'  -- server not reached
  WHEN l.address IS NULL      THEN 'dead'     -- reached; address absent
  ELSE                             'live'
END
FROM sessions s
JOIN processes p             ON p.id = s.process_id
LEFT JOIN observed_servers o USING (kind_id, server_uuid)
LEFT JOIN live_processes  l  USING (kind_id, server_uuid, address)
```

Expose as a view (`session_liveness`) so no consumer re-derives it.

Liveness is now PURELY OBSERVATIONAL: "is this address present on a server we
actually reached?" There is no remaining inference in it. That is the property
that makes I1 and I2 checkable rather than argued.

`unknown` is the safe branch: render last-known, condemn nothing. Per I2, no
consumer may map it to `dead`. The site that needs care is the spawn/claim
ownership guard — under `unknown` it must assume STILL OWNED and refuse. A
wrong refusal is an annoyance; the inverse steals a live worktree.

### Why the shell test is NOT part of liveness

The previous plan's death test was "address absent OR the pane runs a known
shell", to catch a killed harness whose pane survives. It is dropped from
liveness, because it is an inference and it can be wrong about a LIVE session:

- Verified 2026-08-09: a live Claude pane reports its version string
  (`2.1.220`) as `pane_current_command`, even mid-Bash-tool-call. So it does
  not collide with the shell set during normal operation.
- But **Ctrl+Z** puts the shell back in the foreground. A suspended-but-alive
  Claude session's pane reports `zsh`. Under the shell test that session reads
  `dead`, which drops its status line to the placeholder and — the part that
  matters — lets the spawn/claim ownership guard treat its task as free and
  hand the worktree to another session.

Cost of dropping it: a harness killed with its pane still open (SIGKILL, no
SessionEnd) leaves a stale-`live` row until the pane closes. That is a wrong
read in the SAFE direction — a refusal, never a theft — and E-1807's actual
case had a dead pane, which address-absence still catches.

`live_processes.command` is still collected, but is used ONLY for the cosmetic
"pane is running Claude but has no session row" status-line hint. An inference
is acceptable for a hint that misleads nobody and owns nothing; it is not
acceptable for liveness. That line is the rule, and the code must not blur it.

## Snapshot population

Refresh at the start of each **unit of work** — a CLI/hook invocation, an HTTP
request, a monitor repaint — inside the transaction that reads it, so a single
statement never sees two different observations.

For tmux: list sockets in `dirname $(tmux display-message -p '#{socket_path}')`;
for each, read `@server_uuid` and, when present, one
`tmux -S <sock> list-panes -a -F '#{pane_id} #{pane_current_command} #{pane_pid}'`.
Each successfully-read server contributes a row to `observed_servers`.

Enumeration stays, but is no longer load-bearing for safety: a server we cannot
reach (`tmux -S` outside the socket dir, relocated `TMUX_TMPDIR`) yields
`unknown` for its rows, not a verdict. This is the entire difference from the
previous plan's peer-enumeration gate, which had to be complete to be safe.

## Binding: where server_uuid comes from

The hook runs inside the pane. It reads `@server_uuid`; if absent it generates
and stamps one, exactly as `tmux init` does. Every binding therefore carries a
real server identity, and the previous plan's "refuse when uninitialized" gate
is unnecessary — identity is always present rather than sometimes checked.

## Deleted

- `monitor.ReapDeadTmuxPanes` and `internal/monitor/reap.go`, including the
  `len(alive) == 0` mass-UPDATE that ended every tmux row in one statement.
- `runInit`'s `runReset(nil)` call — the documented trigger for the 37-row batch.
- `endless tmux reset` ENTIRELY — the Go verb (`internal/tmuxcmd/reset.go`,
  its `tmux.go` dispatch), the Python wrappers (`cli.py` `tmux_reset`,
  `tmux_cmd.py` `run_reset`), the remedy line in `task_cmd.py:3304` that tells
  users to run it, and the assertion on that line in
  `tests/test_check_task_ownership.py:91`. No read-only replacement is
  introduced: `endless session list` and `endless sql` already read the view,
  and the ownership guard can no longer refuse over a gone pane — the snapshot
  shows it gone — so the remedy it advertised has nothing left to remedy.
- `TouchSession`'s collision invalidation. A reused pane is a different
  `processes` row, so the pane-reuse case cannot arise; a genuine same-server
  collision leaves both rows and the reader orders by `last_activity`.
- From the previous plan: D1, D2, D5, D6, D9 and their tests. D3's insight is
  kept as a read-time classifier; D7 and D8 survive as below.

## Kept from the previous plan

- **D7** — `runInit` no longer reaps (now: there is nothing to reap).
- **D8** — `runStatusLine` records a fault instead of silently rendering the
  placeholder on error. One correction to that decision: because
  `faults.Bind` is wired to `monitor.DB` (main.go:144) and `faults.Record`
  swallows its own DB failure by contract, this covers the non-DB fail-closed
  exits, not all of them. Worth doing; do not claim full coverage.
- The **ledger-safety assertion** in the verify suite.

## Migration

1. Create `process_kinds`, `processes`, add `sessions.process_id`.
2. Backfill, in TWO steps.

   2a. One `processes` row per distinct non-null `sessions.process`, with
   `server_uuid = NULL` (the binding server is not knowable retroactively) and
   `kind` derived from the string shape (`%N` -> tmux, `pid:N` -> pid).

   2b. ADOPT what is observable: for every pane live on the running tmux
   server, repoint the non-ended session bound to that address onto that
   server (`monitor.AdoptPaneBindings`).

   **Step 2b was missing from the first cut, and its absence took the board
   down on 2026-08-10.** This plan claimed the NULL-server rows would
   "self-heal on the session's next hook" and that live sessions would
   "recover within seconds without any repair verb". That is true only for
   sessions that FIRE hooks. An idle window fires none, and idle is the normal
   state, so every pre-existing session became unresolvable at once and STAYED
   unresolvable — the pane lookup matches on (current server uuid, address),
   and a NULL-server row matches no server at all. Measured on the real ledger
   when it bit: 64 sessions bound, 1 healed (the one firing hooks), 63 dark.

   Adoption is an observation, not a repair heuristic: a pane in the live set
   exists on the named server NOW. Two guards keep it honest — it refuses any
   address claimed by more than one non-ended session (that ambiguity is
   exactly what E-1898 exists to stop resolving by guesswork), and it creates
   a NEW row rather than stamping a server onto the shared NULL-server record,
   which the backfill deduplicates by address and which therefore carries
   history from every server that ever issued that pane.

   Panes that are not live, and every binding when no tmux server is
   reachable, keep `server_uuid` NULL and read `unknown` — never `dead`. On
   the measured ledger that left exactly one row: a genuine leftover from a
   dead server, which is precisely the case where `unknown` is the true
   answer. No repair verb is needed, but the reason is adoption, not healing.
3. Convert the ~35 call sites comparing `process` to a raw pane id. The type
   changes, so a missed site is a COMPILE ERROR — the property that made this
   safe to do where string-encoding `<uuid>:<pane>` would not have been.
4. Drop `sessions.process`.

`channels` is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE and keeps its string key; see E-1936.
It becomes the last consumer of the old key, deliberately, pending that
brainstorm's decision on whether it should exist at all.

## Tests — `tests/tasks/e-1898-verify.sh`

**Layer A — liveness truth table (FAIL-FAST, pure SQL fixtures, no tmux).**
Seed `processes`, `sessions`, `live_processes`, `observed_servers` directly and
assert every cell: server unobserved -> `unknown`; observed + address present ->
`live`; observed + address absent -> `dead`. Same pane id under two different
`server_uuid`s resolves independently (I3). Assert a pane running a shell reads
`live` while its session row stands — pinning that the shell inference is NOT in
the liveness path and cannot be reintroduced without failing this test.

**Layer B — invariants as tests, not as prose.**
- **I1:** grep the tree for any write of `state='ended'` or a binding clear
  outside the SessionEnd path; assert zero. Then drive a full hook cycle against
  an EMPTY `live_processes` (the exact 2026-08-05 shape: observer sees nothing)
  and assert **zero rows changed**. This is the regression test for the incident.
- **I2:** with `observed_servers` empty, assert no row reads `dead` and the
  ownership guard refuses rather than freeing.
- **I4:** the whole of A and B runs with `tmux` absent from `$PATH`.

**Layer C — one E2E** against a private tmux server (`-f /dev/null`, throwaway
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) proving the populator fills the snapshot from a real server.
Exactly one, because the logic under test is now SQL, not tmux plumbing.

**Layer D — project-wide regression:** `go test ./...`, `just test`, `just build`.

**Ledger-safety assertion (mandatory).** Count non-ended sessions holding a
binding in the REAL database before and after the suite; they must be equal.

## Out of scope

- `channels` and the `endless-channel` MCP server (E-1936).
- Idle-timeout / session-duration truthfulness. Positive observation covers
  "Claude died, pane lives" without inferring death from silence.
- Non-tmux (`pid:`) liveness. The model has a slot for it; no populator ships here.
- Repairing rows damaged on 2026-08-05. Repaired by hand; migration step 2
  heals the rest on the next hook.

fields.analysis:
# Analysis

One root cause with four faces: **code and database versions diverge across the
worktree / main / real-ledger boundary, and nothing guards the seam.** All four
were hit for real on 2026-08-10, in one sitting, landing E-1898.

## Face 1 — the land uses a binary built from stale source

`just land` (justfile ~167-250) does, in order:

1. `just go` in the worktree — rebuild endless-go
2. `endless db apply-change` against the REAL DB, using that binary
3. `endless worktree land` — which rebases onto main and fast-forwards

Step 1 came from E-1709, whose comment names this failure: "A worktree rebased
onto a newer main ... but not rebuilt would land with a STALE binary whose
embedded enums no longer match the real DB's rows ... (the E-1664 guard only
checks the binary is PRESENT, not CURRENT)."

E-1709 solved half. It makes the binary match the worktree's SOURCE. Nothing
makes the source match MAIN. With the branch 147 commits behind, `just go`
faithfully rebuilt a still-stale binary and step 2 hit the same wall:

    Error: apply-change failed: open db: gate_kinds integrity check on
      ~/.config/endless/endless.db: gatekind: gate_kinds row id="2" slug="relay"
      has no matching enum constant

Nothing was wrong with gate_kinds. Main's E-1901 had added `GateKindRelay` and
applied the row; the worktree's source predated it. The rebase that would fix
this is step 3 — after the step that needs it.

## Face 2 — apply-change succeeds, the merge fails, the DB is left ahead

After rebasing by hand, the land was re-run. This time step 2 SUCCEEDED and the
land then failed, so main never got the code. Result: the real DB was migrated
to a schema only the unlanded branch understands, while every installed binary
still expected the old one. Every session query referenced a dropped column, so
all 64 sessions went unresolvable and session tracking froze machine-wide (0
writes in the following 7 minutes).

The justfile comment asserts: "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances (clean recovery)." It reasons only about apply FAILING. Apply
succeeding and the merge then failing is the unhandled — and worse — case,
because it is the one that is irreversible.

## Face 3 — no supported way back

`endless db backup` exists and the land calls it. There is no `endless db
restore`. Recovery was an unguided `cp`, and it went wrong twice:

- Copied over a live database with six open connections, leaving a hot
  `endless.db-journal`. A read-only connection cannot roll back a hot journal,
  so every reader returned `database is locked` and the status bar flickered.
- The backup is produced by `VACUUM INTO`, which writes a **rollback-journal**
  database. The live DB was WAL. Restoring silently changed journal mode, and
  every connection then fought over an exclusive lock to switch it back.

Recovery took: `pkill -f 'endless task show'` (four abandoned pagers holding
connections for up to 22 days), killing two `session-status --monitor`
processes, then `sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'`
to roll back the journal and restore WAL. None of that is discoverable.

A backup you cannot safely restore is not insurance.

## Face 4 — the worktree hook runs candidate code against the real ledger

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's Claude hook at `<worktree>/bin/endless-go`,
and hooks force the REAL DB (E-1450). That is correct for ordinary branches and
BROKEN for any branch carrying an unlanded schema change: the candidate binary
writes a schema the real ledger does not have yet.

    endless-go hook: claude: touching session: upsert session:
      SQL logic error: table sessions has no column named process_id

Fired on every tool use for the duration. Non-blocking, so it degrades quietly:
the session simply stops being recorded. Worked around by hand-editing the
worktree's `.claude/settings.json` to point at `/usr/local/bin/endless-go`.

## Directions (not locked)

- **Currency precondition.** Before step 1, refuse when
  `git rev-list --count HEAD..main` != 0. Refusing beats auto-rebasing: E-1898's
  own rebase stopped on a conflict in the append-only db-ledger JSONL, and a
  rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.
- **Ordering / atomicity.** Apply schema changes only once the merge is
  guaranteed, or make the pair recoverable as a unit. Face 2 is the expensive
  one; fix it even if nothing else here is done.
- **`endless db restore <backup>`.** A verb that stops DB users, restores, and
  re-establishes WAL — encoding what had to be reverse-engineered under
  pressure. Pairs with the backup the land already takes.
- **Schema-aware hook override.** When the worktree's branch adds an unapplied
  change file, `just claude-settings-init` should point the hook at the global
  binary rather than the candidate, and say so.
- **Diagnosis.** Every `VerifyIntegrity` call site can name the likely cause
  when the DB has rows the binary lacks: "this binary predates the database;
  rebase onto main and rebuild." That direction of drift is always staleness,
  never corruption. The reverse (binary has constants the DB lacks) is a
  genuinely missing migration and should keep reading as it does now.

## Out of scope

E-1898 itself, which is fixed and re-verified. `endless task show -p` pinning a
DB connection for the life of its pager is a real but separate nuisance; file it
on its own if it bites again.

payload.title: Add endless db restore to recover from a backup safely
payload.description: `endless db backup` exists and `just land` calls it, but there is no way to USE a backup — recovery is an unguided `cp`. On 2026-08-10 that went wrong twice: copying over a database with six open connections left a hot journal that made every reader fail with 'database is locked', and `VACUUM INTO` backups are rollback-journal while the live DB is WAL, so connections then fought over switching it back. Add `endless db restore [<backup>]` that defaults to the newest backup, REPORTS open connections by pid/command rather than killing them silently, keeps the pre-restore file aside, and afterwards re-establishes WAL and runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` failing loudly on anything but 'ok'. A dry-run mode printing holders and journal mode is what you actually want mid-incident.
payload.analysis:
# Analysis

## Why this is needed

`just land` takes a backup before applying a schema change, so the safety net is
already half-built. The other half does not exist: there is no way to use it.

On 2026-08-10 a land applied E-1898's migration to the real ledger and then
failed before merging, leaving the database on a schema no installed binary
understood. Session tracking froze machine-wide. Recovery was an ad-hoc `cp`,
and it went wrong twice before it went right:

1. **Copied over a live database.** Six connections were open (two
   `session-status --monitor`, four `endless task show -p` abandoned in pagers
   for up to 22 days). That left a hot `endless.db-journal`. A read-only
   connection cannot roll back a hot journal, so every reader returned
   `database is locked` and the tmux status bar flickered on and off.

2. **Journal mode silently changed.** `endless db backup` uses `VACUUM INTO`,
   which writes a **rollback-journal** database. The live DB was WAL. After the
   restore every connection fought for an exclusive lock trying to switch back.

What finally worked, none of it discoverable:

    pkill -f 'endless task show'          # abandoned pagers holding connections
    kill <session-status --monitor pids>
    sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'

## What the verb should do

`endless db restore [<backup>]` — default to the most recent backup.

1. Refuse unless the target is a real Endless DB and the backup opens clean.
2. Enumerate open connections (the equivalent of `lsof` on the db file) and
   REPORT them by pid and command. Do not kill anything silently; either refuse
   with the list, or require an explicit flag to proceed.
3. Restore the file.
4. Re-establish `journal_mode=WAL` and run `PRAGMA integrity_check`, failing
   loudly if it is not `ok`.
5. Keep the pre-restore database aside (timestamped) so the restore itself is
   reversible.

## Notes

- Step 2 is the load-bearing one. Every failure above came from copying over a
  file other processes had open, not from the copy itself.
- A dry-run mode that prints what it would do (holders, journal mode, sizes)
  costs little and is what you actually want at 5am mid-incident.
- Related: E-1941 covers the land-flow ordering that creates the need for a
  restore in the first place. This task is the recovery tool; that one is the
  prevention. They are independent — the tool is worth having regardless.

fields.text:
# E-1940 — Make the unsettled probe stop reporting "I could not tell" as "you are clear"

Absorbs E-1166. Decisions below are settled unless flagged OPEN.

## Problem

`UnsettledDetail.Unsettled()` returns false — the all-clear — whenever its git
probes could not run. The reaper runs the SAME two probes and already fails
closed ("Any git error while running 4 or 5 is treated as 'in use' — the reaper
would rather skip a candidate it can't reason about than destroy in-flight
work"). So the two surfaces the code claims agree on what "done and landed"
means actually diverge exactly where it matters, and the display picked the
unsafe polarity.

The hardcoded `main` is what makes this permanent rather than rare: on a repo
whose default branch differs, `git rev-list main..HEAD` exits 128 every time,
so `◆` can never appear and the reaper never reaps.

## Settled decisions

| # | Decision | Rejected alternative |
|---|----------|----------------------|
| 1 | Probe failure records a **fault** (E-698's system, already landed). | A new `?` glyph and legend entry. |
| 2 | Default branch resolved by one **shared helper**, used by the unsettled probe AND the reaper. | Fixing the display only and leaving the reaper on `main`. |
| 3 | E-1166 is **absorbed**: the Python `_default_base_branch` fix lands here too, under one strategy. | Two independent resolvers, one per language. |
| 4 | A probe failure marks the task's own row `◆`, alongside the fault. | Badge-only: `◆` keeps its narrow meaning and the row renders as if clean. |

## A. Shared default-branch resolver

New `monitor.DefaultBranch(repoDir) (string, error)`. Resolution order:

1. `.endless/config.json` `default_branch`, when set — explicit beats detection.
2. `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, stripped of `origin/`.
3. `git config init.defaultBranch`.
4. Probe `main`, then `master`, for an existing local ref.
5. Otherwise a real error — the caller decides, and no caller may silently
   substitute `main`.

Step 2 is unset on fresh clones (it needs `git remote set-head`) — that is
E-1166's original finding and why steps 3–5 exist. Resolution is per-repo and
should be memoized for the process; `session monitor` calls the probe every 2s
per row and must not add a git call per row per tick.

## B. Call sites

- `internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go` — `worktreeUnsettledAt`'s probe 2.
- `internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go` — `maybeReapWorktree` condition 4.
- `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` — `_default_base_branch` (absorbed E-1166).

The Go and Python implementations must agree on the order above; assert that in
the tests rather than trusting prose.

## C. Polarity and reporting

`UnsettledDetail` gains an explicit undetermined state rather than overloading
the existing booleans:

- `Unsettled()` returns **true** when a probe failed, so the task's own row is
  marked. The alternative — report only in the badge and leave the row looking
  clean — was rejected: the row is the surface actually scanned, and a row that
  renders identically to a verified-clean one is the exact failure this task
  exists to remove. Marking the row is what tells you WHICH task is
  unverifiable without opening the fault.
- This widens `◆` from "you have work to land" to "look at this task — unlanded
  or uncheckable". That is a deliberate trade, and it is why the distinction
  below must be retrievable.
- `IsUndetermined()` reports it distinctly, so `task unsettled <id>` says which
  probe failed and why. `Reason()` already prints the error text today — that
  half is honest and stays. The list view collapses; the detail view explains.
- No new glyph, and no legend change beyond the fault badge E-698 already
  renders.

A fault is recorded on probe failure, so the condition is visible even when no
one is looking at that row, and is clearable. Faults are deduped by
fingerprint — key on (task id, failing probe) so a monitor ticking every 2s
raises one incident, not thousands.

## D. Fault codes

Two new entries in `internal/faults/codes.go` (numbers never reused; take the
next free ids):

- **worktree-probe-failed** — `git status` or `rev-list` failed for a worktree.
  Severity `error`: the user asked "is my work safe?" and Endless could not
  answer.
- **default-branch-unresolved** — resolution fell through every step in A.
  Severity `error`, same reasoning; it disables the probe entirely.

Both carry the task id, worktree path, failing command, and git's stderr in
`Fields`/`Detail`.

## E. Reaper

Condition 4 takes the resolver. Its fail-closed handling is already correct and
must not be touched. Fixing the branch resolution is what lets a non-`main`
project reap at all — today every candidate errors and is skipped forever.

This change touches the code path that DELETES worktrees, so the tests must pin
that a resolver error still yields "skip", never "reap".

## Verification

**Durable tests** (these outlive the task):

- Go: resolver returns each step's answer in order, and errors rather than
  defaulting to `main` when all fail; `Unsettled()` is true on `StatusErr` and
  on `RevListErr`; `IsUndetermined()` separates that from real unsettled work;
  a fault is recorded once per (task, probe) rather than per tick; the reaper
  skips on resolver error.
- pytest: the Python resolver agrees with the Go order.
- A `master`-based fixture repo: `◆` appears for genuinely unlanded work and
  the reaper can reap. This is the regression that proves the product works
  outside `main`.

**`tests/tasks/e-1940-verify.sh`** — acceptance. **Author a script, NOT a
`.endless/tasks/e-1940/verify.toml`**: the manifest form is not the norm until
the verification-suite epic lands.

## Absorbed

- **E-1166** — absorbed; mark obsolete with an outcome naming this task.

## Not in scope

Local-vs-remote divergence (unpushed commits, `origin/main` ahead/behind).
`session status` answers "is this worktree's work landed into main?" — landing
is a local rebase + fast-forward, so LOCAL `main` is the correct reference and
the current comparison is right.

payload.title: Decide how landed task branches stop accumulating already-landed commits
payload.description: A task branch keeps its pre-rebase commits after landing, because land rebases onto main (rewriting SHAs) and nothing resets the branch. It accumulates commits whose patches are already upstream while main moves ahead, so every later land replays the pile and the append-only ledger jsonl segments conflict once per ledger commit — recovery-and-retry never converges. Decide the mechanism: reset-after-land, drop patch-equivalent commits before replaying, refuse early with a named diagnosis, a union merge driver for the ledger files, extending reap to diverged branches, or a salvage-and-abandon path. See analysis for candidates, evidence, and the three gaps that fall out of the choice.
payload.analysis:
A task branch that has landed keeps its pre-rebase commits, because land
rebases onto main (rewriting SHAs) and nothing resets the branch afterward. The
branch therefore accumulates commits whose patches are already upstream, while
main moves ahead independently. Every later land from that worktree replays the
whole pile, and the append-only ledger jsonl segments conflict because both
sides appended different lines to the same file — one conflict per ledger
commit, so recovery-and-retry never converges.

Observed on the e-801 worktree, forked ten days earlier: `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its branch commits as patch-equivalent to commits
already on main, and the land aborted on the first ledger conflict. Comparing
trees rather than commits showed only two files where the branch was genuinely
ahead. That is the diagnostic worth generalizing: commit counts mislead here,
tree comparison and `git cherry` tell the truth.

Decide the mechanism. Candidates, none pre-selected:

- Reset the branch to main after a successful land, so the next land starts
  clean. Cheapest, but destroys anything genuinely unlanded that was not part
  of the landed set.
- Teach land to drop commits already patch-equivalent upstream before
  replaying, rather than replaying and conflicting.
- Detect the condition and refuse early with a named diagnosis, instead of
  discovering it as a mid-rebase conflict.
- Give the ledger jsonl files a union merge driver so concurrent appends stop
  conflicting at all. Fixes the symptom without addressing duplicate history.
- Extend the reap sweep to catch diverged branches, not only stale landed
  worktrees.
- Add a salvage-and-abandon path: take the files a stale branch is genuinely
  ahead on, record the landing, drop the worktree and branch. Today this is
  hand-run git plus `worktree land --record-only`.

Three concrete gaps are evidence, not separate tasks — their right fix falls
out of whichever mechanism wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.
- No command performs the salvage composite, and `drop` leaves the branch
  behind, so abandoning a stale worktree cleanly still takes raw git.

Relates to E-1941, which fixes a different failure arising from the same root
condition: `just land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from
still-stale worktree source, because the rebase onto main happens afterward.
That task makes currency a precondition of one step; this one asks why branches
go stale and stay stale at all.

Out of scope: the immediate disposition of any particular stranded worktree.

payload.title: Decide who may define, migrate, and use the DB schema, and when
payload.description: The 2026-08-10 incident produced four distinct failures from one question. `monitor.DB()` applies schema.sql on EVERY connection, so any binary additively migrates whatever DB it opens; E-1818's schema-passive mode stops that for pinned surfaces but only protects the DB from the binary, never the binary from the DB — a candidate binary against a main-schema ledger (or vice versa) passes connect cleanly and then fails at runtime writing or reading columns that aren't there. That is what took session tracking down for 30 minutes. Two hypotheses to evaluate: a migration-only executable built from the landing branch that does DDL and never DML; and replacing apply-on-connect with an explicit `endless db upgrade`, with ordinary connects verifying the schema version and refusing rather than silently fixing it. Analysis carries the full state tables. Deliverable is a decision plus follow-on tasks, not an implementation.
payload.analysis:
# Analysis

Provoked by the 2026-08-10 incident landing E-1898, which produced four distinct
failures in one sitting from one underlying question: **who is allowed to define,
migrate, and use the schema, and when.**

## What governs schema writes today

`monitor.DB()` applies `schema.SQL` — all additive `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` —
on EVERY connection, plus five enum `VerifyIntegrity` gates that fail closed.
Destructive one-off change files run separately, once, at land time via
`endless db apply-change`.

E-1818 added **schema-passive**: when `dbPathOverride != ""` (set by
`PinMainDB`/`ForceRealDB`, i.e. the hook, tmux and channel surfaces) the connect
skips both the schema apply and every gate.

**The gap.** Schema-passive protects the DB from the binary. It does nothing to
protect the binary from the DB. The hook error on 2026-08-10 proves it: the
candidate binary did not migrate anything, it simply failed writing `process_id`
into a table that lacked the column. E-1818 solved one half; the unsolved half
is the one that caused the outage.

## A. What each executable does on connect

| Executable | Surface | Pins real DB? | Applies schema.sql | Runs enum gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| global (main) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| global (main) | task, sql, event, ... | no | yes | yes |
| worktree (candidate) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| worktree (candidate) | event apply-change | no | YES | YES  <- the gate_kinds abort |
| worktree (candidate) | anything with --config-dir | no | yes (that DB) | yes |
| Python CLI | all | n/a | own bootstrap | none |

## B. Binary schema vs. DB schema

| Binary expects | DB has | Connect | Runtime DML | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | main | ok | ok | normal |
| candidate | candidate | ok | ok | sandbox only |
| candidate | main | ok (passive) | FAILS: writes absent columns | hook errors, 30 min |
| main | candidate | ok (passive) | FAILS: reads dropped columns | blank board, 30 min |

Rows 3 and 4 are one defect seen from either side. NEITHER is detected at
connect; both surface as runtime SQL errors on hot paths. The enum gates cover
enum tables only and would never catch a dropped column.

## C. Landing phases

| Phase | Binary | DB | Schema | What failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 rebuild worktree bin | worktree | - | - | built from stale source (147 behind) |
| 2 backup | Python | real | pre | - |
| 3 apply-change | worktree | real | pre -> post | gate abort; later succeeded |
| 4 merge | git | - | - | FAILED -> DB post, code pre |
| 5 record landing | worktree | real | post | never reached |
| 6 just build | - | - | - | never reached; global stayed pre |

## Hypotheses to evaluate

**H1 — a migration-only executable.** Built from the landing branch, does DDL
only, never DML, so it has no runtime schema expectations to be wrong about.
Cleanly resolves phase 3. Does NOT touch table B rows 3/4, which are ordinary
binaries at runtime.

**H2 — explicit upgrade; connects verify instead of migrate.** Replace
apply-on-connect with an `endless db upgrade` verb; ordinary connects compare
the DB's schema version against the binary's and REFUSE with a clear message.
This is the one that collapses table B: rows 3 and 4 become a precise
connect-time refusal, and no binary can mutate the real ledger by opening it —
which also makes schema-passive unnecessary. Costs users an explicit step after
upgrade, and every entry point needs a good "your database needs upgrading"
message.

**Neither resolves everything, and that should be stated up front:**
- Ordering (phase 3 vs 4) is independent — see E-1941. H2 arguably makes a
  half-landed state MORE visibly broken (everything refuses) rather than less.
- Recovery is independent — see E-1942, whose shape depends on this decision:
  "copy a backup back" vs "upgrade --rollback" are different verbs.
- Whether candidate hook code should write to the real ledger at all (the
  E-998 / E-1450 tension) is a policy question this may inform but does not
  answer.

## The tension, named

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's hook at CANDIDATE code so it gets exercised.
E-1450 forces hooks to write to the REAL ledger so activity is real. Each is
correct alone; together they mean unlanded code writes production data, which
is safe exactly while the schema is unchanged and unsafe the moment it is not.

It is not a genuine catch-22. It is unresolvable only while one binary defines,
migrates, and uses the schema at once. Separating define/migrate from use — H1
and H2 together — collapses it.

## Deliverable

A decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies. Not an implementation.

triage.rationale: the description names five+ candidate mechanisms without choosing among them, leaving the core design decision (and its three dependent gaps) unresolved.

fields.text:
# Documents on disk for external tools

## What is parked here

Only one thing: if a tool Endless has to work alongside requires markdown files
on disk in prescribed locations, Endless needs a way to keep those files current
without a human re-typing content that already lives in the ledger.

That is a generation-and-sync problem — one authoritative source rendered out to
one or more files — and nothing more. It does not need a document entity, event
kinds, section identifiers, Lexorank ordering, a proposal/review workflow, or
conflict surfacing.

## Why the original epic died

The epic was written to solve design-doc drift: ask an AI to revise a design
document and it regenerates the whole document instead of evolving the existing
one, leaving two versions that partly agree and require manual reconciliation.
The proposed fix was documents as event-sourced entities peer to tasks, with
section-level events making whole-document regeneration structurally impossible.

Brainstorm tasks solved that problem by another route. A brainstorm task is a
topic whose thinking evolves in place across sessions, in a field the tooling
already treats as authoritative, under a lifecycle that already has human review
in it. That is what the document entity was for. Once brainstorms existed, the
section-level event machinery had no problem left to solve, and every child of
this epic was obsoleted.

Two children died for reasons of their own as well. The dashboard views die with
the decision to rewrite the web surface from scratch. The ADR workflow lost to
decisions as a capability, whose storage shape is being re-decided under E-1868.

## What would revive this

A concrete external tool that reads markdown from a fixed path, where the
content it needs is already maintained in Endless. When that shows up, the tool
specifies the requirement — file layout, section conventions, refresh trigger —
far better than this placeholder can, so the right move is a fresh task written
against that tool rather than reopening the shape sketched here.

The in-repo precedent for what the mechanism would look like is the canonical
status-lifecycle mermaid block, which is duplicated byte-identically across
several documentation files and held in sync by a verification script rather
than by generation. That pattern generalizes: one source, rendered out, checked
at land time.

## Superseded design

`docs/private/endless-documents-design.md` describes the abandoned approach. It
is retained as a record of the reasoning, not as a spec. Its analysis of the
drift problem still holds; its proposed mechanism does not.

## Note on how this branch was landed

This branch could not be landed as it stood. It had been used for ten days
without ever being reset after its earlier lands, so it carried a large number
of commits whose patches were already upstream on main, plus main had moved
well ahead independently. Replaying that pile conflicted on the append-only
ledger segments — both sides had appended different lines to the same file —
once per ledger commit, so recovering and retrying could not converge.

Comparing trees rather than counting commits showed the branch was genuinely
ahead of main on exactly two files. The branch was therefore reset onto main
and those two changes re-applied, so the landing replays two clean commits
instead of the accumulated history. The discarded commits remain reachable
through the reflog from the pre-reset tip if anything is ever found missing.

The two salvaged changes are this plan itself, and the README tagline — the
newer positioning, naming AI tasks generally rather than Claude Code
specifically, which had been stranded on this branch unlanded. The tagline is
unrelated to this task's subject and rides along only because this branch is
where it was orphaned.

Why the branch went stale in the first place, and what should prevent it, is
E-1943. The narrower failure where a stale branch aborts a land on enum drift
is E-1941.

fields.title: Decide how worktree branches stop being orphaned by amended ledger commits on main
fields.description: Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as events append, so the tip SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main has equivalent superset content under a new SHA, the branch points at the superseded one, and the land rebase replays the orphan and conflicts on the append-only ledger segment. E-1342's _drop_orphan_amendable_commits covers a contiguous run at the branch base only, mid-branch orphans deliberately out of scope. Decide whether to treat this as a rebase problem (widen the helper, refuse early with a named diagnosis, union merge driver, reset onto main) or as a commit-shape problem (stop amending commits other refs are forked from). See analysis.
fields.analysis:
Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as new events append, so the
tip commit's SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those
SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main holds
equivalent (superset) content under a different SHA, and the branch still
points at the superseded one. On land, the rebase replays the orphan and
conflicts on the append-only ledger segment.

`_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` (E-1342) already handles this for a
contiguous run of orphans at the branch base. Its docstring puts mid-branch
orphans out of scope deliberately: a non-amendable commit followed by an
amendable one only arose from pre-E-1309 contamination, and dropping a
mid-branch commit risks deleting intended work. The open question is what to do
when that assumption no longer holds.

Observed on the e-801 worktree. Its branch reflog showed `Created from main`
with no commits of its own before the session's, yet `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its commits as patch-equivalent to commits on main —
the inherited run of amended ledger commits. The land reported dropping base
auto-amend commits and then conflicted anyway, so the existing helper did not
cover this shape. Recovery-and-retry could not converge because each replayed
ledger commit conflicts in turn.

Two framings, and the choice between them is the point of this brainstorm.

Treat it as a rebase problem, and the levers are: widen the E-1342 helper past
contiguous-at-base once it can distinguish an inherited orphan from real work;
detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis rather
than discovering it mid-conflict; give the ledger segments a union merge driver
so concurrent appends stop conflicting; or reset a branch onto main when its
base is known-orphaned and only its own commits need replaying.

Treat it as a commit-shape problem, and the lever is upstream of all of that:
amending a commit that other refs may be built on is what manufactures the
orphans. Appending a new ledger commit instead of amending would cost more
commits on main but leave every fork point stable. Whether the amend behavior
earns its keep, and what it was buying, needs establishing before the rebase-side
options are worth ranking.

Two gaps are evidence rather than separate tasks, since their fix depends on
which framing wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.

Relates to E-1941, a different failure from the same root condition: `just
land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from still-stale worktree
source, because the rebase onto main runs afterward.

A correction worth keeping, because it cost this session three wrong
conclusions: commit counts mislead here. A branch can read as hundreds of
commits ahead while being an ancestor of main in content. `git cherry` and a
tree comparison tell the truth; `git reflog show <branch>` tells you where the
branch actually came from, which is what finally identified the cause.

fields.title: Rework just land's ordering so no failure can leave the DB ahead of the code
fields.description: Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 produced two failures in the land recipe itself. First, `just land` rebuilds the worktree binary but never checks the worktree's SOURCE is current with main, so a branch 147 commits behind rebuilt a still-stale binary and aborted on an unrelated enum-drift error naming gate_kinds. Second — and the expensive one — apply-change then SUCCEEDED and the merge failed, leaving the real database migrated to a schema no installed binary understood; session tracking froze machine-wide and recovery needed a manual restore. The justfile only reasons about apply FAILING ("the land aborts before main advances"); apply succeeding and the merge failing is the unhandled, irreversible case. Fix: refuse the land when the branch is behind main, rehearse the merge on a throwaway branch, fast-forward main to that result, and apply schema changes AFTER the merge so a failed apply is merely a retry. Analysis carries the full sequence.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

One root cause with four faces: **code and database versions diverge across the
worktree / main / real-ledger boundary, and nothing guards the seam.** All four
were hit for real on 2026-08-10, in one sitting, landing E-1898.

## Face 1 — the land uses a binary built from stale source

`just land` (justfile ~167-250) does, in order:

1. `just go` in the worktree — rebuild endless-go
2. `endless db apply-change` against the REAL DB, using that binary
3. `endless worktree land` — which rebases onto main and fast-forwards

Step 1 came from E-1709, whose comment names this failure: "A worktree rebased
onto a newer main ... but not rebuilt would land with a STALE binary whose
embedded enums no longer match the real DB's rows ... (the E-1664 guard only
checks the binary is PRESENT, not CURRENT)."

E-1709 solved half. It makes the binary match the worktree's SOURCE. Nothing
makes the source match MAIN. With the branch 147 commits behind, `just go`
faithfully rebuilt a still-stale binary and step 2 hit the same wall:

    Error: apply-change failed: open db: gate_kinds integrity check on
      ~/.config/endless/endless.db: gatekind: gate_kinds row id="2" slug="relay"
      has no matching enum constant

Nothing was wrong with gate_kinds. Main's E-1901 had added `GateKindRelay` and
applied the row; the worktree's source predated it. The rebase that would fix
this is step 3 — after the step that needs it.

## Face 2 — apply-change succeeds, the merge fails, the DB is left ahead

After rebasing by hand, the land was re-run. This time step 2 SUCCEEDED and the
land then failed, so main never got the code. Result: the real DB was migrated
to a schema only the unlanded branch understands, while every installed binary
still expected the old one. Every session query referenced a dropped column, so
all 64 sessions went unresolvable and session tracking froze machine-wide (0
writes in the following 7 minutes).

The justfile comment asserts: "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances (clean recovery)." It reasons only about apply FAILING. Apply
succeeding and the merge then failing is the unhandled — and worse — case,
because it is the one that is irreversible.

## Face 3 — no supported way back (SPLIT OUT to E-1942)

`endless db backup` exists and the land calls it. There is no `endless db
restore`. Recovery was an unguided `cp`, and it went wrong twice:

- Copied over a live database with six open connections, leaving a hot
  `endless.db-journal`. A read-only connection cannot roll back a hot journal,
  so every reader returned `database is locked` and the status bar flickered.
- The backup is produced by `VACUUM INTO`, which writes a **rollback-journal**
  database. The live DB was WAL. Restoring silently changed journal mode, and
  every connection then fought over an exclusive lock to switch it back.

Recovery took: `pkill -f 'endless task show'` (four abandoned pagers holding
connections for up to 22 days), killing two `session-status --monitor`
processes, then `sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'`
to roll back the journal and restore WAL. None of that is discoverable.

A backup you cannot safely restore is not insurance.

## Face 4 — MOVED to E-1944

The worktree's Claude hook runs candidate code against the real ledger (E-998
points the hook at the candidate binary; E-1450 forces hooks to the real DB).
That pair is safe only while the schema is unchanged, and deciding it means
deciding who may define, migrate and use the schema — which is E-1944. It is
out of scope HERE so this task stays spawnable.

## Decided approach

**Face 1 — refuse, do not auto-rebase.** Before rebuilding the worktree binary,
refuse the land when `git rev-list --count HEAD..main` != 0, telling the user to
rebase. Auto-rebasing mid-land is rejected: E-1898's own rebase stopped on a
conflict in the append-only db-ledger JSONL, and a rebase that stalls with main
partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

**Face 2 — rehearse the merge, then reorder.** Do the merge on a throwaway
branch first (`endless-land-<taskid>-<rand>`, removed in a trap, so concurrent
lands cannot collide):

  1. branch off main, merge/rebase the task branch onto it
  2. it fails -> delete the branch, abort. The DB was never touched.
  3. it succeeds -> FAST-FORWARD main to that result. A pointer move, so there
     is no window where main advances and something else does not. Do NOT redo
     the merge; re-merging reopens the gap it just closed.
  4. THEN apply the schema changes, then record the landing, then rebuild.

Applying AFTER the fast-forward inverts the asymmetry that caused the incident:

  - apply fails after the merge -> main has the code, the DB lacks the
    migration. Re-run `endless db apply-change`; it is idempotent and gated by
    `_schema_version`. Recoverable.
  - merge fails after apply -> what happened on 2026-08-10. Not recoverable
    without a restore.

**Diagnosis, independent of the above.** Every `VerifyIntegrity` call site can
name the likely cause when the DB has rows the binary lacks: "this binary
predates the database; rebase onto main and rebuild." That direction of drift is
always staleness, never corruption. The reverse (binary has constants the DB
lacks) is a genuinely missing migration and should keep reading as it does now.

## Out of scope

E-1898 itself, which is fixed and re-verified. `endless task show -p` pinning a
DB connection for the life of its pager is a real but separate nuisance; file it
on its own if it bites again.

triage.rationale: The description explicitly poses an open choice between multiple materially different solution directions (widen the helper, refuse early, union merge driver, reset onto main, or stop amending commits) without deciding among them.

A worktree branch forked from one of those SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main has equivalent superset content under a new SHA, the branch points at the superseded one, and the land rebase replays the orphan and conflicts on the append-only ledger segment. E-1342's _drop_orphan_amendable_commits covers a contiguous run at the branch base only, mid-branch orphans deliberately out of scope. Decide whether to treat this as a rebase problem (widen the helper, refuse early with a named diagnosis, union merge driver, reset onto main), a commit-shape problem (stop amending commits other refs are forked from), or a maintenance problem (periodically bring settled worktrees current, hook-driven on session inactivity). payload.title: Allow task update --status submitted
payload.description: endless task update --status rejects 'submitted', accepting only untriaged, unplanned, ready, underway, unverified, confirmed, assumed, completed, blocked, revisit, declined, obsolete. Every other agent-settable status can ride along with a description edit in one call; submitted cannot, so routing a task to submitted after editing its description takes a second command (task submit). That asymmetry is a direct cause of agents leaving edited tasks sitting in untriaged: the one-call path exists for 'needs a plan' but not for 'description is sufficient'. Add submitted to the accepted values; task submit stays as the standalone verb.

triage.rationale: The fix is fully specified — add 'submitted' to the accepted --status values list in task update's validation, mirroring existing agent-settable statuses.

payload.title: Fix the triager routing brainstorm tasks to unplanned
payload.description: The triager routed E-1943 (type brainstorm, description plus full analysis, no plan attached) to unplanned. For a brainstorm the plan IS the deliverable, so 'no plan attached' can never mean 'needs a plan first' — a brainstorm whose problem statement is sufficient should route to submitted and be spawnable. The triager appears to apply the same plan-attached heuristic across all task types. Make the routing type-aware: for brainstorm, judge whether the problem statement and constraints are sufficient to explore from, not whether a plan exists. Check research tasks for the same mis-read, since their deliverable is the outcome rather than a plan.

triage.rationale: The description pins down the exact fix (make triage routing type-aware, judging brainstorm/research tasks by problem-statement sufficiency rather than plan-attachment) and names the specific case to check for the same mis-read.

payload.title: Add drop's missing live-cwd and unlanded guards that reap already has
payload.description: endless worktree drop removes a worktree whose directory a live process is sitting in, orphaning that session's cwd — hit for real, and recovered only by mkdir'ing the directory back. monitor's reap path already refuses exactly this (no live process holding cwd inside) and drop does not; drop checks foreign state and uncommitted changes only. Same repo, same concern, one has the guard. Reuse reap's check in drop. While there, deliver the unlanded refusal drop's own docstring and the module header both promise ('refuses modified/unlanded/foreign without --force') but which the implementation never performs. Coordinate with E-1898 and E-1941, which are still moving through this code.

payload.title: Make status routing read as the agent's job at every point of occurrence
payload.description: Agents repeatedly narrate 'this sends it back through triage' after a description edit, treating the reset as a system outcome they must route around rather than a routing call they should make. Two sources teach that. CLAUDE.md documents that triage runs automatically (task add triages in the background, a sweep drains the rest), which reads as exclusivity — knowing the mechanism gives an agent nothing actionable and actively invites deferral. And task update's transition message offers only --keep-status to suppress, never naming the decision. Reword both to lead with DECIDE YOURSELF, with the background sweep named as a worst-case fallback rather than the normal path. Drop the automation mechanics from CLAUDE.md; agents need the duty, not the machinery.

triage.rationale: The description pins down both edit sites (CLAUDE.md's triage-automation text and task update's transition message), the exact framing to adopt (lead with "decide yourself," demote the sweep to fallback), and the concrete instruction to drop automation mechanics, leaving no open design choice.

payload.title: Explore how a self-dev session reports Endless blocking it instead of working around it
payload.description: When an agent using Endless hits something that should work but does not, the reflex is to work around it silently and keep going — the user never learns the product blocked them. Observed this session: task update --status rejected submitted, and the workaround (a second task submit call) was applied without comment until asked. In self_dev mode especially, an agent is a user of the product and its friction is product signal that should surface, not be absorbed. Decide the mechanism: what counts as blocked-but-should-work versus ordinary error, how the agent surfaces it (report to the user, auto-file, a hook-collected friction log), how to avoid drowning the user in noise, and whether this applies only when self_dev is set or to any project.

triage.rationale: the description explicitly poses open design questions (blocked-vs-error criteria, surfacing mechanism, noise control, scope) without deciding among them.

payload.title: Fix session status fault badge: stuck warning, wasted hint row, unreadable WARNING chip
payload.description: The fault badge on `endless session status` has three defects: (1) a stale one-occurrence SQLITE_BUSY warning is pinned to the badge forever with no visible way to resolve it — the badge names only `endless errors show`, never `endless errors clear`; (2) the command hint burns an entire screen row on its own; (3) the WARNING chip's black-on-yellow renders as an unreadable orange block. See analysis for detail.
payload.analysis:
`endless session status` currently renders three problems in its fault badge area, reported from a live session on 2026-08-11.

## 1. A transient fault is stuck on the badge with no visible way to resolve it

The badge shows:

```
 WARNING  1 warning — ERR-0004 job scheduling row could not be created: "triage-sufficien…
        endless errors show
```

The underlying incident is a single SQLITE_BUSY ("database is locked (5)") while creating the `triage-sufficiency` job scheduling row, first and last seen 2026-08-10T09:49:09 — one occurrence, a day stale, self-healed. By design (`internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge.go`) an incident stays on the badge until `endless errors clear`, but nothing on the badge says that, so the user reads it as a permanent error with no idea how to fix it. The badge names only `endless errors show`, which explains the fault but does not offer any resolution — and `errors show` itself does not mention `errors clear` either.

Needs a decision on the fix: surface the clear command, auto-expire/auto-clear stale self-healed warnings, make single-occurrence SQLITE_BUSY on job scheduling non-faulting (it's retried anyway), or some combination.

## 2. The hint line wastes a whole screen row

`renderFaultBadge` prints a second line containing nothing but the dim string `        endless errors show`. In a status pane every row is scarce. The command hint should live on the badge line itself (right-aligned or appended) rather than consuming its own row.

## 3. The WARNING chip is unreadable

`badgeWarning = "\033[30;43m"` (black on yellow) renders as a low-contrast orange block in the user's terminal — the label is effectively invisible. Reported preference: invert the entire badge row, with a foreground/background pair that is actually readable across light and dark terminal themes.

## Files

- `internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge.go` — badge rendering, colors, hint line
- `internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge_test.go`
- `internal/faults/` — fault store, overview, detail log
- `internal/errorscmd/errors.go` — `errors show` / `clear` / `codes`
- `internal/jobs/run.go` — the ERR-0004 raise site

Three things teach that. And task update --status rejects 'submitted', so the one-call path exists for 'needs a plan' but not for 'the description is sufficient', making the right answer the harder one to reach. Fix all three: accept submitted in --status (task submit stays as the standalone verb), reword the transition message to lead with DECIDE YOURSELF and name the background sweep as a worst-case fallback, and drop the automation mechanics from CLAUDE.md — agents need the duty, not the machinery.

fields.text:
# E-1950 — session-status fault badge

Three reported defects, discussed with Mike before implementation. Decisions he
made are marked **[Mike]**.

## Defect 1 — a transient fault pinned to the badge with no way to resolve it

The incident was a single `SQLITE_BUSY` while creating the `triage-sufficiency`
job scheduling row, one occurrence, self-healed, still badged a day later.

Two independent causes:

**1a. It should never have been a fault.** `runOne` raised ERR-0004 on any
`ensureRow` failure, while `docs/errors.md` already said of that code: "no job
state is corrupted ... the next invocation retries. A persistent occurrence
means something is wrong with the database itself." Losing a single lock race is
what a database with concurrent writers does.

*Fix:* `ensureRowWithRetry` — three attempts, each behind the connection's
existing `PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000`, 250ms apart. `isBusy` matches on message
text, so a missing table or disk error still faults immediately without
retrying. **[Mike: ok]**

**1b. The dismissal was undiscoverable.** The badge named only
`endless errors show`, and `errors show` never mentioned `errors clear`. Mike
read the dim hint line as an oversight rather than an instruction.

*Fix:* `printClearHint` closes `errors show` with both forms of `errors clear`
plus the clear-is-not-retry distinction. Suppressed when nothing open.

**1c. Stale warnings age off the badge.** The E-698 design comment said clearing
is manual "so an intermittent fault cannot heal itself out of view". That rule is
right for a fault that is still happening and wrong for one that fired once and
healed. **[Mike: agreed — the existing comment contradicts his original
intention.]**

*Fix:* a warning stops being badged once **one hour of active time** has passed
since its last occurrence. Errors never age off. The incident is not cleared or
deleted — `errors show` still lists it.

**[Mike: the hour must not elapse while he is away from the computer.]** So the
clock is `monitor.ActiveSecondsSince`, which sums only the gaps between
consecutive `activity` rows shorter than `IdleGap` (5 min), plus the open segment
up to now. Idle stretches contribute nothing, so a warning cannot expire
overnight unseen. Not scoped to a project — "was the user at the machine" is not
a per-repo question.

*Placement:* the policy lives in `sessionstatuscmd`, not in `faults`. The
`faults` package deliberately imports nothing from the rest of Endless, and its
storage contract ("nothing is hidden or deleted") is unchanged — the badge simply
decides what is worth a row. `faults.Summarize` was split out of `Open` so the
filtered set produces counts consistent with what is displayed. `badgeworthy`
takes the clock as a parameter so the policy is testable without a DB.

*Failure direction:* an unreadable activity table or an unparseable timestamp
keeps the incident. Never hide what cannot be justified hiding.

## Defect 2 — the hint burned a whole screen row

`renderFaultBadge` emitted a second `Fprintln` containing only a dim
`        endless errors show`.

*Fix:* one row — chip, incident text, hint right-aligned. The hint is reserved
out of the width budget *before* the text, so it survives truncation; on a
terminal too narrow for both, the text wins and the hint is dropped rather than
wrapping.

**[Mike: `See: endless errors --help` is too long — add a shell helper `eeh` and
render it in a different background.]** So the hint is `Run eeh`, and
`eeh` joins `esu`/`esp`/`esf`/`esm` in `endless shell-init` as a wrapper for
`errors show`. The "different background" falls out of the chip inversion below.

The row fills `cols-1`, not `cols`: a line ending exactly at the right margin
sits on the deferred-wrap boundary where tmux panes can emit a spurious second
row, and the monitor sizes its pane from `frameLines`, which counts newlines and
would not see it.

**[Mike: "WARNING 1 warning" is redundant.]** Agreed — `badgeCounts` now returns
"" when there is a single incident, since the chip already says the severity. The
tally appears only when `Total >= 2`, where it says something the one chip cannot.

## Defect 3 — the WARNING chip was an unreadable orange block

Root cause: `\033[30;43m` uses the 30-47 ANSI range, which the terminal **theme
remaps**. Mike's theme renders `43` as a dark orange; black on it is invisible.
The existing code comment shows this was already tuned once in the opposite
direction for a different theme — chasing the palette cannot win.

*Fix:* fixed 256-color indices, which themes do not remap.

| | row | chip (inverts the row) |
|---|---|---|
| warning | `48;5;220` / `38;5;16` — black on gold | `48;5;16` / `38;5;220` |
| error | `48;5;160` / `38;5;231` — white on red | `48;5;231` / `38;5;160` |

**[Mike: invert the entire row — yes.]** The whole row carries the reversed
background so the badge reads as a bar; the chip inverts the row's own pair,
which delineates it without a third color that would have to be legible against
both.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge.go` | rewritten: one row, 256-color inverse, stale-warning filter |
| `internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go` | `frameLines` comment (badge is 1 line now, not 2) |
| `internal/monitor/activity.go` | `ActiveSecondsSince`, `IdleGap` |
| `internal/faults/read.go` | `Summarize` split out of `Open` |
| `internal/jobs/run.go` | `ensureRowWithRetry`, `isBusy` |
| `internal/errorscmd/errors.go` | `printClearHint` |
| `src/endless/cli.py` | `eeh` shell helper |
| `docs/errors.md`, `docs/guide/reference.md`, `docs/guide/orchestration.md` | retry, age-off, `eeh` |

## Verification

`esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1950-verify.sh` — 8 sections, fail-fast on the Go unit
tests, then per-defect assertions, a live render, and the docs gates.

Confirmed against Mike's real data: incident 1 (last seen 2026-08-10T09:49:09,
235 activity rows since) no longer renders on the badge, and is still open and
listed in `errors show`.

Observed this session: task update --status rejected submitted, and the workaround (a second task submit call) was applied without comment until asked. In self_dev mode especially the agent is a user of the product, and its friction is product signal. payload.title: Cull the open backlog: close, decline, or park every task that would not be missed
payload.description: Sweep every open task and close, decline, or park it, keeping only what someone would genuinely miss. Filed because the measured file-to-close ratio is roughly 1.5 over the last sixty days and 1.9 over the project's life; above 1.0 the backlog diverges and the project has no completion date regardless of work rate. Filing discipline is necessary but slow-acting, so the open backlog is the fast lever. Phase has also stopped discriminating, with most open tasks sitting in 'now', so re-phasing is part of the sweep.
