payload.text:
# Systematic backlog cull

## Why this exists

Measured over the sixty days before this task was filed: 391 tasks filed
against 264 resolved (landed plus killed). That is roughly 1.5 filed for every
one closed; over the project's life it is closer to 1.9. Any ratio above 1.0
means the backlog diverges and the project has no completion date, no matter
how fast work proceeds — working harder raises both sides of the ratio.

Near 1.0 the sensitivity is severe. Against the open count at filing time,
a sustained ratio of 0.5 clears the backlog in roughly nine months; 0.9 takes
over three years; 1.0 leaves it permanently where it is.

Filing discipline going forward is necessary but slow-acting. This task is the
fast lever: the open backlog itself.

## What to do

Sweep every open task and assign one of four dispositions. Close or park
aggressively; the bar for keeping a task open is that someone would genuinely
be worse off if it vanished.

- **obsolete** — superseded, or aimed at code or a design that no longer
  exists. Record why in the outcome, not just the status.
- **declined** — understood and deliberately not doing it. Requires a reason.
- **maybe** — plausibly wanted someday, nothing to act on now. Parking is not
  a defeat; it is what the phase is for.
- **keep** — leave open, and be able to say what makes it worth carrying.

Phase has stopped discriminating: at filing time the great majority of open
tasks sat in `now`, which makes the field carry no information. Re-phasing is
part of the sweep, not a separate pass.

## Hard constraint

**File nothing.** This task closes and parks; it does not open. A discovery
made mid-sweep belongs in an existing task's analysis, or in the report to the
user at the end — never in a new task. A sweep that files as it goes defeats
its own purpose.

Batch related tasks under one shared outcome where a group dies for one
reason; that is both faster and produces a better record than per-task prose.

## Suggested approach

Work in coherent groups rather than by ID order — by subsystem, by originating
epic, or by the design they assumed. A group that shares a premise usually
shares a fate, and judging it once is more accurate than judging its members
separately.

Prior art worth reading before starting: the sweep that obsoleted the
documents epic and the web dashboard subtree, recorded on E-801 and E-1939.
Both killed large coherent groups on a single stated premise.

## Verification

Report the before and after open counts, the split across dispositions, and
the resulting file-to-close ratio for the sweep itself. The sweep succeeds if
the open count falls materially and no new tasks were created.

payload.title: Agents must close more tasks than they file; filing is the exception and reporting never means filing
payload.description: A project whose agents file more tasks than they close has no completion date. Arithmetic, not preference: while the file-to-close ratio exceeds 1.0 the backlog diverges, and working faster raises both sides. Measured here over sixty days, 391 filed against 264 closed (~1.5); lifetime ~1.9. Agents cause this, so agents carry the rules. (1) Filing is the exception; the default response to a finding is to tell the user in chat. Noticing something true does not earn a task. (2) Fold before filing: a finding supporting existing work is evidence in that task's analysis, and several symptoms of one cause are one task. (3) Search for the task already owning the area first. (4) A request to file is not unlimited; say which items are better recorded as evidence, file the rest. (5) Reporting never means filing. Any mechanism surfacing friction or discovery must surface it in conversation, never auto-file. (6) Closing is work: obsolete, decline, and park are the only fast lever on the ratio.

fields.analysis:
Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as new events append, so the
tip commit's SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those
SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main holds
equivalent (superset) content under a different SHA, and the branch still
points at the superseded one. On land, the rebase replays the orphan and
conflicts on the append-only ledger segment.

`_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` (E-1342) already handles this for a
contiguous run of orphans at the branch base. Its docstring puts mid-branch
orphans out of scope deliberately: a non-amendable commit followed by an
amendable one only arose from pre-E-1309 contamination, and dropping a
mid-branch commit risks deleting intended work. The open question is what to do
when that assumption no longer holds.

Observed on the e-801 worktree. Its branch reflog showed `Created from main`
with no commits of its own before the session's, yet `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its commits as patch-equivalent to commits on main —
the inherited run of amended ledger commits. The land reported dropping base
auto-amend commits and then conflicted anyway, so the existing helper did not
cover this shape. Recovery-and-retry could not converge because each replayed
ledger commit conflicts in turn.

Two framings, and the choice between them is the point of this brainstorm.

Treat it as a rebase problem, and the levers are: widen the E-1342 helper past
contiguous-at-base once it can distinguish an inherited orphan from real work;
detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis rather
than discovering it mid-conflict; give the ledger segments a union merge driver
so concurrent appends stop conflicting; or reset a branch onto main when its
base is known-orphaned and only its own commits need replaying.

Treat it as a commit-shape problem, and the lever is upstream of all of that:
amending a commit that other refs may be built on is what manufactures the
orphans. Appending a new ledger commit instead of amending would cost more
commits on main but leave every fork point stable. Whether the amend behavior
earns its keep, and what it was buying, needs establishing before the rebase-side
options are worth ranking.

Two gaps are evidence rather than separate tasks, since their fix depends on
which framing wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.

Relates to E-1941, a different failure from the same root condition: `just
land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from still-stale worktree
source, because the rebase onto main runs afterward.

A correction worth keeping, because it cost this session three wrong
conclusions: commit counts mislead here. A branch can read as hundreds of
commits ahead while being an ancestor of main in content. `git cherry` and a
tree comparison tell the truth; `git reflog show <branch>` tells you where the
branch actually came from, which is what finally identified the cause.

## Root cause identified: `pull.rebase=true` blinds canAmend's guard (E-1941 session, 2026-08-11)

The orphan is not produced by amending per se. `canAmend`
(internal/events/commit.go:205-223) already refuses to amend a tip another ref
can reach — precondition 2, "HEAD must not be reachable from any ref BESIDES the
current branch." A worktree branch forked from main's ledger tip normally
triggers that refusal and endless appends instead. The commit-shape lever this
brainstorm proposes is therefore already implemented; the question is why it did
not fire.

Because it implements reachability as a SHA test: `git for-each-ref --contains
HEAD`. `git pull --rebase` rewrites every local main commit to a new SHA. The
task branch still points into the old, now-unreachable SHAs, so it no longer
"contains" main's HEAD. The guard is not bypassed and does not error — it
answers a reachability question the rewrite made meaningless, returns "safe to
amend," and the next amend diverges main from every task branch.

Reproduced in scratchpad/exp-canamend-guard.sh (re-implements precondition 2
faithfully and reports its decision either side of a pull):

    G1  no pull:          guard -> APPEND (saw refs/heads/task/900)   land: OK
    G2  after git pull:   guard -> AMEND  (saw no other ref)          land: CONFLICT
                                          conflicts: .endless/db-ledger/seg.jsonl

Mike set `pull.rebase true` manually at repo scope on 2026-08-10. main's reflog
carries the resulting rewrite: `e3ef6acb main@{2026-08-10 05:07:46}: rebase
(finish): refs/heads/main onto 43f238a9`, ~330 commits, about 3.5 hours before
E-1941 was filed. `pull.rebase=false` preserves local SHAs (it adds a merge
commit), so the guard keeps working — the merge strategy is an unstated,
load-bearing precondition of a safety check, not a style preference. Mike's ask
is that endless support either setting.

Consequences for the levers listed above:

- **The union merge driver for ledger segments must be struck.** It would
  corrupt the ledger. `Event` (internal/events/event.go:17-26) carries no unique
  id, and neither `ReadAllEvents` nor the projector dedups; union merge's defining
  behavior is to keep both sides' lines in a conflicted region, manufacturing
  duplicate entries that replay double-applies. `verbs.jsonl` tolerates union only
  because `matchers._add_verb_to_file` dedups at load. It also contradicts
  standing policy: land Step 3.75 refuses branch-side ledger commits and E-1342
  drops orphaned ones, so a merge driver would legitimize the cross-branch ledger
  merging the rest of the system refuses. (`ReadAllEvents` does re-sort by kairos
  TS, so the corruption vector is duplication rather than ordering — that does not
  rescue the idea.)
- **Any fix that stays SHA-reachability-based inherits the bug.** Widening the
  E-1342 helper, or refusing early with a named diagnosis, both still ask "is this
  commit reachable from another ref," which a rewrite answers wrongly. A durable
  fix needs an identity for a fork point that survives a history rewrite, or it
  needs to stop the rewrite from reaching ledger commits.
- **The framing choice may be moot.** This is not "rebase problem vs commit-shape
  problem" — the commit-shape guard exists and is correct; an external history
  rewrite defeats it. The live question is how endless behaves when main's history
  is rewritten under it, under either `pull.rebase` setting.

Also tested and negative, for whoever prices the E-1941 plan: rehearsing the land
on a throwaway branch off main and *merging* the task branch into it conflicts on
the same file, in the same cases, as the current rebase does
(scratchpad/exp-rebase-vs-merge.sh, PATH A and PATH B identical in every row).
Changing the merge shape does not help a guard that has gone blind.

fields.text:
# E-1941 — Rework `just land`'s ordering so no failure can leave the DB ahead of the code

## Context

Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 migrated the real database to a schema no installed
binary understood, then failed to merge. Session tracking froze machine-wide and
recovery needed a hand-rolled `cp` restore.

The cause is ordering in the dev-only `just land` recipe. It runs, in order:
rebuild the worktree binary → **`endless db apply-change` against the real DB** →
`endless worktree land` (rebase + ff-merge). The recipe's own comment reasons
only about apply *failing* ("the land aborts before main advances"). Apply
*succeeding* and the merge then failing is the unhandled case, and it is the
irreversible one.

Reproduced (`scratchpad/repro.sh` runs the real recipe body against a throwaway
repo with stubbed tools; task branch 3 commits behind main, the land stubbed to
fail as it did on 2026-08-10):

```
just go (cwd=e-9999) → endless db backup → endless db apply-change → endless worktree land ✗
DB state: MIGRATED      main advanced: NO
```

Two defects, both confirmed: there is no check that the branch is current with
main before the binary is rebuilt, and the DB is migrated before anything
irreversible is known to succeed.

**Outcome:** invert the asymmetry. Apply schema changes only after main has
actually advanced, so a failed apply is a retry rather than a restore; and
refuse the land outright when the branch is behind main, so the binary that runs
against the real DB is built from source that matches main.

## Approach

### 1. Refuse a behind-main land (justfile)

In the `land` recipe, inside the `if [ -d "$wt" ]` block and **before**
`( cd "$wt" && just go )`:

```sh
behind=$(git -C "$wt" rev-list --count HEAD..main)
if [ "$behind" -ne 0 ]; then   # refuse; tell the user to rebase
```

Refuse, do not auto-rebase — E-1898's own rebase stopped on a conflict, and a
rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

This stays in the justfile and **must not** move into `endless worktree land`: a
downstream user's branch being behind main is the normal case that the land's
rebase exists to handle. Refusing there would break ordinary product usage.

### 2. Move the schema apply into `land_worktree`, after the merge

`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`, `land_worktree()`. The apply cannot simply move
later in the justfile: Step 6 (`_record_landing`) runs the *worktree* binary
against the *real* DB, and for an enum-adding branch that binary carries a
constant the DB lacks until the change is applied — E-1664's failure inverted.
So it belongs between Step 5 and Step 6.

- **Compute the change list before Step 5**, into a local. This is load-bearing:
  after the ff-merge `main` and the branch are the same commit, so
  `git diff main...HEAD` returns empty and the changes would be silently skipped.
  Reuse the justfile's existing pathspec verbatim:
  `--diff-filter=A --name-only -- internal/schema/changes/
  ':(exclude)internal/schema/changes/runner/'`, filtered to `*.sql`/`*.go`.
- **After the ff-merge succeeds**, and only when
  `config.project_is_self_dev(main_root)`: back up, then apply each change file
  in order, pinning `endless_go_bin` (already resolved at line 2085 by
  `_resolve_land_endless_go`).
- **On apply failure**, raise a ClickException in the shape `_record_landing`
  already uses for post-merge failures (worktree_cmd.py:2001-2008): say main was
  advanced, name the cause, and state that `endless db apply-change` is
  idempotent and gated by `_schema_version` so re-running `just land` recovers.

Two new module-level helpers alongside the existing ones:
`_branch_schema_changes(worktree_path, base_branch)` and
`_apply_branch_schema_changes(paths, main_root, endless_go_bin)`.

### 3. Thread the pinned binary through `apply_change` / `backup_db`

`src/endless/event_bridge.py`. Both currently call `_resolve_endless_go()` with
no override, which is why the justfile needs its `PATH="$wt/bin:$PATH"` hack.
Add `endless_go_bin: str | None = None` to each and pass it to
`_resolve_endless_go(override=...)` — exactly the parameter `emit_event` already
threads (line 203). This finishes the job E-1664 started: it explicitly
superseded the E-1660 PATH hack for the record step, and this removes the last
one.

`cli.py`'s `db apply-change` / `db backup` commands keep their current
no-override behavior; the new parameter defaults to `None`.

### 4. Justfile cleanup

Delete the `endless db backup` call and the `for f in $changes` apply loop
(justfile:219-237) — now owned by `land_worktree`. Keep the up-front `just go`
(E-1709) and the trailing `just build`. Update the stale comment block at
justfile:193-198 whose claim "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances" is the reasoning error behind the incident.

## Explicitly out of scope

**The throwaway rehearsal branch is dropped.** The analysis prescribes
rehearsing the merge on `endless-land-<tid>-<rand>`, but this needs your
sign-off to omit, because it is a deliberate departure from the written plan.
Tested in `scratchpad/exp-rebase-vs-merge.sh`: a temp branch off main with the
task branch *merged* into it conflicts on the same file, in the same cases, as
the current rebase does — PATH A and PATH B are identical in all four scenarios.
Step 4 already rebases in the worktree (main untouched, clean abort) and Step 5
is already `git merge --ff-only` (a pure pointer move), so the rehearse-then-
pointer-move shape exists. It would cost ~5 test files plus a temp-branch /
task-branch reconciliation question, and change no tested outcome.

**The `canAmend` guard and `pull.rebase` support are not fixed here.**
`scratchpad/exp-canamend-guard.sh` shows `git pull --rebase` blinds canAmend's
shared-tip guard (SHA-reachability based), which is the actual origin of the
orphaned ledger bases. That evidence is folded into E-1943's analysis, which
owns the decision. Per ED-1550 no new task was filed.

Honest limit: the behind-main refusal converts an irreversible DB-ahead disaster
into a clean refusal that says "rebase onto main" — and under a blinded guard
that rebase is the thing that conflicts. This bounds the damage; E-1943 is what
makes the land succeed.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `justfile` (~193-237) | behind-main refusal; remove backup/apply loop; fix stale comment |
| `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` | 2 helpers; pre-merge change list; apply between Steps 5 and 6 |
| `src/endless/event_bridge.py` | `endless_go_bin` param on `apply_change`, `backup_db` |
| `tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` | new |
| `tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh` | new |

## Tests

`tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py`, following the monkeypatch style of
`tests/test_worktree_land_record_landing.py`:

- apply is invoked **after** the ff-merge and **before** `_record_landing`
  (ordering asserted via a shared call log)
- the change list is captured pre-merge and is still non-empty post-merge
- apply failure raises a re-runnable "main was advanced" error and does not
  unwind the merge
- a non-self_dev project skips apply entirely
- the pinned `endless_go_bin` reaches `_resolve_endless_go(override=...)`

## Verification

Single command: `esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh`

Modeled on `tests/tasks/e-1709-verify.sh` (same pass/fail + summary shape,
exit 0/1/2), fail-fast, folding this task's own tests in:

1. **Regression, end-to-end** — the `scratchpad/repro.sh` harness promoted into
   the suite: run the real recipe body against a throwaway repo with stubbed
   `endless`/`just`, land stubbed to fail. Assert the DB was **never** migrated
   and main never advanced. This is the check that fails on today's code.
2. **Behind-main refusal** — same harness with the branch behind main: assert
   the recipe exits non-zero, names the rebase remedy, and never reaches
   `just go` or `apply-change`.
3. **Recipe ordering** (static guard, per E-1709's check 2) — `just --show land`
   contains no `endless db apply-change`, and `just go` still precedes
   `endless worktree land`. Plus `bash -n` on the recipe body.
4. **Unit tests** — `pytest tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` and the
   existing `tests/test_worktree_land_*.py` suite.

Project-wide regression (`just test`, `just test-go`, `just build`,
`just guide-check`) I run myself and report as one line.

# E-1941 — Rework `just land`'s ordering so no failure can leave the DB ahead of the code

## Context

Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 migrated the real database to a schema no installed
binary understood, then failed to merge. Session tracking froze machine-wide and
recovery needed a hand-rolled `cp` restore.

The cause is ordering in the dev-only `just land` recipe. It runs, in order:
rebuild the worktree binary → **`endless db apply-change` against the real DB** →
`endless worktree land` (rebase + ff-merge). The recipe's own comment reasons
only about apply *failing* ("the land aborts before main advances"). Apply
*succeeding* and the merge then failing is the unhandled case, and it is the
irreversible one.

Reproduced by extracting the real recipe body with `just --show land` and running
it against a throwaway repo with stubbed `endless`/`just`; task branch 3 commits
behind main, the land stubbed to fail as it did on 2026-08-10 (this harness
becomes check 1 of the verify script below):

```
just go (cwd=e-9999) → endless db backup → endless db apply-change → endless worktree land ✗
DB state: MIGRATED      main advanced: NO
```

Two defects, both confirmed: there is no check that the branch is current with
main before the binary is rebuilt, and the DB is migrated before anything
irreversible is known to succeed.

**Outcome:** invert the asymmetry. Apply schema changes only after main has
actually advanced, so a failed apply is a retry rather than a restore; and
refuse the land outright when the branch is behind main, so the binary that runs
against the real DB is built from source that matches main.

## Approach

### 1. Refuse a behind-main land (justfile)

In the `land` recipe, inside the `if [ -d "$wt" ]` block and **before**
`( cd "$wt" && just go )`:

```sh
behind=$(git -C "$wt" rev-list --count HEAD..main)
if [ "$behind" -ne 0 ]; then   # refuse; tell the user to rebase
```

Refuse, do not auto-rebase — E-1898's own rebase stopped on a conflict, and a
rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

This stays in the justfile and **must not** move into `endless worktree land`: a
downstream user's branch being behind main is the normal case that the land's
rebase exists to handle. Refusing there would break ordinary product usage.

### 2. Move the schema apply into `land_worktree`, after the merge

`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`, `land_worktree()`. The apply cannot simply move
later in the justfile: Step 6 (`_record_landing`) runs the *worktree* binary
against the *real* DB, and for an enum-adding branch that binary carries a
constant the DB lacks until the change is applied — E-1664's failure inverted.
So it belongs between Step 5 and Step 6.

- **Compute the change list before Step 5**, into a local. This is load-bearing:
  after the ff-merge `main` and the branch are the same commit, so
  `git diff main...HEAD` returns empty and the changes would be silently skipped.
  Reuse the justfile's existing pathspec verbatim:
  `--diff-filter=A --name-only -- internal/schema/changes/
  ':(exclude)internal/schema/changes/runner/'`, filtered to `*.sql`/`*.go`.
- **After the ff-merge succeeds**, and only when
  `config.project_is_self_dev(main_root)`: back up, then apply each change file
  in order, pinning `endless_go_bin` (already resolved at line 2085 by
  `_resolve_land_endless_go`).
- **On apply failure**, raise a ClickException in the shape `_record_landing`
  already uses for post-merge failures (worktree_cmd.py:2001-2008): say main was
  advanced, name the cause, and state that `endless db apply-change` is
  idempotent and gated by `_schema_version` so re-running `just land` recovers.

Two new module-level helpers alongside the existing ones:
`_branch_schema_changes(worktree_path, base_branch)` and
`_apply_branch_schema_changes(paths, main_root, endless_go_bin)`.

### 3. Thread the pinned binary through `apply_change` / `backup_db`

`src/endless/event_bridge.py`. Both currently call `_resolve_endless_go()` with
no override, which is why the justfile needs its `PATH="$wt/bin:$PATH"` hack.
Add `endless_go_bin: str | None = None` to each and pass it to
`_resolve_endless_go(override=...)` — exactly the parameter `emit_event` already
threads (line 203). This finishes the job E-1664 started: it explicitly
superseded the E-1660 PATH hack for the record step, and this removes the last
one.

`cli.py`'s `db apply-change` / `db backup` commands keep their current
no-override behavior; the new parameter defaults to `None`.

### 4. Justfile cleanup

Delete the `endless db backup` call and the `for f in $changes` apply loop
(justfile:219-237) — now owned by `land_worktree`. Keep the up-front `just go`
(E-1709) and the trailing `just build`. Update the stale comment block at
justfile:193-198 whose claim "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances" is the reasoning error behind the incident.

## Explicitly out of scope

**The throwaway rehearsal branch is dropped.** The analysis prescribes
rehearsing the merge on `endless-land-<tid>-<rand>`, but this needs your
sign-off to omit, because it is a deliberate departure from the written plan.
Tested across four scenarios (amend alone; `pull --rebase` alone; both; both with
a union driver) against two strategies — rebase the task branch onto main, versus
branch off main and merge the task branch in. The two gave an identical verdict
in every scenario: a temp branch with the task branch *merged* into it conflicts
on the same file, in the same cases, as the current rebase does.
Step 4 already rebases in the worktree (main untouched, clean abort) and Step 5
is already `git merge --ff-only` (a pure pointer move), so the rehearse-then-
pointer-move shape exists. It would cost ~5 test files plus a temp-branch /
task-branch reconciliation question, and change no tested outcome.

**The `canAmend` guard and `pull.rebase` support are not fixed here.**
`git pull --rebase` blinds canAmend's shared-tip guard (it is SHA-reachability
based), which is the actual origin of the orphaned ledger bases. That evidence —
the guard experiment, the struck union-merge lever, and the arguments already
tried and discarded — is folded into E-1943's analysis, which owns the decision.
Per ED-1550 no new task was filed.

Honest limit: the behind-main refusal converts an irreversible DB-ahead disaster
into a clean refusal that says "rebase onto main" — and under a blinded guard
that rebase is the thing that conflicts. This bounds the damage; E-1943 is what
makes the land succeed.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `justfile` (~193-237) | behind-main refusal; remove backup/apply loop; fix stale comment |
| `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` | 2 helpers; pre-merge change list; apply between Steps 5 and 6 |
| `src/endless/event_bridge.py` | `endless_go_bin` param on `apply_change`, `backup_db` |
| `tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` | new |
| `tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh` | new |

## Tests

`tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py`, following the monkeypatch style of
`tests/test_worktree_land_record_landing.py`:

- apply is invoked **after** the ff-merge and **before** `_record_landing`
  (ordering asserted via a shared call log)
- the change list is captured pre-merge and is still non-empty post-merge
- apply failure raises a re-runnable "main was advanced" error and does not
  unwind the merge
- a non-self_dev project skips apply entirely
- the pinned `endless_go_bin` reaches `_resolve_endless_go(override=...)`

## Verification

Single command: `esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh`

Modeled on `tests/tasks/e-1709-verify.sh` (same pass/fail + summary shape,
exit 0/1/2), fail-fast, folding this task's own tests in:

1. **Regression, end-to-end** — the reproduction harness from Context, promoted
   into the suite: extract the recipe body with `just --show land`, run it against
   a throwaway repo with stubbed `endless`/`just`, land stubbed to fail. Assert
   the DB was **never** migrated and main never advanced. This is the check that
   fails on today's code.
2. **Behind-main refusal** — same harness with the branch behind main: assert
   the recipe exits non-zero, names the rebase remedy, and never reaches
   `just go` or `apply-change`.
3. **Recipe ordering** (static guard, per E-1709's check 2) — `just --show land`
   contains no `endless db apply-change`, and `just go` still precedes
   `endless worktree land`. Plus `bash -n` on the recipe body.
4. **Unit tests** — `pytest tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` and the
   existing `tests/test_worktree_land_*.py` suite.

Project-wide regression (`just test`, `just test-go`, `just build`,
`just guide-check`) I run myself and report as one line.

fields.outcome: Obsolete before starting. A dedicated cull is itself a task, and working a task to reduce tasks is self-defeating at this backlog size. The cheaper path is per-session: a session reviewing its own session status considers whether the tasks in front of it can be merged, which spreads the same work across sessions that are already loaded with the context to judge it. ED-1550 carries the standing rules; this task added ceremony on top of them.

# Analysis

Provoked by the 2026-08-10 incident landing E-1898, which produced four distinct
failures in one sitting from one underlying question: **who is allowed to define,
migrate, and use the schema, and when.**

## What governs schema writes today

`monitor.DB()` applies `schema.SQL` — all additive `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` —
on EVERY connection, plus five enum `VerifyIntegrity` gates that fail closed.
Destructive one-off change files run separately, once, at land time via
`endless db apply-change`.

E-1818 added **schema-passive**: when `dbPathOverride != ""` (set by
`PinMainDB`/`ForceRealDB`, i.e. the hook, tmux and channel surfaces) the connect
skips both the schema apply and every gate.

**The gap.** Schema-passive protects the DB from the binary. It does nothing to
protect the binary from the DB. The hook error on 2026-08-10 proves it: the
candidate binary did not migrate anything, it simply failed writing `process_id`
into a table that lacked the column. E-1818 solved one half; the unsolved half
is the one that caused the outage.

## A. What each executable does on connect

| Executable | Surface | Pins real DB? | Applies schema.sql | Runs enum gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| global (main) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| global (main) | task, sql, event, ... | no | yes | yes |
| worktree (candidate) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| worktree (candidate) | event apply-change | no | YES | YES  <- the gate_kinds abort |
| worktree (candidate) | anything with --config-dir | no | yes (that DB) | yes |
| Python CLI | all | n/a | own bootstrap | none |

## B. Binary schema vs. DB schema

| Binary expects | DB has | Connect | Runtime DML | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | main | ok | ok | normal |
| candidate | candidate | ok | ok | sandbox only |
| candidate | main | ok (passive) | FAILS: writes absent columns | hook errors, 30 min |
| main | candidate | ok (passive) | FAILS: reads dropped columns | blank board, 30 min |

Rows 3 and 4 are one defect seen from either side. NEITHER is detected at
connect; both surface as runtime SQL errors on hot paths. The enum gates cover
enum tables only and would never catch a dropped column.

## C. Landing phases

| Phase | Binary | DB | Schema | What failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 rebuild worktree bin | worktree | - | - | built from stale source (147 behind) |
| 2 backup | Python | real | pre | - |
| 3 apply-change | worktree | real | pre -> post | gate abort; later succeeded |
| 4 merge | git | - | - | FAILED -> DB post, code pre |
| 5 record landing | worktree | real | post | never reached |
| 6 just build | - | - | - | never reached; global stayed pre |

## Hypotheses to evaluate

**H1 — a migration-only executable.** Built from the landing branch, does DDL
only, never DML, so it has no runtime schema expectations to be wrong about.
Cleanly resolves phase 3. Does NOT touch table B rows 3/4, which are ordinary
binaries at runtime.

**H2 — explicit upgrade; connects verify instead of migrate.** Replace
apply-on-connect with an `endless db upgrade` verb; ordinary connects compare
the DB's schema version against the binary's and REFUSE with a clear message.
This is the one that collapses table B: rows 3 and 4 become a precise
connect-time refusal, and no binary can mutate the real ledger by opening it —
which also makes schema-passive unnecessary. Costs users an explicit step after
upgrade, and every entry point needs a good "your database needs upgrading"
message.

**Neither resolves everything, and that should be stated up front:**
- Ordering (phase 3 vs 4) is independent — see E-1941. H2 arguably makes a
  half-landed state MORE visibly broken (everything refuses) rather than less.
- Recovery is independent — see E-1942, whose shape depends on this decision:
  "copy a backup back" vs "upgrade --rollback" are different verbs.
- Whether candidate hook code should write to the real ledger at all (the
  E-998 / E-1450 tension) is a policy question this may inform but does not
  answer.

## The tension, named

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's hook at CANDIDATE code so it gets exercised.
E-1450 forces hooks to write to the REAL ledger so activity is real. Each is
correct alone; together they mean unlanded code writes production data, which
is safe exactly while the schema is unchanged and unsafe the moment it is not.

It is not a genuine catch-22. It is unresolvable only while one binary defines,
migrates, and uses the schema at once. Separating define/migrate from use — H1
and H2 together — collapses it.

## Deliverable

A decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies. Not an implementation.



## Folded in from E-1922: the concrete form of H2

E-1922 was filed separately as an implementation of exactly H2's connect-time
check, and is folded here because it presupposes a decision this task has not
yet made. Its evidence stands regardless of which hypothesis wins, and is worth
keeping in front of whoever decides:

`monitor.DB()` executes its embedded schema SQL on every owned connection with
no check that the DB carries the change files that schema assumes. Nothing
connects a binary's expectations to the DB's actual state, so a binary
installed before its change file is applied can create schema objects
referencing columns that do not exist. E-1917's trigger reads
`NEW.changed_by_session`, and SQLite resolves trigger bodies at fire time, so
every `UPDATE tasks` would fail — the failure is not at connect, it is at the
next write, which is what makes it hard to attribute.

Today that is avoided only by convention: land, which runs apply-change, before
`just install`. A convention is not a guard, and the ordering requirement is
invisible to anyone who has not been bitten by it.

E-1922 proposed a gate that either auto-applies pending changes on connect or
refuses with a clear error. Note that those are two different answers, not one:
auto-applying keeps a binary able to migrate whatever DB it opens, which is the
property H1 and H2 are both trying to remove; refusing is H2 proper. If H2 is
chosen, this becomes its first follow-on task. If H1 is chosen instead, the
convention-only ordering requirement still needs an answer, and this evidence
is where that answer starts.

payload.outcome: Folded into E-1944, whose analysis now carries this evidence. E-1922 implemented one of E-1944's two hypotheses (replace apply-on-connect with a connect-time schema-version check that refuses rather than silently fixing) before E-1944 had decided between them. E-1944 states its deliverable is a decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies, so this re-emerges as a follow-on if that hypothesis wins, and is obsolete if the migration-only-executable hypothesis wins instead. The underlying evidence — monitor.DB() applying schema on every connection with nothing tying a binary's expectations to the DB's state, and the ordering requirement being convention rather than a guard — survives either way and is preserved there.

fields.title: Decide how worktree branches survive a rewrite of main's history

fields.description: Worktree branches lose their base when main's history is rewritten under them — not from amending. canAmend already refuses to amend a tip another ref can reach, but implements that as SHA reachability, so once `git pull --rebase` rewrites main the guard answers a question the rewrite made meaningless, permits the amend, and the land rebase then conflicts on the append-only ledger segment. Endless must work under either `pull.rebase` setting: rebase-style pull is mainstream, and a guard that silently degrades under it is a defect regardless of which setting this repo uses. Decide how — give a fork point an identity that survives a rewrite, keep rewrites away from ledger commits, or detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis. Any SHA-reachability-based fix inherits the same blindness; the union-merge-driver option is struck (it would corrupt the ledger). Analysis carries the evidence. Deliverable is a decision plus follow-on tasks.

## Approach

### 1. Refuse a behind-main land

The rule lives in `land_worktree`, **gated on `config.project_is_self_dev`**, so
a direct `endless worktree land` gets it too — not only `just land`. It must stay
self_dev-gated: a downstream user's branch being behind main is the normal case
the land's rebase exists to handle, and refusing there would break ordinary
product usage.

The justfile keeps a cheap `git -C "$wt" rev-list --count HEAD..main` pre-check
before `( cd "$wt" && just go )` purely to avoid a pointless rebuild before the
refusal fires. Deliberate duplication of one git command; the rule itself has a
single home.

Refuse, do not auto-rebase — E-1898's own rebase stopped on a conflict, and a
rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

**The message must not just say "rebase."** Under a rewritten main the rebase is
itself the thing that conflicts, so a bare instruction sends the user into the
failure. It should state the drift, say why the land is refused (the binary about
to touch the real DB must be built from source matching main), and then name both
cases: an ordinary behind-main branch rebases cleanly; a branch whose base was
rewritten (`git reflog show main` showing a `rebase (finish)` entry, or
`git cherry main HEAD` reporting patch-equivalent commits) may conflict on
`.endless/db-ledger/`, which is E-1943 and not yet solved.

### 2. Move the schema apply into `land_worktree`, after the merge

`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`, `land_worktree()`. The apply cannot simply move
later in the justfile: Step 6 (`_record_landing`) runs the *worktree* binary
against the *real* DB, and for an enum-adding branch that binary carries a
constant the DB lacks until the change is applied — E-1664's failure inverted.

  `_resolve_land_endless_go`).

  already uses for post-merge failures (worktree_cmd.py:2001-2008): say main was

`_branch_schema_changes(worktree_path, base_branch)` and
`_apply_branch_schema_changes(paths, main_root, endless_go_bin)`.

`cli.py`'s `db apply-change` / `db backup` commands keep their current
no-override behavior; the new parameter defaults to `None`.

**The backup is not removed — it moves.** The `endless db backup` call and the
`for f in $changes` apply loop (justfile:219-237) both relocate into
`land_worktree` per section 2. The backup stays warranted: a change set can be
several files, so file 1 can apply and file 2 fail, leaving a partially migrated
DB no re-run heals, and E-1942 means there is still no `endless db restore`.

**Close the remaining window.** If the apply succeeds and `_record_landing` then
fails, the recipe aborts before `just build` — leaving old global binaries against
a *new* DB, which is the incident's shape. That window exists today (wider: it
spans the merge too). Main advancing is the fact that obliges a rebuild; the
land's exit code is not. So capture main's SHA before and after the land and
rebuild whenever it moved, propagating the land's exit code:

```sh
before=$(git -C "$main_root" rev-parse main)
endless worktree land "$tid"
land_rc=$?
after=$(git -C "$main_root" rev-parse main)
if [ "$before" != "$after" ]; then ( cd "$main_root" && just build ); fi
exit "$land_rc"
```

explicitly. It is banned in this project — `pipefail` turns SIGPIPE from an
early-exiting `head`/`grep -q` into a crash, and `set -e` has inconsistent
semantics in subshells, loops, and conditionals. The logic above depends on
observing a non-zero exit rather than dying at it, so the conversion is part of
this change, not incidental cleanup. Every command whose failure matters gets an
explicit check; `${PIPESTATUS[@]}` where a pipeline's stage matters. Load the
`shell-script-author` skill before writing it, and ShellCheck the result.

The other 5 recipes using strict mode are left alone — out of scope here.

Also update the stale comment block at justfile:193-198, whose claim "If any
apply fails, the land aborts before main advances" is the reasoning error behind
the incident. Keep the up-front `just go` (E-1709).

payload.title: The db-ledger JSONL segments must never be given a git union merge driver; branch-side ledger divergence is resolved by dropping or refusing, never by merging
payload.description: Union merge keeps both sides' lines in a conflicted region, so it manufactures duplicate ledger entries. Event (internal/events/event.go) carries no unique id and neither ReadAllEvents nor the projector dedups, so duplicates double-apply on replay — silent data corruption, not a merge artifact. verbs.jsonl tolerates the driver only because matchers._add_verb_to_file dedups at load; the ledger has no equivalent. It also contradicts standing policy: land Step 3.75 refuses branch-side ledger commits and E-1342 drops orphaned ones, so a merge driver would legitimize the cross-branch ledger merging the rest of the system refuses. Noted for accuracy: ReadAllEvents re-sorts by kairos TS, so the corruption vector is duplication rather than ordering — that does not rescue the idea. Struck as a candidate lever in E-1943's analysis on 2026-08-11 after the rebase-vs-merge experiments; recorded here because it constrains any future ledger-merge work, not just E-1943.

payload.title: Redesign `task report` around partial success instead of an all-or-nothing render
payload.description: `task report` renders a report in one shot with no partial success and no persisted state, so any rejected or absent field costs a whole extra invocation — one turn of an E-1939 session needed three calls to emit one block. A rejected note discards the valid `verify` field with it; the statelessness is undiscoverable given the id-addressed, payload-taking surface; a bare run at `unverified` asserts `Nothing to report.` for a task whose handoff mandates a verify command; and the PostToolUse hook fires on `--help`. Filed as one task because all four share that root cause.
payload.analysis:
`task report` models a report as a one-shot render with no partial success and
no persisted state, so any rejected or absent field costs a full extra
invocation. One task rather than four: the symptoms below share that cause.

Evidence — one turn of an E-1939 session took three calls to emit one block:

1. ALL-OR-NOTHING VALIDATION. A payload of {verify, notes} had its note bounced
   by the ceremony check, and the command emitted NO block at all — the valid
   `verify` field was discarded alongside the rejected note. Rendering the block
   from the accepted fields, plus a rejection notice naming what was dropped and
   why, would have made this the last call instead of the middle one.

   The check's judgment was CORRECT: the note recounted a rebase and its
   conflict resolution, which a reviewer can read off the commits. The defect is
   the blast radius of a rejection, not the rejection itself.

2. STATELESSNESS IS UNDISCOVERABLE. The command is addressed by task id, takes a
   structured payload, and sits beside `task update` / `task submit`, which
   persist. It does not persist — a payload supplied in one call is gone by the
   next. The session spent a call running it bare to find that out. Either
   persist the payload on the task, or make the one-shot nature evident in the
   help text and the `--json` option description.

3. AN EMPTY BLOCK AT `unverified` IS NEAR-CERTAINLY WRONG. Run bare on a task
   just flipped to `unverified`, it prints `Nothing to report.` — for a task
   whose handoff mandates a verify command. It cannot know that command, but it
   does know the status and that no `verify` entry was passed, so it can say so
   rather than assert a null result the handoff forbids.

4. THE PostToolUse HOOK FIRES ON `--help`. Running `task report --help` to look
   up the `--json` shape injects the full "now append the block, unchanged,
   after the separator" instruction when no block was rendered. The hook matches
   the command name rather than a successful render.

Deliberately out of scope: the ceremony check's judgment criteria. They are
working, and loosening them to reduce round-trips would trade a real quality
gate for a cheap one.

triage.rationale: The description names four symptoms of a root cause but leaves open how partial-success state should be persisted, how the new payload/interface should be shaped, and how the four fixes should be sequenced or bundled into one design.

payload.title: Rebuild `task report` as an enforced minimizer over the agent's full draft reply
payload.description: Replace `task report`'s payload-and-render model: the command takes the agent's ENTIRE freeform draft reply, an adversarial agent minimizes it, and a Stop hook requires the agent to reply with that output verbatim. Subsumes the four render defects in E-1952's seed, which are symptoms of the agent routing content into prose instead of the block. Design synthesized in E-1952's outcome; see --analysis for the build shape.
payload.analysis:
Replace `task report`'s payload-and-render model with a minimizer over the
agent's entire draft reply. Design synthesized in E-1952's outcome — read that
first; this task is the build.

Why the current command fails: the agent writes the verify command in prose and
then tells `task report` there is nothing to report. Two output channels exist
and content lands in the cheap one. Any design where the agent volunteers a
structured payload fails identically, which is why the four defects named in
E-1952's seed are subsumed rather than fixed individually.

Shape:

- `task report --draft-file <path>` takes the agent's ENTIRE freeform draft
  reply as plain markdown. No JSON/XML, no field tagging — any format requiring
  the agent to pre-structure the draft reintroduces the restatement tax that
  caused the routing failure.
- An adversarial agent minimizes it. Objective: "delete what the user didn't
  ask for," NOT "make it short" — a pure minimizer guts a requested discussion.
  It occupies the slot the current ceremony check occupies.

  and also catches "never called it," which is otherwise the trivial bypass.
- Every turn, not just handoffs.

  the training corpus, and it is what lets the minimizer be aggressive at zero
  risk.
- Bounded appeal: one, and the appeal text is itself minimized.

  command name (it currently fires on `--help`).

  survives, direct questions get direct answers) plus anti-puffery/anti-jargon
  guidance go in the `//go:embed`ed default. The anti-puffery half is a stated
  product benefit, not personal config; the user template holds additions.

fields.outcome:
# E-1952 — Synthesis: `task report` is the wrong shape, not the wrong implementation

## The seed was too small

The task was filed around four render defects in `task report`: all-or-nothing
validation, undiscoverable statelessness, a false `Nothing to report.` at
`unverified`, and the PostToolUse hook firing on `--help`. (The last one
reproduced live during this session: running `task report --help` injected the
full "append the block, unchanged" instruction with no block rendered.)

All four are real. None of them are why the command has failed. The requester
converted this to a brainstorm specifically to widen it past that list.

## What the command was actually for

`task report` was requested out of exasperation at agent verbosity. Its purpose
was never "produce a report" — it was **bound the agent's output**. Three
attempts, three failures:

1. Report replaces the reply → the agent editorialized around it anyway.
2. Report is appended after freeform prose → the block is `Nothing to report.`
   most of the time, and noise the rest.
3. The block's spec grew content the requester never asked for (filed
   follow-ups), which `session status` already renders. That was unilateral
   scope, not a feature.

## The diagnosis

The verify command *existed*. The agent wrote it in prose, then told
`task report` there was nothing to report.

The block is not failing to find content. **The agent is failing to route
content into it**, because the command requires re-stating in a structured
field something already said in freeform. Given two output channels and no
enforcement, everything lands in the cheap one.

The consequence is decisive: **any design where the agent volunteers the
payload fails identically.** Partial success, persistence, better help text —
none of the four seed fixes touch the actual defect. They would all ship, and
the agent would still put the verify command in prose and pass nothing.

Restated: there are two channels and content lands in the wrong one. Every
attempt so far added rules to the block. The alternative is to **delete a
channel**.

## The design the requester proposed

`task report` accepts whatever the agent wants to send. An adversarial agent
aggressively minimizes it. The agent must reply with that output verbatim, and
a hook errors if it does not.

This dissolves the four seed symptoms for free — nothing is rejected, so there
is no all-or-nothing render and no ceremony bounce — but that is incidental.
What it fixes is the enforcer. The spec ("report only what the user cannot
compute themselves") was always right; the agent was the wrong party to apply
it, judging its own output in the same breath as writing it.

### Settled during the session

- **Input is the entire freeform draft reply**, not payload fields. Fields keep
  a second channel alive; the draft *is* the reply.
- **`--draft-file <path>`, plain markdown.** Not JSON/XML, not heredoc, not
  inline arg. Any format requiring the agent to pre-structure or tag the draft
  reintroduces the exact restatement tax that caused the routing failure; and
  escaping failures (backticks, quotes, `$`) become retries. The minimizer
  *extracts* structure; the agent does not mark it up.
- **Every turn**, not just handoffs. The 5000-character task review that
  triggered this was a mid-conversation turn.
- **The objective is "delete what the user didn't ask for," not "make it
  short."** A pure minimizer guts a requested discussion — this brainstorm is
  the counterexample. One objective, no turn-type switch.
- **Enforcement is at Stop**, where the hook can see the final message. The
  same hook must catch "never called it," or that is the trivial bypass.
- **Latency is accepted.** Endless is built for many parallel sessions; the
  requester works elsewhere while a turn is being minimized.

### Escape hatches (requester's three, refined)

1. **Appeal** — bounded hard. One appeal, and the appeal text goes through the
   minimizer too. An unbounded appeal is a second bite the agent will always
   take.
2. **Raw draft persisted and retrievable on demand** — the one that matters.
   With the raw preserved, the minimizer can be maximally aggressive at zero
   risk, because nothing is destroyed, only hidden.
3. **A structured pointer** in the output when the minimizer judges more detail
   exists — nearly free once (2) holds.

## The prompt is the product, so it needs an iteration loop

The requester's expectation is that the minimizer prompt will take substantial
tuning. Two parts with different lifecycles:

- **Invariants** — tables verbatim, code blocks intact, the verify command
  always survives, a direct question gets its direct answer. Few, stable,
  shipped.
- **Anti-puffery / anti-jargon guidance** — *also shipped*, and deliberately so.
  The requester wants "Endless filters out that crap" as a stated product
  benefit, not a personal config file. The user template holds additions.

Both are **guidelines to the adversarial agent, not gates**. A regex gate would
mangle a legitimate quotation of a banned phrase.

A phrase denylist alone never converges (ban "load-bearing", get "does the
heavy lifting"). It needs a generative rule — *delete any sentence that
characterizes the reasoning or narrates the analysis rather than delivering
information the user needs* — with the phrase list as concrete anchors beneath
it. First three entries, all from this session's own output: "the thing that
survives from your instinct", "that reframes the decision", "load-bearing".

### Mechanics

- The template is user-customizable config; editing it needs no task and no
  land. **Ceremony is reserved for promoting a proven override back into the
  `//go:embed`ed default**, which is what the long-lived `underway` task is for.
- **Promotion should be triggered objectively** — the override beats the
  embedded default on the corpus — not by feel.

### The corpus

Every turn yields (prompting user message, raw draft, minimized output). The
triple is **already free**: hatch (2) forces persisting the raw draft, the
minimized text is the command's own stdout, and the user message is at hand.
One extra column, not a capture pipeline.

Prefer this over mining transcripts with a periodic job (cf. E-698): the
persisted triple is exact, where transcript-mining must infer which turns had a
report and reconstruct the draft.

What neither provides is the **label**.

### Labels: a four-word signal vocabulary

Recognized only as the first token of a line, standalone or followed by free
text (`$CUT you dropped the verify command`):

- `$CUT` — you dropped something I needed (show me the raw)
- `$BLOAT` — still too long, or said things I didn't ask for
- `$WRONG` — off-target regardless of length
- `$GOOD` — it worked

The sigil is not decoration. `CUT:` at line start is nearly safe, but `WRONG:`
and `GOOD:` are exactly what a user naturally types as a prose label. One
character buys immunity. `!cut` and `/cut` are unusable — Claude Code already
claims both prefixes.

`$GOOD` is not politeness. A corpus made only of complaints trains the
minimizer toward verbosity, because every recorded failure is a cut the user
resented.

Detection is a **UserPromptSubmit hook**, not the agent noticing — same
argument as everything else here. `$BLOAT` with a quoted phrase can append
straight to the denylist, turning annoyance into config without a round trip.

## Rejected: self-launched subagents and workflows

The requester asked whether the agent's own Agent/Workflow capability could do
the minimizing instead of a command. Recorded as a decision.

The requester's assumption was partly correct — a `fork` agent variant inherits
the parent's context, and `SendMessage` continues an agent with context intact —
but there is no embedding channel; tool I/O is text either way.

Context fidelity was never the problem. The agent chooses whether to call a
subagent, what draft to hand it, and whether to keep its output; the return
value lands in context as editable text. No enforcement point exists. A hook
needs a stable anchor ("the last `endless task report` stdout"); a subagent
result is indistinguishable from any other Agent call unless a marker
convention is invented — at which point the command has been rebuilt, worse and
unversioned. Workflows are a harder no: heavyweight, background, opt-in,
notification-returning.

Not impossible. Unenforceable.

The salvaged half: the command should *call* a model internally. `task report`
already runs a ceremony check over free text — that slot becomes the minimizer.
The bouncer is replaced by an editor.

## Deliberately out of scope

- **Task inflation** (>1 task filed per task completed). Raised here with force,
  but the requester is pursuing it in other sessions. It is not a `task report`
  problem and would have swallowed this one.
- **The four seed defects as standalone fixes.** They are subsumed. Repairing
  them independently would ship four correct patches that leave the actual
  failure untouched.

## Open, not settled

- Whether `task report` should be disabled outright while the minimizer is
  built. The requester weighed it; by his own account the current command
  delivers nothing 9/10 times, so disabling costs nothing — but it was not
  decided.
- The exact wording of the minimizer's objective and the invariant list. Expected
  to be substantial work, and the reason the iteration loop above exists.
- Whether the block/minimized output ever carries anything the user did not
  request (the filed-follow-ups mistake suggests: no, by default).

payload.description: Turn off `task report` and its PostToolUse hook. It emits "Nothing to report." most of the time and unrequested noise the rest, so the hook currently demands agents append a block carrying no signal. payload.title: Identify a worktree fork point by ledger content, not by SHA
payload.description: canAmend's precondition 2 asks "is HEAD reachable from another ref" (`git for-each-ref --contains HEAD`) — a SHA-level question that any history rewrite invalidates, after which the guard permits an amend that diverges main from every task branch's base and conflicts on the ledger segment at land. Add a second, content-level reason to refuse: before amending a ledger tip, compare the `.endless/db-ledger` tree hash at HEAD against every `refs/heads/task/*` tip; if any branch holds a byte-identical ledger tree, append instead. A tree hash is content-addressed, so it survives any rewrite — the durable fork-point identity the SHA test lacks. Precondition 2 is retained, not replaced: the content test scans only task branches, so it is blind to a ledger commit already pushed or tagged. The two are OR'd. Measured at 16ms across 145 branches; the patch-id alternative costs 71s per event and is struck. Amend is preserved and self-releases, costing one extra commit per rewrite.

# Add a content-identity precondition to canAmend

Implements ED-1553. Root cause, evidence and rejected alternatives are in
E-1943's outcome.

## What to change

`canAmend` in `internal/events/commit.go` currently refuses to amend on three
preconditions. Add a fourth, checked only when the tip subject is
`LedgerCommitSubject`:

> Refuse to amend if any `refs/heads/task/*` tip holds a `.endless/db-ledger`
> tree byte-identical to the one at HEAD.

Rationale: a tree hash is content-addressed, so it is unchanged by any history
rewrite. `git pull --rebase` (or interactive rebase, or a hand `commit --amend`
on main) reassigns every local SHA, which makes precondition 2's
`for-each-ref --contains HEAD` test answer a question the rewrite made
meaningless. The content test asks the same question — "does a task branch
depend on the commit I am about to amend?" — in terms a rewrite cannot
invalidate.

## What NOT to change

Precondition 2 stays. The two are OR'd; either refusing means append. The
content test scans only `refs/heads/task/*`, so it is structurally blind to a
ledger commit already pushed to `origin/main` or carrying a tag — exactly the
cases precondition 2 gets right. Do not replace it.

## Implementation notes

Use a single batched process, not one `rev-parse` per branch:

    git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short):.endless/db-ledger' refs/heads/task \
      | git cat-file --batch-check

Compare each resulting tree OID against `HEAD:.endless/db-ledger`. Measured on
the endless repo (145 task branches, 130 worktrees) at 16ms for the batched
form vs ~1s for 146 spawns. A `git patch-id` scan answers the same question
but costs 71s per ledger event and is struck — its cost scales with the size
of the rewrite it is looking for, so it is slowest exactly when it matters.

Follow existing house error handling in the file: a subprocess failure is an
error; a "no" answer to the precondition returns `(false, nil)`. Treat a
missing `.endless/db-ledger` tree at HEAD (empty OID) as "no match, do not
suppress" rather than an error.

Mirror the existing comment style in `canAmend` — the surrounding
preconditions each carry a short rationale comment, and this one needs to say
why a tree hash rather than a SHA.

## How to verify

The reproduction is a self-contained git harness; the shape is:

1. Record two ledger events on main so the tip is an amended ledger commit.
2. Fork `task/900` at that tip and give it one real work commit.
3. Advance a remote, then `git pull --rebase` on main.
4. Record another ledger event, letting the guard decide.
5. `git rebase main` in the task worktree.

Before the change, step 4 amends and step 5 conflicts on the ledger segment.
After it, step 4 appends and step 5 is clean. Two properties matter beyond the
basic fix and should both be covered:

- **Self-release.** Repeat step 4 five and twenty more times after the first
  suppressed amend. The guard must return to amending (it does — main's tip is
  then a commit no branch holds) and the land must stay clean. This is what
  keeps amend's flood-suppression value intact; the cost is one extra commit on
  main per rewrite, not per event.
- **No false suppression.** With no pull, and with `pull.rebase=false`
  (merge-style pull), behaviour must be unchanged from today.

A Go unit test in `internal/events` following the existing `commit_test.go`
fixtures is the right home.

fields.outcome:
# How worktree branches survive a rewrite of main's history

Decided: **ED-1553** — identify a fork point by ledger *content*, not by SHA.
Implemented by: **E-1955**.

## The finding that reframed the task

The prior analysis reported two harness verdicts (no-pull → clean;
pull+amend → conflict) out of four scenarios run. Re-running the harness with
the missing scenarios changed the shape of the problem:

    S1 no pull, ledger events (guard)     guard=APPEND (saw task/900)   land=OK
    S2 pull --rebase, ledger (guard)      guard=AMEND                   land=CONFLICT
    S3 pull --rebase, NO further ledger   guard=-                       land=OK
    S4 pull --rebase, ledger FORCED append guard=APPEND                 land=OK
    S5 pull --merge, ledger (guard)       guard=APPEND                  land=OK
    S6 no pull, NO further ledger         guard=-                       land=OK

    S7 pull --rebase, append once, +5 more guard-driven events   land=OK
    S8 pull --rebase, guard only,  +5 more guard-driven events   land=CONFLICT
    S9 pull --rebase, append once, +20 more guard-driven events  land=OK

S3 and S4 are the ones that had not been reported, and they are decisive.

**The rewrite alone is harmless (S3).** `pull --rebase` orphans every fork
point, and the land still succeeds: rebase drops commits patch-equivalent to
upstream, and a rewritten-but-unamended ledger commit is patch-identical to
its old copy.

**The rewrite plus continued ledger activity is still harmless (S4)**, so long
as the first post-rewrite event appends rather than amends. So the amend is
not a co-factor. It is the entire converter from "survivable" to "broken."

**One append per rewrite is enough, permanently (S7, S9).** After a single
append, main's tip is a commit no branch holds; 5 and 20 subsequent amends all
proceed and the land stays clean. The suppression needed is one append per
history rewrite — not one per event, and not one per live branch.

S5 confirms `pull.rebase=false` masks the defect entirely, which is why it
surfaced only after that setting was changed on 2026-08-10.

## Why the guard fails, precisely

`canAmend` (`internal/events/commit.go`) is not bypassed and does not error.
Its precondition 2 asks "is HEAD reachable from any ref besides the current
branch" via `git for-each-ref --contains HEAD`. That is a SHA-level question.
`git pull --rebase` reassigns every local SHA, so a task branch forked from
main's ledger tip stops "containing" main's HEAD. The guard answers a question
the rewrite made meaningless, returns "safe to amend," and the next amend
diverges main from every task branch's base.

This generalises past `pull.rebase`: interactive rebase, a hand
`commit --amend` on main, and a force-pull after someone rewrote origin all do
the same thing. The task's title was already the right framing.

## The decision

Add a second, content-level reason to refuse the amend: before amending a
ledger tip, compare the `.endless/db-ledger` tree hash at HEAD against every
`refs/heads/task/*` tip. If any branch holds a byte-identical ledger tree,
that branch's base is content-identical to the commit about to be amended —
append instead.

A tree hash is content-addressed, so no history rewrite can change it. That is
the durable fork-point identity the SHA test lacks, and it is the first of the
three options the task description named.

Three properties made this the choice rather than a compromise:

- **It is cheaper than what it supplements.** 16ms across 145 task branches
  and 130 worktrees, via a single `git cat-file --batch-check` process.
- **It self-releases.** Once one append has occurred the test stops matching
  and amending resumes (S7/S9). Amend's flood-suppression value is preserved
  in full; the measured cost is one extra commit on main per rewrite.
- **It is additive, not a replacement.** Precondition 2 is retained. The
  content test scans only task branches, so it is structurally blind to a
  ledger commit already pushed to `origin/main` or carrying a tag — cases the
  reachability test gets right. The two are OR'd.

## Rejected

**A `git patch-id` scan.** Answers the same question and is equally
rewrite-immune, but costs **71s per ledger event** (measured; 34s even when
restricted to ledger-touching commits). Its cost scales with the size of the
rewrite it is looking for, because a rewrite pushes every branch's merge-base
back behind it — so it is slowest exactly when it matters. Disqualifying for a
check that runs on every event.

**"Any task branch exists → append."** Considered and priced wrong at first.
It would suppress amend on essentially every event, reinstating the commit
flood amend exists to prevent.

**A sidecar record of main's tip SHA.** Detects the rewrite directly and is
O(1), but requires stored state and forces an append that the content test
shows is unnecessary in most cases. Strictly worse than a content test that
costs 16ms and needs no state.

**Land-side detection as the primary gate.** A detector keyed on "was this
branch's base rewritten" would refuse S3, S4, S7 and S9 — four false alarms
against one true positive. An honest land-side gate has to be keyed on
divergence rather than on the rewrite, which needs a rebase rehearsal to
answer. Prevention at write time is both cheaper and more accurate.

**A union merge driver on the ledger segments.** Struck in the prior analysis
and still struck: `Event` carries no unique id and neither `ReadAllEvents` nor
the projector dedups, so union's duplicate lines would double-apply on replay.

## Repair: not needed

The aggregate figure — 195 ledger commits carried by task branches that main
lacks — is noise, not damage. Scanning all 109 unmerged task branches with
`git cherry`:

- The large live branches carrying 100–150 inherited ledger commits
  (`task/1889`, `task/1929`, `task/1934`, …) are **clean**. Rebase drops every
  inherited commit as patch-equivalent and replays only their 2 real work
  commits, neither touching the ledger.
- 29 branches have a non-patch-equivalent ledger commit. Every one has
  **exactly one** replaying commit, it is a single `Endless: record ledger
  entry`, and it touches nothing but `.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`. Zero real
  work is at stake — these are spent plumbing whose work already landed.

So no live branch with pending work is at risk, and a repair path would exist
only to rescue branches that are disposable. The widened orphan-drop that was
under consideration (extending `_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` past its
contiguous-at-base limit) is therefore not filed: with prevention in place, no
branch carrying real work can acquire the condition.

Worth keeping: across all 29, there are **zero** commits touching both the
ledger and real source. The mixed-commit hazard that E-1342's docstring backs
away from does not occur in practice.

## Deliberately not filed

`worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
the failure it exists to preview. Named in E-1943's analysis as evidence
pending the framing choice. The framing is now settled, and the gap turns out
to be independent of it — a dry-run that does not simulate the rebase cannot
predict *any* conflict, ledger or ordinary. It is a separate defect with a
separate root cause and should be filed on its own merits, not as cleanup
of E-1943.

## Correction to the prior analysis

Its closing note warned that commit counts mislead. That holds, and this
session found the sharper form: `git cherry` distinguishes "ahead by 326
commits" from "ahead by 2 commits and 324 patch-equivalent copies," and the
difference between those two readings is the difference between a branch that
lands clean and one that does not.

# Verification

Two increments, verified separately.

## Increment 1 — disable

```sh
endless task report E-1952            # command refuses / reports disabled
endless task report --help            # PostToolUse hook does NOT fire
```

Pass: neither invocation injects the "append the block, unchanged" instruction,
and no session is asked to emit a block.

## Increment 2 — minimizer

Fixture: a draft containing (a) a markdown table, (b) a fenced code block,
(c) a one-line verify command, (d) three paragraphs narrating the analysis,
(e) a direct answer to a direct question.

```sh
endless task report E-NNN --draft-file tests/fixtures/report-draft.md
```

Pass criteria, asserted by a golden test over the fixture:

1. The table survives byte-for-byte.
2. The fenced code block survives byte-for-byte.
3. The verify command appears in the output.
4. The direct answer appears in the output.
5. The three narrating paragraphs are gone.
6. Output is shorter than input.

Then:

```sh
endless task report E-NNN --raw        # prints the persisted draft in full
```

Pass: the raw draft round-trips unchanged, so nothing the minimizer cut is lost.

## Increment 2 — enforcement

A Stop-hook test, not a CLI test:

- Reply verbatim with the minimized output → allowed.
- Reply with the minimized output plus one appended sentence → rejected.
- Reply without having called `task report` at all → rejected.

The third case is the one that matters; the first two are the easy half.

## Increment 2 — signals

```sh
# simulate a user prompt beginning "$CUT you dropped the verify command"
```

Pass: the UserPromptSubmit hook records the label against the preceding turn's
triple. `$CUT` / `$BLOAT` / `$WRONG` with no following text are rejected;
`$GOOD` alone is accepted. `CUT the scope` and `WRONG: ...` do not fire.

## Not verifiable by test

The minimizer's judgment quality. That is what the eval corpus and the promotion
gate exist for — an override is promoted into the `//go:embed`ed default only
when it beats the current default over the corpus. No golden test substitutes
for that.

# Reproduction harness (E-1943)

Self-contained. Simulates canAmend's precondition 2 faithfully and, under
LEDGER_ID_TEST=1, the proposed content-identity precondition. Proves the idea;
does NOT exercise real endless code — E-1955's verify script must do that.

Results:

    SHA guard only (today)                     + content-identity test
    S1 no pull, ledger (guard)      land=OK    land=OK
    S2 pull --rebase, ledger        land=CONFLICT   land=OK  (saw task/900 by content)
    S3 pull --rebase, no more       land=OK    land=OK
    S4 pull --rebase, forced append land=OK    land=OK
    S5 pull --merge, ledger         land=OK    land=OK
    S6 no pull, no more             land=OK    land=OK
    S7 rebase, append once, +5      land=OK    land=OK  (amend resumed)
    S8 rebase, guard only,  +5      land=CONFLICT   land=OK  (amend resumed)
    S9 rebase, append once, +20     land=OK    land=OK  (amend resumed)

S8 is the load-bearing one: after the single suppressed amend, the guard
returns to amending and the land stays clean — the fix self-releases.

Run: `LEDGER_ID_TEST=0 bash harness.sh` then `LEDGER_ID_TEST=1 bash harness.sh`

## Script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# E-1943 harness: does `git pull --rebase` alone break a land, or only pull+amend?
#
# Re-implements canAmend precondition 1+2 (subject match; for-each-ref --contains
# HEAD skipping the current branch), reports its decision, then attempts land's
# rebase and reports OK / CONFLICT.
set -uo pipefail

ROOT="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$ROOT"' EXIT

LEDGER=".endless/db-ledger/db-entries-aaaa-000001.jsonl"
SUBJ="Endless: record ledger entry"
DECISION=""
SAW=""
N=0
TAIL=0

g() { git -C "$@"; }

can_amend() {
  local repo head_subj cur_ref refs r
  repo="$1"
  head_subj="$(git -C "$repo" log -1 --format=%s 2>/dev/null)" || return 1
  [ "$head_subj" = "$SUBJ" ] || return 1
  cur_ref="$(git -C "$repo" symbolic-ref --quiet HEAD 2>/dev/null)"
  refs="$(git -C "$repo" for-each-ref --contains HEAD --format='%(refname)' 2>/dev/null)"
  SAW=""
  while IFS= read -r r; do
    [ -z "$r" ] && continue
    [ "$r" = "$cur_ref" ] && continue
    SAW="$r(sha)"
    return 1
  done <<< "$refs"
  if [ "${LEDGER_ID_TEST:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    local tip_tree b b_tree
    tip_tree="$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse "HEAD:.endless/db-ledger" 2>/dev/null)"
    if [ -n "$tip_tree" ]; then
      for b in $(git -C "$repo" for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads/task 2>/dev/null); do
        b_tree="$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse "$b:.endless/db-ledger" 2>/dev/null)"
        if [ "$b_tree" = "$tip_tree" ]; then
          SAW="$b(content)"
          return 1
        fi
      done
    fi
  fi
  return 0
}

record_event() {
  local repo mode payload
  repo="$1"; mode="$2"; payload="$3"
  mkdir -p "$repo/.endless/db-ledger"
  echo "{\"ev\":\"$payload\"}" >> "$repo/$LEDGER"
  git -C "$repo" add "$LEDGER"
  if [ "$mode" = "guard" ] && can_amend "$repo"; then
    git -C "$repo" commit -q --amend --no-edit
    DECISION="AMEND"
  else
    git -C "$repo" commit -q -m "$SUBJ"
    DECISION="APPEND"
  fi
}

REPO=""; WT=""; UP=""
setup() {
  N=$((N+1))
  UP="$ROOT/up$N"
  REPO="$ROOT/repo$N"
  WT="$ROOT/wt$N"
  git init -q --bare "$UP"
  git init -q -b main "$REPO"
  git -C "$REPO" config user.email t@t
  git -C "$REPO" config user.name t
  git -C "$REPO" config commit.gpgsign false
  mkdir -p "$REPO/.endless/db-ledger"
  echo base > "$REPO/src.txt"
  git -C "$REPO" add -A
  git -C "$REPO" commit -q -m "base commit"
  git -C "$REPO" remote add origin "$UP"
  git -C "$REPO" push -q -u origin main
}

upstream_advance() {
  local tmp
  tmp="$ROOT/clone$N"
  git clone -q "$UP" "$tmp"
  git -C "$tmp" config user.email o@o
  git -C "$tmp" config user.name o
  git -C "$tmp" config commit.gpgsign false
  echo upstream >> "$tmp/other.txt"
  git -C "$tmp" add -A
  git -C "$tmp" commit -q -m "upstream: someone else's work"
  git -C "$tmp" push -q origin main
  rm -rf "$tmp"
}

make_task_branch() {
  git -C "$REPO" branch task/900
  git -C "$REPO" worktree add -q "$WT" task/900
  echo "task work" >> "$WT/src.txt"
  git -C "$WT" add -A
  git -C "$WT" commit -q -m "E-900: real user work"
}

try_land() {
  local files
  if git -C "$WT" rebase main >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "OK"
  else
    files="$(git -C "$WT" diff --name-only --diff-filter=U 2>/dev/null | tr '\n' ' ')"
    git -C "$WT" rebase --abort >/dev/null 2>&1
    echo "CONFLICT [${files% }]"
  fi
}

run() {
  local label pull post pre_dec land
  label="$1"; pull="$2"; post="$3"; TAIL="${4:-0}"
  setup

  # ledger events BEFORE the branch exists: no other ref contains HEAD, so the
  # guard permits amend — this is how main's tip becomes an amended commit.
  record_event "$REPO" guard e1
  record_event "$REPO" guard e2

  # Branch forks AT main's ledger tip and stays there — the real shape.
  make_task_branch

  # Probe the guard without mutating anything: expect APPEND (branch is visible).
  if can_amend "$REPO"; then pre_dec="AMEND"; else pre_dec="APPEND"; fi

  upstream_advance
  case "$pull" in
    rebase) git -C "$REPO" -c pull.rebase=true  pull -q --rebase origin main >/dev/null 2>&1 ;;
    merge)  git -C "$REPO" -c pull.rebase=false pull -q --no-rebase --no-edit origin main >/dev/null 2>&1 ;;
    none) : ;;
  esac

  DECISION="-"; SAW=""
  if [ "$post" != "none" ]; then
    record_event "$REPO" "$post" e3
  fi

  # TAIL: further ledger events, always guard-driven, AFTER the post-pull one.
  # Tests whether a single append is enough to re-anchor main permanently.
  local i
  for (( i=0; i<TAIL; i++ )); do
    record_event "$REPO" guard "tail$i"
  done

  land="$(try_land)"
  printf '%-38s | pull=%-6s | post-ledger=%-6s | pre-pull guard=%-6s | post-pull guard=%-6s%s | land=%s\n' \
    "$label" "$pull" "$post" "$pre_dec" "$DECISION" \
    "$([ -n "$SAW" ] && echo " (saw ${SAW##*/})" || echo "")" "$land"
}

run "S1 no pull, ledger (guard)"        none   guard
run "S2 pull --rebase, ledger (guard)"  rebase guard
run "S3 pull --rebase, NO more ledger"  rebase none
run "S4 pull --rebase, FORCED append"   rebase append
run "S5 pull --merge, ledger (guard)"   merge  guard
run "S6 no pull, NO more ledger"        none   none
echo
echo "--- does ONE append after the rewrite re-anchor main permanently? ---"
run "S7 rebase, append once, +5 guard"  rebase append 5
run "S8 rebase, guard only, +5 guard"   rebase guard  5
run "S9 rebase, append once, +20 guard" rebase append 20
```
