# How worktree branches survive a rewrite of main's history

Decided: **ED-1553** — identify a fork point by ledger *content*, not by SHA.
Implemented by: **E-1955**.

## The finding that reframed the task

The prior analysis reported two harness verdicts (no-pull → clean;
pull+amend → conflict) out of four scenarios run. Re-running the harness with
the missing scenarios changed the shape of the problem:

    S1 no pull, ledger events (guard)     guard=APPEND (saw task/900)   land=OK
    S2 pull --rebase, ledger (guard)      guard=AMEND                   land=CONFLICT
    S3 pull --rebase, NO further ledger   guard=-                       land=OK
    S4 pull --rebase, ledger FORCED append guard=APPEND                 land=OK
    S5 pull --merge, ledger (guard)       guard=APPEND                  land=OK
    S6 no pull, NO further ledger         guard=-                       land=OK

    S7 pull --rebase, append once, +5 more guard-driven events   land=OK
    S8 pull --rebase, guard only,  +5 more guard-driven events   land=CONFLICT
    S9 pull --rebase, append once, +20 more guard-driven events  land=OK

S3 and S4 are the ones that had not been reported, and they are decisive.

**The rewrite alone is harmless (S3).** `pull --rebase` orphans every fork
point, and the land still succeeds: rebase drops commits patch-equivalent to
upstream, and a rewritten-but-unamended ledger commit is patch-identical to
its old copy.

**The rewrite plus continued ledger activity is still harmless (S4)**, so long
as the first post-rewrite event appends rather than amends. So the amend is
not a co-factor. It is the entire converter from "survivable" to "broken."

**One append per rewrite is enough, permanently (S7, S9).** After a single
append, main's tip is a commit no branch holds; 5 and 20 subsequent amends all
proceed and the land stays clean. The suppression needed is one append per
history rewrite — not one per event, and not one per live branch.

S5 confirms `pull.rebase=false` masks the defect entirely, which is why it
surfaced only after that setting was changed on 2026-08-10.

## Why the guard fails, precisely

`canAmend` (`internal/events/commit.go`) is not bypassed and does not error.
Its precondition 2 asks "is HEAD reachable from any ref besides the current
branch" via `git for-each-ref --contains HEAD`. That is a SHA-level question.
`git pull --rebase` reassigns every local SHA, so a task branch forked from
main's ledger tip stops "containing" main's HEAD. The guard answers a question
the rewrite made meaningless, returns "safe to amend," and the next amend
diverges main from every task branch's base.

This generalises past `pull.rebase`: interactive rebase, a hand
`commit --amend` on main, and a force-pull after someone rewrote origin all do
the same thing. The task's title was already the right framing.

## The decision

Add a second, content-level reason to refuse the amend: before amending a
ledger tip, compare the `.endless/db-ledger` tree hash at HEAD against every
`refs/heads/task/*` tip. If any branch holds a byte-identical ledger tree,
that branch's base is content-identical to the commit about to be amended —
append instead.

A tree hash is content-addressed, so no history rewrite can change it. That is
the durable fork-point identity the SHA test lacks, and it is the first of the
three options the task description named.

Three properties made this the choice rather than a compromise:

- **It is cheaper than what it supplements.** 16ms across 145 task branches
  and 130 worktrees, via a single `git cat-file --batch-check` process.
- **It self-releases.** Once one append has occurred the test stops matching
  and amending resumes (S7/S9). Amend's flood-suppression value is preserved
  in full; the measured cost is one extra commit on main per rewrite.
- **It is additive, not a replacement.** Precondition 2 is retained. The
  content test scans only task branches, so it is structurally blind to a
  ledger commit already pushed to `origin/main` or carrying a tag — cases the
  reachability test gets right. The two are OR'd.

## Rejected

**A `git patch-id` scan.** Answers the same question and is equally
rewrite-immune, but costs **71s per ledger event** (measured; 34s even when
restricted to ledger-touching commits). Its cost scales with the size of the
rewrite it is looking for, because a rewrite pushes every branch's merge-base
back behind it — so it is slowest exactly when it matters. Disqualifying for a
check that runs on every event.

**"Any task branch exists → append."** Considered and priced wrong at first.
It would suppress amend on essentially every event, reinstating the commit
flood amend exists to prevent.

**A sidecar record of main's tip SHA.** Detects the rewrite directly and is
O(1), but requires stored state and forces an append that the content test
shows is unnecessary in most cases. Strictly worse than a content test that
costs 16ms and needs no state.

**Land-side detection as the primary gate.** A detector keyed on "was this
branch's base rewritten" would refuse S3, S4, S7 and S9 — four false alarms
against one true positive. An honest land-side gate has to be keyed on
divergence rather than on the rewrite, which needs a rebase rehearsal to
answer. Prevention at write time is both cheaper and more accurate.

**A union merge driver on the ledger segments.** Struck in the prior analysis
and still struck: `Event` carries no unique id and neither `ReadAllEvents` nor
the projector dedups, so union's duplicate lines would double-apply on replay.

## Repair: not needed

The aggregate figure — 195 ledger commits carried by task branches that main
lacks — is noise, not damage. Scanning all 109 unmerged task branches with
`git cherry`:

- The large live branches carrying 100–150 inherited ledger commits
  (`task/1889`, `task/1929`, `task/1934`, …) are **clean**. Rebase drops every
  inherited commit as patch-equivalent and replays only their 2 real work
  commits, neither touching the ledger.
- 29 branches have a non-patch-equivalent ledger commit. Every one has
  **exactly one** replaying commit, it is a single `Endless: record ledger
  entry`, and it touches nothing but `.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`. Zero real
  work is at stake — these are spent plumbing whose work already landed.

So no live branch with pending work is at risk, and a repair path would exist
only to rescue branches that are disposable. The widened orphan-drop that was
under consideration (extending `_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` past its
contiguous-at-base limit) is therefore not filed: with prevention in place, no
branch carrying real work can acquire the condition.

Worth keeping: across all 29, there are **zero** commits touching both the
ledger and real source. The mixed-commit hazard that E-1342's docstring backs
away from does not occur in practice.

## Deliberately not filed

`worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
the failure it exists to preview. Named in E-1943's analysis as evidence
pending the framing choice. The framing is now settled, and the gap turns out
to be independent of it — a dry-run that does not simulate the rebase cannot
predict *any* conflict, ledger or ordinary. It is a separate defect with a
separate root cause and should be filed on its own merits, not as cleanup
of E-1943.

## Correction to the prior analysis

Its closing note warned that commit counts mislead. That holds, and this
session found the sharper form: `git cherry` distinguishes "ahead by 326
commits" from "ahead by 2 commits and 324 patch-equivalent copies," and the
difference between those two readings is the difference between a branch that
lands clean and one that does not.

## Scope addition: the behind-base refusal is auto-resolved (2026-08-12)

Folded in per ED-1550 rather than filed. Landing E-1943's own branch tripped
E-1941's behind-base refusal, which raised the question of how often that
happens: **106 of 109 unmerged task branches are behind main on Go paths right
now** — 97%, against 57 Go-path commits on main in 30 days (~1.9/day) and 82
lands. It is the normal case, not an exception.

The refusal is correct: a self_dev land runs the worktree's endless-go against
the real DB, and a binary built from stale source fails VerifyIntegrity. What
made it friction rather than protection is that the recovery it demanded —
`git rebase main` by hand — is the same rebase land's Step 4 already performs.
Only ORDER prevented land from satisfying its own guard: `just land` builds
the worktree binary BEFORE calling land, so Step 4's rebase arrives too late
to affect that build.

Fixed by doing the rebase earlier instead of asking for it. `endless worktree
sync <id>` (new) rebases the branch onto base when behind on
BINARY_SOURCE_PATHS; the justfile calls it before `just go`, so the build
reads current source and Step 4 reduces to a no-op. Automating it is safe at
that point for exactly the reason the refusal was written to preserve —
nothing has been built, migrated or merged, so a conflicting rebase aborts
with main untouched.

Two deliberate choices:

- **The refusal stays**, as the backstop for a land invoked without the sync
  step, so the rule keeps one home. Its message now names `worktree sync`
  instead of a bare `git rebase`.
- **The rewritten-history diagnosis moved with the rebase**, into sync's
  conflict path, where it inspects the actual conflicting paths and fires only
  when one is under the ledger dir — rather than being appended speculatively
  to every behind-base refusal as before.

Also confirmed: the first refusal seen when landing from the worktree ("branch
is 20 commit(s) behind main") was NOT the live guard. It came from the
worktree's own 20-commit-stale justfile — the duplicate pre-check E-1941 had
already deleted in 301965bc/f73722df, which counted ledger auto-commits and so
inflated the count. Rebasing the branch removed it.

Verification: `tests/tasks/e-1943-verify.sh` (11 checks, mutation-tested — 5
fail when the rebase is disabled), plus 4 tests in
`tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py`. Full suite 1339 passed.

Not covered by the script and stated rather than omitted: the self_dev gate
lives above `sync_branch_to_base`, in the resolution layer, which routes
through `config.default_db_to_main()` — that deliberately ignores
XDG_CONFIG_HOME, so no test below it can use a throwaway DB. That property is
why the function is split at all.

payload.title: Add a task status meaning "shipped, but superseded"
payload.description: `obsolete` currently covers both "never happened" and "shipped, then replaced" — the two read identically in the ledger, so marking superseded work obsolete erases the fact that it ever ran. Surfaced while closing E-1952: E-1901's Stop-gate machinery shipped and is being adopted by E-1953, yet E-1901 is marked obsolete, which implies it never landed. Needs a distinct terminal status (and a rule for when each applies).

triage.rationale: The task names the problem but leaves open the new status's name, its exact semantics/rule versus `obsolete`, and how existing tasks and tooling should migrate.

fields.title: Show `replaced_by` inline with terminal status; guard `obsolete` on shipped work
fields.description: `obsolete` reads as "never happened," so there is no way to see at a glance that shipped work was superseded — the fact lives in a `replaced_by` relation that status displays omit, which tempts users to mark shipped tasks obsolete and lose that history. No new status needed. Three parts: (1) render the relation inline with terminal statuses everywhere status is shown — `assumed (replaced by E-1953)` — in `task show`, `task list` and `session status`; (2) guard `obsolete` on any task that reached unverified/confirmed/assumed/completed, refusing or warning and pointing at `replaced_by` (confirmed absent: setting an `assumed` task to `obsolete` succeeds silently); (3) fix `task update --help`, whose --status list omits `submitted` and `completed` though both are accepted.

# Verification

Two increments, verified separately.

## Increment 1 — disable

```sh
endless task report E-1952            # command refuses / reports disabled
endless task report --help            # PostToolUse hook does NOT fire
```

Pass: neither invocation injects the "append the block, unchanged" instruction,
and no session is asked to emit a block.

## Increment 2 — minimizer

Fixture: a draft containing (a) a markdown table, (b) a fenced code block,
(c) a one-line verify command, (d) three paragraphs narrating the analysis,
(e) a direct answer to a direct question.

```sh
endless task report E-NNN --draft-file tests/fixtures/report-draft.md
```

Pass criteria, asserted by a golden test over the fixture:

1. The table survives byte-for-byte.
2. The fenced code block survives byte-for-byte.
3. The verify command appears in the output.
4. The direct answer appears in the output.
5. The three narrating paragraphs are gone.
6. Output is shorter than input.

Then:

```sh
endless task report E-NNN --raw        # prints the persisted draft in full
```

Pass: the raw draft round-trips unchanged, so nothing the minimizer cut is lost.

## Increment 2 — enforcement

A Stop-hook test, not a CLI test:

- Reply verbatim with the minimized output → allowed.
- Reply with the minimized output plus one appended sentence → rejected.
- Reply without having called `task report` at all → rejected.

The third case is the one that matters; the first two are the easy half.

## Increment 2 — signals

```sh
# simulate a user prompt beginning "$CUT you dropped the verify command"
```

Pass: the UserPromptSubmit hook records the label against the preceding turn's
triple. `$CUT` / `$BLOAT` / `$WRONG` with no following text are rejected;
`$GOOD` alone is accepted. `CUT the scope` and `WRONG: ...` do not fire.

## Not verifiable by test

The minimizer's judgment quality. That is what the eval corpus and the promotion
gate exist for — an override is promoted into the `//go:embed`ed default only
when it beats the current default over the corpus. No golden test substitutes
for that.

---

# Answers to build-session questions (from E-1952 requester)

**1. Sessions with no claimed task — (b), id-less allowed.**
Exempting unclaimed sessions exempts most of the verbosity the gate exists to
stop; unclaimed quick questions are exactly where sprawl happens. Don't force a
claim either — that taxes a one-line question. Make the id optional: the corpus
row keys on the session, which always exists; the task id is attribution only.
Scope the gate to registered projects. Command stays `task report` for now.

**2. "Every turn" — fire only when assistant text exists.**
A clarifying-question turn has text and goes through. A tool-only turn has
nothing to minimize. Keep empty `last_assistant_message` as fail-open: "said
nothing" versus "field unpopulated" is not a distinction worth guessing on.

**3. Agent-tool subagents — still exempt.**
A subagent's final message is a return value, not a handoff. Nothing may sit
between an agent and its subagent. The parent's own reply — the thing the user
reads — is already gated.

**4. FULL STATUS — replaced by `$FULL`, and it is a full one-turn exemption
from the gate.**
FULL STATUS was built against the old placeholder scheme; revise it to the
sigil vocabulary. `$FULL` is a *directive*, not a label, so unlike
`$CUT`/`$BLOAT`/`$WRONG` it may stand alone or carry the question with it —
`$FULL why did the rebase conflict?`. Same sigil, different class; the hook
routes on the word. The licensed reply does not go through the minimizer —
routing it through would contradict the license.

**5. Loop guard — session-scoped counter mirroring `RelayBounceLimit`.**
Add one thing: once the budget is spent, fail open **and record it**. A silent
livelock and a silent surrender are indistinguishable from outside, and the
second is how a gate rots unnoticed.

**6. Ships enabled — make the switch configuration, not a code constant, and
default it on.**
This overturns the analysis's "the switch belongs in code." The switch belongs
in `.endless/config.json`, endless's canonical per-project config, and **ships
enabled for product users** — the pain of not having it is what drives
adoption, so there is no case for shipping it inert. Endless's own
`.endless/config.json` can set it off while the prompt is being tuned, which is
the one place that needs to opt out.

`.endless/config.json` is also the right home because a gate an agent can
switch off is not a gate — this must not live anywhere an agent edits in the
course of normal work, `.claude/settings.json` included.

**Also:** `relay_gate.go` belongs to E-1901, which is `assumed` and landed at
`aa83a0c`; its `relayGateEnabled` constant is currently `false`. Link
`E-1953 replaces E-1901` so the supersession is visible.

Its closing note warned that commit counts mislead. That holds, and this
session found the sharper form: `git cherry` distinguishes "ahead by 326
commits" from "ahead by 2 commits and 324 patch-equivalent copies," and the
difference between those two readings is the difference between a branch that
lands clean and one that does not.

## Scope addition attempted, then superseded (2026-08-12)

Folded in per ED-1550 rather than filed, then dropped. Recorded because the
measurement stands even though the implementation did not.

Landing E-1943's own branch tripped E-1941's behind-base refusal, which raised
the question of how often that happens: **106 of 109 unmerged task branches
are behind main on Go paths** — 97%, against 57 Go-path commits on main in 30
days (~1.9/day) and 82 lands. It is the normal case, not an exception, so the
refusal was friction rather than protection almost every time it fired.

builds the worktree binary BEFORE calling land, so Step 4's rebase — which
already exists and already aborts cleanly — arrives too late to affect that
build. That diagnosis was right and is now settled.

The implementation was wrong. This session added `endless worktree sync` to
rebase the branch BEFORE the build, keeping the refusal as a backstop. In
parallel, the E-1941 session removed the staleness instead of sequencing
around it: main's Step 4.2 (`_rebuild_worktree_binary`, commit ef5ae25a)
rebuilds the binary AFTER Step 4's rebase and before Step 5's ff-merge, so a
stale binary cannot arise and `_refuse_if_behind_base` and
`BINARY_SOURCE_PATHS` were deleted outright.

That is strictly better. It deletes a guard, a constant, a command and a
justfile step; the sync approach added a command and a justfile step to
satisfy a guard that did not need to exist. Removing a failure mode beats
ordering around it.

Commit 34dc226b (`endless worktree sync` + verify script + 4 tests) is
therefore discarded, not merged — it references `_refuse_if_behind_base` and
`BINARY_SOURCE_PATHS`, both now gone, so merging it would ship a command that
raises NameError on first use. Recoverable from the branch reflog if ever
wanted; nothing in it should be.

this area: `config.default_db_to_main()` resolves through `main_config_dir()`,
which deliberately ignores `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (escaping the sandbox is its
purpose). No test above that call can run against a throwaway DB, which is why
land-level behaviour is tested by calling inner functions directly rather than
through the CLI.

# Replace the land's guessed rebase recoveries with evidence

## Context

`endless worktree land` fails on a rebase conflict by printing two recovery
options as *candidates for the user to choose between*:

1. resolve the conflict in place, `git rebase --continue`
2. capture the delta, `git reset --hard main`, re-apply, re-commit

Both can be actively harmful. Landing E-1943 on 2026-08-12 hit a conflict whose
branch side referenced `BINARY_SOURCE_PATHS` and `_refuse_if_behind_base`,
identifiers E-1941 had just deleted from main. Either recovery reintroduces them
into a function whose global no longer exists, so the land would have
"succeeded" while shipping an `endless worktree sync` that raises `NameError` on
first use. A recovery that can silently ship broken code must not be offered at
all.

The current shape was itself a deliberate correction — `_rebase_conflict_message`'s
docstring says it offers candidates "never one confident prescription… the
confident misattribution is exactly the failure mode this task removes." That
fixed real misattribution and introduced this hazard. The way out is not a third
rewording: stop speculating and go get evidence.

**The fork, already resolved:** classification is deterministic even though
resolution is not. The tool can prove *which kind* of conflict this is; only
genuine semantic overlap needs human judgment, and in that one case guessing is
exactly what should not be offered.

## Deliverables

### 1. `_rebase_conflict_message` stops prescribing

Keep the facts it already reports well — phase, the commit that failed to
replay (`REBASE_HEAD`), the conflicting paths. Delete the two numbered
candidates. End with one instruction: run `endless worktree diagnose`.

Keep the existing confident path: when every conflicting path is an
endless-managed auto-file, the mechanical recovery is already proven and stays.

Both call sites are affected — Step 3.7 (orphan replay) and Step 4 (base
rebase).

### 2. Persist the conflict evidence before aborting

The message is built mid-rebase and then `git rebase --abort` runs, so
`REBASE_HEAD` and the unmerged set are gone by the time anyone diagnoses.
Write the evidence first:

- path: `config.main_cache_dir() / "land" / "E-NNNN" / "conflict.json"`
  (mirrors `~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/<worktree>/`; use the helper, do not
  hand-build the path)
- contents: phase, base branch, branch, `REBASE_HEAD` sha + subject, unmerged
  paths, both sides of each conflicting hunk, `git cherry <base> HEAD` output,
  and the base tip sha at failure time
- overwrite per task; a later successful land removes the file

### 3. `endless worktree diagnose [E-NNNN]`

Derives the task ID exactly as `land` does, so a bare call works in-session.
Human-readable by default, `--json` for agent consumption (matches the rest of
the CLI). Reads the persisted evidence; if none exists, says so and exits
non-zero rather than reproducing anything.

**Contract: prescribe only what is proven. Where the class is not provable,
print the evidence and say judgment is required — never a menu of candidates.**

Classifiers, each proven or not attempted:

| Class | Test | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Already-landed content | `git cherry <base> HEAD` marks `REBASE_HEAD` `-` | Reset-and-reapply is correct; in-place resolve provably duplicates |
| Auto-file-only | every unmerged path satisfies `_is_auto_file` | Existing mechanical recovery |
| Orphaned ledger base | content-based fork-point identity (ED-1553) | `_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` already covers contiguous-at-base; report if the run is mid-branch |
| Symbol supersession | identifiers in the branch side of each hunk that have no definition on base | Neither recovery is safe; the branch's work is superseded — discard or re-author against base |
| Semantic overlap | none of the above | **No prescription.** Show both sides, name the overlapping symbols, and say a human or agent must choose |

Reuse ED-1553's detector rather than reimplementing it: E-1955 landed the
content-based fork-point test in `internal/events/commit.go`. Shell out through
`endless-go` the way `event_bridge` already does; do not port it to Python.

### 4. `worktree land --dry-run` rehearses the rebase

Today `--dry-run` only prints the worktree, branch, base and main paths — it
cannot preview the failure it exists to preview. Make it rehearse the rebase on
a throwaway branch off the task branch, report the same classification the
diagnostic does, and delete the branch in a `finally`. Never touches base, the
task branch, or the DB.

This is the same machinery as deliverables 2-3 — one rehearsal producing the
same evidence structure, serving prevention (before) and post-mortem (after).

## Sequencing

Deliverable 1 is a few lines and removes a live hazard from main; land it first
rather than holding it behind the rest.

## Out of scope

The behind-base refusal (deleted in E-1941 — do not resurrect it) and the ledger
conflict itself (E-1943 / ED-1553, shipped as E-1955).

## Verification

`tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh`, modeled on `tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh`
(pass/fail per check, summary, exit 0/1/2, fail-fast, `set -u` only — no bash
strict mode).

1. **The hazard is gone** — build a throwaway repo whose branch references a
   symbol deleted on base, drive a real land, assert the message contains
   neither numbered recovery and does name `endless worktree diagnose`. Fails on
   today's code.
2. **Evidence survives the abort** — after that failed land, the conflict.json
   exists, and `REBASE_HEAD` is recorded even though the rebase was aborted.
3. **Each classifier** — one throwaway repo per row of the table above,
   asserting the class and that a prescription appears only for the provable
   ones. Symbol supersession must reproduce the E-1943 shape and must NOT
   prescribe either recovery.
4. **Semantic overlap prints no prescription** — the negative case, explicitly.
5. **`--dry-run` predicts** — a branch that will conflict is reported by
   `--dry-run` with the same class the post-mortem gives; base, the task branch
   and the DB are all unchanged afterwards, and the throwaway branch is gone.
6. **pytest** for the classifier units and the persistence round-trip.

Project-wide regression (`just test`, `just test-go`, `just build`,
`just guide-check`) run by the implementing session and reported in one line.

payload.title: Make per-worktree sandboxes available to all projects, not just self_dev
payload.description: Sandbox provisioning is gated on `self_dev: true`, so only Endless itself gets per-worktree sandboxes: `_maybe_auto_sandbox_bind` (worktree_cmd.py) returns early for other projects and `config.py` resolves the sandbox root to None for them. That gate was never an intended design decision — the intent was that EVERY project gets a sandbox, because a sandbox is where a worktree stores the configuration a task needs in order to be verified, and essentially no real software project has zero configuration files. What is genuinely Endless-specific is only the `endless.db` routing (downstream worktree tasks must still land in the real ledger as real audit data, not a throwaway copy). So the two concerns are conflated and need separating: per-worktree scratch/config storage should be universal, while sandbox DB routing stays opt-in via self_dev. Decide the split, then make sandboxes available to all projects.

triage.rationale: There is no description at all, so the shape of the "read surface" (format, tool, UI vs. CLI vs. doc) is entirely undecided.

fields.description: E-1953 persists the eval-corpus triple (prompting message, raw draft, minimized output) and its $CUT/$BLOAT/$WRONG/$GOOD label on session_gates, but nothing reads it back for a human. `task report --raw` is agent-side and resolves the calling session, so from a shell it cannot show another session's draft; reviewing the corpus today means hand-written SQL. fields.analysis:
E-1953 persists the eval-corpus triple (prompting user message, raw draft,
minimized output) plus the `$CUT`/`$BLOAT`/`$WRONG`/`$GOOD` label on
`session_gates`, but nothing reads it back for a human. `task report --raw` is
agent-side and resolves the *calling* session, so from a shell it cannot show
another session's draft. Reviewing the corpus today means hand-written SQL and
a `length()` call to guess whether a cut was reasonable.

That blocks the loop the whole design rests on. The minimizer prompt is
explicitly expected to need substantial tuning, and promotion of an override
into the embedded default is supposed to be gated on beating the current
default OVER THE CORPUS. Neither judging a cut nor running that comparison is
possible without being able to read raw and minimized side by side.

Needed, roughly:

- List recent triples across sessions — when, which session, which task (may be
  null), prompt excerpt, raw/minimized sizes, label. Filterable by label, so
  "show me everything I marked $CUT" is one command.
- Show one triple in full, with raw and minimized presented for comparison
  rather than concatenated. A diff view is the obvious default given the
  minimizer only deletes; a side-by-side is the alternative.
- Read-only, and it must reach the real ledger from a plain shell (the reviewer
  is a human at a terminal, not a session).

Open questions for whoever takes it:

- Command shape. `endless report log` / `endless report show <id>` reads
  naturally but `report` is currently a `task` subcommand, so `endless task
  report --log` may fit the existing tree better at the cost of overloading a
  command that is otherwise agent-facing.
- Whether it also needs an export (JSONL) for running the promotion comparison
  offline, or whether that is a separate concern.

Note for anyone reading the table early: most existing rows predate E-1953 and
carry only `sanctioned_text` — they are E-1901-era relay checkpoints, not
corpus samples. Filtering to rows with a non-null `raw_draft` is what selects
real triples.

triage.rationale: The description states the problem (no way to view another session's stored draft/minimized/label triples) but leaves open the command's interface and design—e.g. whether it's a new CLI flag, a new subcommand, filtering/query options, and output format for side-by-side comparison.

and adding `project_id` to `errors` (raised, deliberately not folded in).

## Verification

`tests/tasks/e-1957-verify.sh`, modeled on `tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh`:
pass/fail per check, summary, exit 0/1/2, fail-fast, `set -u` only — no bash
strict mode (house rule; load the `shell-script-author` skill first).

1. **The hazard is gone** — throwaway repo whose branch references a symbol
   deleted on base; drive a real land; assert the message contains neither
   numbered recovery and does name `endless worktree diagnose`. Fails on
   today's code.
2. **Evidence survives the abort** — after that failed land, `REBASE_HEAD` is
   recoverable from the capture even though the rebase was aborted.
3. **Each classifier** — one throwaway repo per row, asserting the class and
   that a prescription appears ONLY for the provable rows.
4. **The two unprovable classes prescribe nothing** — symbol supersession
   reproduces the E-1943 shape; semantic overlap is the explicit negative case.
5. **`--dry-run` predicts** — a branch that will conflict is reported by
   `--dry-run` with the same class the post-mortem gives; base, the task branch
   and the DB are unchanged afterwards, and the throwaway branch is gone.
6. **pytest** for the classifier units and the capture round-trip.

Project-wide regression (`just test`, `just test-go`, `just build`,
`just guide-check`) run by the implementing session and reported in one line.

# Analysis

Findings from the E-1941 session (2026-08-12) that surfaced this task. Evidence,
not a plan — the working session owns the design.

## How the gate is implemented today

- `_maybe_auto_sandbox_bind` (`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`) returns early when
  `config.project_is_self_dev(project_root)` is false, so `task claim` /
  `task spawn` provision a sandbox only for Endless itself.
- `config.py` resolves the sandbox root to `None` for non-self-dev projects
  (`return root if project_is_self_dev(root) else None`).
- `.endless/config.json` carries the flag; only Endless sets it.

So a downstream project's worktree gets no sandbox at all — not merely no
sandbox *DB*.

## The two concerns the flag conflates

1. **Per-worktree scratch/config storage.** A worktree needs somewhere to keep
   the configuration a task requires in order to be *verified*. Essentially no
   real software project has zero configuration files, so this is universal.
2. **DB routing.** Endless-specific, and correctly opt-in: a downstream
   project's worktree tasks must land in the real ledger as real audit data, not
   in a throwaway copy. Sandboxing *that* for downstream users would be wrong.

Today one flag governs both. Separating them is the decision this task exists to
make.

## Why E-1957 is blocked on this: the fault surface is project-blind

E-1957 needs somewhere to persist git conflict evidence when a land fails. The
obvious existing home was the fault subsystem (`internal/faults`), which already
does the right shape of thing — `Fault.Code` + `Fault.Source` discriminate the
producer, and `Fault.Detail` / `Fault.Fields` carry long structured capture to a
JSONL log by design, explicitly "never the DB". No schema change needed.

It was rejected for now because none of it is project-scoped:

- the `errors` table (`internal/schema/schema.sql:882`) has **no `project_id`
  column** — columns are id, code, severity, source, fingerprint, summary,
  occurrences, first_seen_at, last_seen_at, cleared_at, cleared_by
- the JSONL `Detail` struct (`internal/faults/detaillog.go`) has **no project
  field**
- `monitor.ConfigDir()` (`internal/monitor/db.go:61`) returns `dbContextDir`
  when set, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/endless`. A land pins `--db main`, which sets
  `dbContextDir` to the real config dir — so the detail log is **one shared
  location for every project**, `~/.config/endless/log/`

Attributing anything there means smuggling task/project through `Fields` and the
fingerprint: a workaround for a missing column.

If this task gives every project a per-worktree sandbox, per-worktree fault and
evidence storage becomes the natural home and no smuggling is needed. That is
why E-1957 defers its storage decision to this task's outcome rather than
picking a location now.

Two adjacent gaps, noted and deliberately NOT folded in (Mike's call):

- Neither the `errors` table nor the JSONL detail log has any retention sweep.
  `appendDetail` does `MkdirAll` + append with no rotation; only manual
  `endless errors clear` exists. Left for when it is needed.
- Adding `project_id` to `errors` would fix the blindness directly and benefit
  every fault source, independent of sandboxes. Raised, not filed — it may be
  the cheaper answer than universal sandboxes for E-1957's needs specifically,
  and this task should say which it prefers.

payload.title: Add the missing project qualifier to the errors table and fault detail log
payload.description: The `errors` table (internal/schema/schema.sql:882) has no project_id column, and the JSONL `Detail` struct (internal/faults/detaillog.go) has no project field. One Endless database holds many projects, so every recorded fault from every project lands in one undifferentiated table, and the detail log compounds it: monitor.ConfigDir() (internal/monitor/db.go:61) resolves to the single shared ~/.config/endless for any caller pinning --db main. Consequences: `endless errors show` cannot filter by project, the session-status error badge cannot be project-scoped, the unique index on (source, code, fingerprint) can collide across unrelated projects, and any new fault producer must smuggle attribution through Source or Fields. This reads as an oversight in E-698 rather than a deliberate choice. Add project_id to errors and a project field to the Detail line, decide backfill vs NULL for existing rows, and update the read paths and the index.

# Outcome

## Pre-work scoping decisions (E-1941 session, 2026-08-12)

Recorded before the design work begins, so the deciding session inherits them
rather than re-deriving them. Everything below was settled with Mike during
filing. The decision this task exists to make — how to split per-worktree
storage from DB routing — is NOT among them and remains open.

**E-1957 stays blocked on this task.** E-1957 needs somewhere to persist git
conflict evidence when a land fails. The alternative considered was to unblock it
by making the existing fault surface project-aware instead. Mike chose to keep
the block: the intent is one coherent storage story — per-worktree storage, once
every project has a sandbox — rather than two mechanisms. So this task's outcome
determines where E-1957 stores evidence.

**The missing `errors.project_id` is a separate defect, not an input to this
decision.** It was initially recorded here as an alternative that had been
"considered and rejected," which was wrong: it conflated *where land evidence
lives* with *the errors table being unable to say which project a fault came
from*. The second is a design oversight in its own right — `endless errors show`
cannot filter by project, the status badge cannot be project-scoped, and the
unique index on `(source, code, fingerprint)` can collide across unrelated
projects — none of which depends on where E-1957 stores anything. Split out as
**E-1960**. This task neither depends on it nor blocks it.

**Fault-surface retention is deliberately out of scope.** Neither the `errors`
table nor the JSONL detail log has any sweep; `appendDetail` appends without
rotation and only manual `endless errors clear` exists. Mike's call: leave it
until it is needed. Do not fold it in here.

## Correction worth keeping

The `self_dev` gate on sandbox provisioning was never an intended design
decision — Mike's stated intent was always that every project gets a sandbox,
because a sandbox is where a worktree keeps the configuration a task needs in
order to be verified. It was recorded in a prior session as though the
downstream-projects-get-no-sandbox behavior were deliberate. Only the
`endless.db` routing is genuinely Endless-specific.

payload.title: Enforce agreement between a task's title verb and its type
payload.description: `validate_title` (src/endless/task_cmd.py) checks only that a title begins with a registered actionable verb from the verb catalog — nothing checks the verb against the task TYPE. So a brainstorm, whose deliverable is a decision, can be titled with a doing-verb and read as implementation work: E-1958 was filed as "Make per-worktree sandboxes available to all projects" and passed validation cleanly, when a brainstorm should read "Decide how...". The title is what everyone scans in `task next`, `task list` and the dashboard, so a mismatched verb misrepresents what the task will produce and invites a session to start building instead of deciding. Decide whether the fix is a per-type allowed-verb set, a per-verb allowed-type set, or a softer warn-and-confirm — the verb catalog already carries definitions that could seed the mapping (decide/evaluate/compare for brainstorm; add/build/remove for todo). Note --type can change after filing, so the check has to run on `task update --type` too, not just `task add`.

payload.title: Gate the report channel to terminal Claude Code sessions only, not the Desktop app
payload.description: The E-1953 report channel is injected into, and enforced against, every Claude Code session on a registered project with report_gate on — including sessions in the Claude Code Desktop app, where the `endless task report` contract is not currently wanted. Endless needs to distinguish a terminal CLI session from a Desktop-app session and gate reportChannelOn() on that surface, so injection and enforcement stay in lockstep.
payload.analysis:
The report channel (E-1953) is delivered to, and enforced against, every Claude
Code session on a registered project whose nearest `.endless/config.json` leaves
`report_gate` on. That is too wide: it also catches sessions running in the
**Claude Code Desktop app**, where the `endless task report` contract is not
currently wanted. The desktop session gets told to route its reply through
`endless task report`, and (if a Stop hook fires there) can be blocked for not
having done so.

Intent: the report channel is a **terminal-only** contract for now. Endless must
be able to tell a terminal CLI session from a Desktop-app session and gate on it.

## Where it is wired

- `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` — `reportChannelOn(projectID, isRegistered, cwd)`
  is the single switch, used deliberately by BOTH halves:
  - `handleTaskContextInjection` → `composeSessionStartContext(..., reportChannelOn(...))`
    injects `reportChannelRule` on SessionStart, and
  - the `Stop` case → `enforceReportGate(...)`, which blocks the turn.
  The comment on `reportChannelOn` states the invariant to preserve: a session
  must never be told to use a channel that will not gate it, nor gated without
  having been told. So the surface detection belongs inside `reportChannelOn`,
  not bolted onto one of the two call sites.
- `internal/monitor/db.go` — `ReportGateEnabledForCwd` / `ReportGateEnabled`
  resolve the per-project `report_gate` key (nearest-config-wins). Surface
  detection is a separate axis from that config key and should compose with it
  (both must say yes).
- `src/endless/config.py:project_report_gate` mirrors the Go resolution.

## The detection signal

CC Desktop told Mike that `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` "does not exist". That is
wrong. Verified empirically from a terminal session on 2026-08-13 (Claude Code
2.1.222): the hook subprocess environment contains

    CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=cli
    CLAUDECODE=1
    CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=1
    CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID=...
    CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH=...
    AI_AGENT=claude-code_2-1-222_agent
    TERM_PROGRAM=tmux            # incidental — Mike's terminal, not a CC signal

`endless-hook` already reads process env directly (`TMUX_PANE`,
`CLAUDE_JOB_DIR`), so reading one more var is in-pattern.

**Unknown that must be resolved before implementing:** what
`CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` (and the rest of the env) actually contains inside a
Claude Code Desktop session. Do not guess a value. Capture it empirically — have
a Desktop session dump its env (or land a temporary diagnostic path in the hook)
and record the observed values in this task before coding the predicate.

Design consequence of that unknown: the predicate should **allow-list the
terminal**, not deny-list the desktop. `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT == "cli"` → gate
on; anything else (desktop, vscode, sdk, remote, unset) → gate off. Failing
closed on an unrecognized surface matches the rest of the gate's design (it
already returns false for unregistered projects and unresolvable paths) and
means a future Claude Code surface does not silently start enforcing the channel.

Sub-question to settle: whether the terminal-only rule is hardcoded or itself a
config key (e.g. `report_gate_surfaces`). Prefer hardcoded + documented until
there is a second consumer — Mike's stated intent is "currently" terminal-only,
which is a policy that may widen later, not a per-project knob.

## Notes

- Endless's own checkout has `"report_gate": false`, so the gate is off here and
  the fix cannot be observed from inside this repo. Verification needs a
  registered project that leaves the key unset, driven once from the terminal
  (rule present) and once from Desktop (rule absent).
- `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` is not part of the hook stdin payload — it is process
  env only. If the payload ever grows a surface field, prefer that.
- Related but distinct: `SessionStart` matchers (`startup`/`resume`/`clear`/
  `compact`/`fork`) describe how a session began, not what surface it runs on;
  they are not a substitute here.

## Done when

- A single predicate in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` decides surface, consulted
  by `reportChannelOn` so injection and enforcement can never disagree.
- Observed Desktop env values recorded in this task.
- Go tests cover: terminal → on, desktop → off, unset → off, and terminal +
  `report_gate: false` → still off.
- Docs updated where the gate is described: `CLAUDE.md` ("Reporting to the user
  — the minimizer gate"), `docs/guide/tasks.md`.

payload.title: Remove sandbox tooling rot: nonexistent endless-sandbox binary and dead ephemeral commands
payload.description: Every error string in `internal/sandboxcmd/` names an `endless-sandbox` binary that does not exist (the surface is `endless-go sandbox <cmd>`), and the ephemeral non-worktree sandbox feature — `run`, `enter`, `prune`, plus modeEphemeral/orphan/supervisor/livewriters — is still live code despite having been judged YAGNI and dropped from the documented surface. CLAUDE.md also instructs `endless-sandbox destroy e-NNN`, which cannot be run. Decide whether to delete the ephemeral path or keep it deliberately, then fix the strings in whatever survives.
payload.analysis:
# Sandbox tooling rot — inventory

Found while brainstorming E-1958. Mike believed the ephemeral sandbox feature had
been removed from Endless entirely ("we realized YAGNI so we eliminated them from
the Endless feature set") and that `sandbox run`/`enter`/`prune` did not exist.
They do — just not where he looked.

## 1. Error strings name a binary that does not exist

Every error and usage string in `internal/sandboxcmd/` is prefixed
`endless-sandbox <cmd>:` — init.go, bind.go, run.go, prune.go, destroy.go,
list.go. There is no such binary:

```
$ which endless-sandbox
endless-sandbox not found
$ ls cmd/
endless-go
```

The real surface is `endless-go sandbox <cmd>`. `endless sandbox` (the Python
CLI) also does not exist, which is what made the whole feature look absent.
So a user hitting any sandbox error is handed a command they cannot run.

## 2. The ephemeral, non-worktree sandbox path is still live code

`endless-go sandbox --help` lists:

```
  run     [--clone] [--name N] [--keep] -- <cmd> [args]
  enter   [--clone] <name>
  init    [--mode empty|worktree|seed|clone] [--force] <name>
  bind    <worktree-path> [<sandbox-name>]
  list
  prune   [--older-than DURATION]
  destroy [--force] [--if-exists] <name>
```

`run` provisions `modeEphemeral` with a random hex name and auto-destroys on
exit; `enter` forks a subshell; `prune` exists solely to reap orphaned
ephemerals (minimum `--older-than 24h`). None of this is reachable from the
worktree lifecycle, which is 1-to-1 with a task.

Falls out if run/enter/prune go: `modeEphemeral`/`modeKeep`, orphan.go,
supervisor.go, livewriters.go, and the `--clone` flags that only warn about
unimplemented E-1087.

Related: `init --mode seed` and `--mode clone` both hard-exit "not yet
implemented". Dead flags on a live command.

## 3. CLAUDE.md documents the nonexistent binary

The "Self-dev DB sandbox — E-1281" section ends with: "manually
`endless-sandbox destroy e-NNN` if the cache needs reclaiming." Cannot be run.

This item may be moot depending on E-1958: if sandboxes move inside the
worktree they die with it, so manual destroy stops being a thing to document
at all.

## 4. `ENDLESS_SANDBOX` semantics are worth a look while in here

`Sandbox.Env()` (sandbox.go:200) injects `ENDLESS_SANDBOX=<dir>` alongside
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, but only on the run/enter paths — never via `bind`. Its
only consumer is the E-1162 refusal gate in `cli.py:301`: when set,
project-bound endless subcommands refuse. If run/enter are deleted, nothing
sets the variable and the gate becomes unreachable. Decide whether the gate
goes too, or gets re-keyed onto something that still exists.

## Decision needed

Whether to delete the ephemeral path or keep it deliberately. If deleted, the
`endless-sandbox` → `endless-go sandbox` string fix shrinks to the files that
survive.

triage.rationale: The description explicitly leaves open whether to delete or keep the ephemeral run/enter/prune path, which is the material design decision that must be made before the fix can be implemented.

fields.analysis:
# Reopen: automatic triage effectively never fires where tasks are filed

Found while brainstorming E-1958 (2026-08-13). Symptom Mike reports: triage
"takes fucking forever" — a task filed by an agent sits `untriaged` long enough
that the agent surfaces the state to him instead of the routing resolving it.

Four defects, all from `f39a6e3a` (E-1859).

## 1. `inline_suppressed()` is over-broad — the primary cause

`src/endless/triage.py:311` suppresses file-time triage when
`gated_worktree_root() is not None and RESOLVED_CONFIG_DIR == main_config_dir()`
— i.e. `--db main` from inside a self-dev worktree. That is exactly how every
agent session in this repo is instructed to file tasks, and agents file ~99% of
them. So in endless's own repo the belt never fastens and everything falls to
the suspenders.

The stated rationale is E-698's: candidate code must not write the real ledger.
That rationale does not hold on this path. Under `--db main` from a worktree:

- The spawned child is `sys.argv[0]` — the `endless` shim, which `just install`
  points at the MAIN checkout's editable source. Never the worktree's Python.
- That child writes via `_resolve_endless_go()` (event_bridge.py:34), which
  prefers `<worktree>/bin/endless-go` ONLY under `--db sandbox`; under
  `--db main` it falls back to the PATH-resolved global.

Both halves are already the landed code. The DB router had already closed this
door; the suppression was pattern-matched off `internal/jobs/suppress.go:52`
(where it IS correct, because hooks invoke the worktree's binary) rather than
derived for this path.

Fix: drop the self-dev-worktree clause from `inline_suppressed()`, keeping the
`ENDLESS_NO_TRIAGE` opt-out. Verify first that the Python CLI in a worktree is
always main's editable install — CLAUDE.md mandates it ("Run `just install`
from the main checkout, never from a worktree") but nothing enforces it. If
that cannot be guaranteed, gate on the resolved CLI path being outside the
worktree instead of on self_dev.

## 2. `spawn_detached` sends all three stdio streams to DEVNULL

`triage.py:358-363`. `triage.run` is already fail-open by design — timeout,
missing `claude`, non-zero exit, unparseable verdict all silently leave the task
`untriaged`. Layering DEVNULL on top means a genuine crash in the child is
indistinguishable from a considered no-verdict, and nothing is recorded
anywhere. Some share of the reported latency may be the child dying unseen.

Fix: redirect stdout/stderr to a log file rather than DEVNULL. Keep
fire-and-forget semantics (the parent still must not wait); only make failure
observable after the fact.

## 3. Sweep interval of 15 minutes was not asked for

`internal/triagejob/triagejob.go:60` sets `interval = 15 * time.Minute`. Mike
does not recall specifying it and would have asked for 1-3 minutes. With defect
#1 present, this interval IS the triage latency for nearly every task, so it
compounds. Even after #1 is fixed the sweep is the fallback for every
suppressed or failed inline run.

Note the tension recorded in the source: `batchLimit` caps a sweep because every
selected task is a model call. A shorter interval raises spend. Pick the
interval with that trade explicit — it may argue for a short interval with a
small batch rather than the current long interval with a large one.

## 4. The reset message offers an undo instead of stating a fact

`src/endless/task_cmd.py:4663` (E-1845's code, folded in here because it is the
same user-visible symptom). On a description-edit reset it prints:

the queue it fills; this task builds the thing that drains it — for each
`untriaged` task, decide whether its description is already a sufficient spec
(→ `submitted`) or design work is needed first (→ `unplanned`), and record the
transition with triager attribution.

Both blockers are clear: E-698's fire-once runner landed (`internal/jobs/`,
registry ships empty — this is its first real client), and E-1845 landed at
`576f948`.

recorded so the implementing session does not have to re-derive it.

orchestration and the model call. Every DB read goes through the Go read helpers
(E-1481), never through Python `sqlite3`; the write already routes through
`emit_event` → the Go executor. This lands the code on the target side of
**E-1486** (`ready`, `next` — "Python has zero SQLite knowledge", DB access in Go
while Click and logic stay Python) from day one, instead of adding to its 38-site
backlog. **E-1063** (port the whole CLI to Go) stays `later` with no forcing
function, and inherits a small bounded surface.

The all-Go alternative was rejected: `run_internal_claude` stays Python under
E-1486's boundary (the verb-check that uses it is Click-layer validation), so a
Go triager would create a second model-invocation harness in a second language —
precisely what **E-1849** would then have to unify.

`endless task add` would add seconds to every filing, interactive ones included.
The inline path is a latency optimization; the background sweep is the
correctness guarantee. File time spawns the triage of that one task detached and
returns at today's speed. If the detached call dies, the task stays `untriaged`
for the sweep — the fallback is the normal path, not an error path.

**Fail-open, always.** Timeout, missing binary, non-zero exit, unparseable reply
→ leave the task `untriaged`, transition nothing, exit zero. Triple duty: it
makes the job idempotent for free (a re-claim after a lapsed lease re-selects
only still-`untriaged` rows — the lease contract's hard requirement at
`internal/jobs/jobs.go:28-32`), it keeps a model outage from corrupting the
ledger, and it makes the worst failure mode the status quo, where a human
triages by hand with `task submit` — which E-1845 already commits to keeping as
the permanent override (`task_cmd.py:2790-2797`).

in `config.py`, reading a `models` map from the layered config with a documented
default per purpose. The verb-check (`task_cmd.py:264`) and the triager both
resolve through it — the same mechanism E-1859 asks for — with distinct defaults,
because "is this description a sufficient spec?" is a materially harder judgment
than "is this word a verb?". A user who wants them identical sets one value.

**The two `report_cmd` gates are not touched.** They stay pinned to Haiku.
**E-1911** (`submitted`) is actively reworking the reporting contract and those
gates; changing model selection there would collide with it.

**The prompt is a Go template, not a JSONL string.** It lives at
`internal/templatecmd/templates/triage/sufficiency.md.tmpl` and renders through
`endless-go template render`. That system (E-1565/E-1822) already gives the
three-layer lookup — `<project>/.endless/templates/<name>.local.tmpl`
(per-developer) → `<name>.tmpl` (committed, materialized from embed on first
render) → embedded fallback — which satisfies ED-1531 Req 5's requirement that
the user tune wording in config rather than product source. It renders from
stdin-supplied JSON variables, so parent, sibling titles, and linked decisions
interpolate natively; a flat JSONL string would force that assembly in Python.

touches nothing E-1911 is rewriting.

become first-class and queryable as such, rather than hiding inside a payload
field on a generic `system` event. This adds one value to the validated set at
`internal/events/event.go:78-82`; the change is purely additive, so every
historical event remains valid under the existing kinds and nothing needs
upcasting. Coordinate the touch with **E-1671** (`unplanned`, `now`), which is
about to rework `internal/events`. The payload still carries the deciding model
and the model's one-line rationale — that is provenance, not attribution, and it

from planning and therefore from triage, exactly as `task_cmd.py:2151` requires.

  broken triager decays toward the cap instead of burning model cost every
  interval. `LeaseTTL` generously exceeds the worst-case sweep (batch limit ×
  per-call timeout).

  **capturing** stdout and stderr rather than inheriting them, because
  `jobs.Job`'s contract forbids writing to either when the trigger is a live TUI.
  Return the error; the runner records it as a fault.

  sweep triages the wrong ledger.

  in the candidate build.

`endless guide tasks` and the status-lifecycle prose say triage is manual ("until
an automatic triager exists, do it by hand"). That sentence appears in
`CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, and `docs/guide/index.md`, and
`tests/tasks/e-1648-verify.sh` asserts the canonical block matches across copies —
re-sync all of them together.

`tests/tasks/e-1859-verify.sh`, self-contained against a throwaway
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and a temp project, shaped after `tests/tasks/e-1880-verify.sh`.

# REOPENED 2026-08-13 — automatic triage never fires where tasks are filed

Reported by Mike during the E-1958 brainstorm: triage "takes fucking forever."
A task an agent files sits `untriaged` long enough that the agent surfaces the
state to Mike instead of the routing quietly resolving it. Four defects, all
from this task's own commit `f39a6e3a`. Fix them here rather than in a new task.

The full evidence trace is in this task's `--analysis`. What to DO is below.

## Fix 1 — `inline_suppressed()` is over-broad (the primary cause)

`src/endless/triage.py:311` suppresses file-time triage when
`gated_worktree_root() is not None and RESOLVED_CONFIG_DIR == main_config_dir()`
— `--db main` from inside a self-dev worktree. That is exactly how every agent
session in this repo is told to file, and agents file ~99% of tasks. So in
endless's own repo the inline path never runs and everything waits on the sweep.

The rationale it copied is E-698's (`internal/jobs/suppress.go:52`): candidate
code must not write the real ledger. Correct there — hooks invoke
`<worktree>/bin/endless-go`. Not true here. Under `--db main` from a worktree:

- the spawned child is `sys.argv[0]`, the `endless` shim, which `just install`
  points at the MAIN checkout's editable source;
- that child writes via `_resolve_endless_go()` (event_bridge.py:34), which
  prefers `<worktree>/bin/endless-go` ONLY under `--db sandbox` and otherwise
  falls back to the PATH-resolved global.

Both halves are already landed code. Confirmed empirically: `just verify`
(justfile:457) runs `endless --db sandbox ...` — the global shim — and only
`uv run pytest` (justfile:440) resolves worktree Python.

The correct rule is a pair, not one condition:

| binary   | DB      | verdict                          |
|----------|---------|----------------------------------|
| candidate| sandbox | fine — this IS the test          |
| candidate| real    | forbidden — the E-698 hazard     |
| landed   | real    | fine — this is triage            |

**Do:** gate on the resolved CLI/binary path lying outside the worktree, NOT on
`self_dev`. Do not simply delete the clause — path-gating stays correct if
anyone later runs `uv run endless` from a worktree, which today nobody does.
Keep the `ENDLESS_NO_TRIAGE` opt-out untouched.

## Fix 2 — child failures must reach the user, not DEVNULL

`triage.py:358-363` sends stdin/stdout/stderr to DEVNULL. `triage.run` is
already fail-open by design (timeout, missing `claude`, non-zero exit,
unparseable verdict all silently leave the task `untriaged`), so DEVNULL on top
makes a crash indistinguishable from a considered no-verdict, recorded nowhere.
Some share of the reported latency may be the child dying unseen.

**Do:** surface failures where a user actually sees them — `session monitor`,
per Mike — not merely a log file. Keep fire-and-forget semantics: the parent
still must not block on the child. Logging is the floor, monitor is the
requirement.

Mike's standing rule, stated here: code must not silently ignore errors. This
is an instance, not an exception.

## Fix 3 — sweep interval

`internal/triagejob/triagejob.go:60` sets `interval = 15 * time.Minute`. Not
specified by Mike; he would have asked for 1-3 minutes.

Correction to an earlier claim in this task's analysis: interval does NOT trade
against model spend. The sweep selects `untriaged` rows first, so an empty queue
costs one query; spend is proportional to tasks filed, not to polling frequency.
The only interval-sensitive risk is double-triage racing the inline path, which
the lease described in the module docstring already covers.

**Do:** drop to 1-3 minutes. Confirm the lease actually holds under the tighter
cadence before landing.

## Fix 4 — the reset message offers an undo instead of naming a cost

`src/endless/task_cmd.py:4663` (E-1845's code; folded in here because it is the
same user-visible symptom). On a description-edit reset it prints:

    E-NNNN was 'ready'; description changed → status set to untriaged (the
    description is the spec that triage and approval were judged against; pass
    --keep-status to suppress for a typo/formatting-only edit).

The status render already shows `Status: ready -> untriaged`. The trailing
`pass --keep-status to suppress` reads as an undo offered after the fact, which
invites an agent to relay a completed, correct transition to the user as a
decision to accept. Observed four times in one session.

Do NOT simply delete the clause. `--keep-status` is a spend control, not a
status convenience: every re-triage is a model call, and a filer who already
knows the edit was cosmetic should skip it. The clause needs reframing so the
decision it offers is about cost rather than about whether the status was right:

    → untriaged; re-triage will run (one model call). Pass --keep-status on a
    typo- or formatting-only edit to skip it.

**Do:** reframe along those lines and keep the "why" short.

## Why one task, not four

They share a root: a filing (or a reset) that cannot self-resolve becomes a
state someone has to narrate. Fixes 1 and 3 are why it does not self-resolve,
2 is why nobody can see that it did not, and 4 is what turns the residue into a
question for the user. Fixing only the message leaves the latency; fixing only
the latency leaves the message inviting undo offers on the paths where triage
legitimately cannot run.

## Out of scope, filed/flagged separately

`just verify` runs main's Python, not the worktree's, so a Python-side change is
verified against landed code. Real asymmetry with the Go side, but a different
defect — not to be fixed under this task.

- **E-1911** — the reporting rework, including `report_cmd`'s Haiku gates.
- **E-1913** — the `--keep-status` fix. Sibling under E-1844, independently owned.
- Any change to `internal/events` beyond adding the one `ActorKind` value.



---

# REOPENED 2026-08-13 — automatic triage never fires where tasks are filed

Reported by Mike during the E-1958 brainstorm: triage "takes fucking forever."
A task an agent files sits `untriaged` long enough that the agent surfaces the
state to Mike instead of the routing quietly resolving it. Five defects, all in
code this task landed. Fix them here rather than in a new task.

Fix them IN ORDER — Fix 1 activates a race that Fix 2 must already cover.

## Fix 1 — `inline_suppressed()` is over-broad (the primary cause)

`triage.inline_suppressed()` suppresses file-time triage whenever
`config.gated_worktree_root()` is non-None and the resolved config dir is the
main one — i.e. `--db main` from inside a self-dev worktree. That is exactly how
every agent session in this repo is told to file, and agents file ~99% of tasks.
So in endless's own repo the inline path never runs and everything waits on the
sweep.

The rationale it copied is E-698's, in `internal/jobs/suppress.go`
(`suppressedWithReason`): candidate code must not write the real ledger. Correct
THERE — the Claude hooks invoke `<worktree>/bin/endless-go`. Not true here.
Under `--db main` from a worktree:

- the child `spawn_detached` launches is `sys.argv[0]`, the `endless` shim,
  which `just install` points at the MAIN checkout's editable source;
- that child writes through `event_bridge._resolve_endless_go()`, which prefers
  the worktree binary ONLY under `--db sandbox` and otherwise falls back to the
  PATH-resolved global.

Both halves are already landed code. Confirmed empirically: the justfile's
`verify` recipe runs `endless --db sandbox task verify` — the global shim — and
only the `test` recipe's `uv run pytest` resolves worktree Python.

The correct rule is a pair, not one condition:

| binary    | DB      | verdict                       |
|-----------|---------|-------------------------------|
| candidate | sandbox | fine — this IS the test       |
| candidate | real    | forbidden — the E-698 hazard  |
| landed    | real    | fine — this is triage         |

**Do:** gate on the resolved CLI/binary path lying outside the worktree, NOT on
`self_dev`. Do not merely delete the clause — path-gating stays correct if
anyone later runs `uv run endless` from a worktree, which today nobody does.
Leave the `ENDLESS_NO_TRIAGE` opt-out untouched.

## Fix 2 — the inline path takes no lease (PREREQUISITE of Fix 1)

Sweep-vs-sweep is already safe: `internal/jobs` claims with a CAS lease (single
conditional UPDATE, SQLite's clock for every due/expiry comparison), so the N
`session monitor` instances across N tmux windows that each call `jobs.RunDue`
contend and exactly one wins. `triagejob`'s Schedule sets `LeaseTTL` explicitly
as `batchLimit * perTaskTimeout + leaseHeadroom`, NOT derived from Interval, so
shortening the interval does not shrink the lease.

The gap is inline-vs-sweep. `triage.spawn_detached` runs `endless triage run
--task N` directly — it never enters the jobs runner and takes no lease at all:

1. task filed; inline child begins a model call (up to `CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`)
2. the sweep fires meanwhile and selects N, still `untriaged` because the child
   has not written yet
3. both call the model for the same task

Python re-reads the row and guards the write, so state does not corrupt — but
the re-read happens AFTER the model call, so the spend is already doubled.

This is latent TODAY only because Fix 1's bug means the inline path never runs
in a worktree. Unsuppressing it makes the window real; shortening the interval
widens it. Mike: "IT WILL HAPPEN, so we can't assume a longer delay will solve
it."

**Do:** take a per-task claim BEFORE the model call, honored by both paths, so
a second attempt from either skips a task already in flight. Must survive a
crashed claimant (time-boxed like the job lease, not an OS lock). Land this
with or before Fix 1.

## Fix 3 — child failures must reach the user, not DEVNULL

`triage.spawn_detached` sends stdin, stdout and stderr to DEVNULL. `triage.run`
is already fail-open by design (timeout, missing `claude`, non-zero exit,
unparseable verdict all silently leave the task `untriaged`), so DEVNULL on top
makes a crash indistinguishable from a considered no-verdict, recorded nowhere.
Some share of the reported latency may be the child dying unseen.

**Do:** surface failures where a user actually sees them — `session monitor`,
per Mike — not merely a log file. Keep fire-and-forget semantics: the parent
still must not block on the child. Logging is the floor; the monitor is the
requirement.

Mike's standing rule, stated here because this violated it: code must not
silently ignore errors.

## Fix 4 — sweep interval

`triagejob`'s `interval` constant is 15 minutes. Not specified by Mike.

Correction to an earlier claim: interval does NOT trade against model spend. The
sweep selects `untriaged` rows first, so an empty queue costs one query; spend is
proportional to tasks filed, not to polling frequency.

**Do:** 5 minutes. Not 1 — with many `session monitor` instances live, tighter
polling buys latency that Fix 2's per-task claim should be providing instead.

## Fix 5 — the reset message offers an undo instead of naming a cost

In `task_cmd`'s update path, the E-1845 auto-untriage note (E-1845's code,
folded in here because it is the same user-visible symptom) prints:

    E-NNNN was 'ready'; description changed → status set to untriaged (the
    description is the spec that triage and approval were judged against; pass
    --keep-status to suppress for a typo/formatting-only edit).

The status render already shows `Status: ready -> untriaged`. The trailing
`pass --keep-status to suppress` reads as an undo offered after the fact, which
invites an agent to relay a completed, correct transition to the user as a
decision to accept. Observed four times in one session.

Do NOT simply delete the clause. `--keep-status` is a spend control, not a
status convenience: every re-triage is a model call, and a filer who already
knows the edit was cosmetic should skip it. Reframe so the decision it offers is
about cost rather than about whether the status was right:

    → untriaged; re-triage will run (one model call). Pass --keep-status on a
    typo- or formatting-only edit to skip it.

**Do:** reframe along those lines and keep the "why" short.

## Why one task, not five

They share a root: a filing (or a reset) that cannot self-resolve becomes a state
someone has to narrate. Fixes 1 and 4 are why it does not self-resolve, 2 is the
race that unblocking 1 exposes, 3 is why nobody can see when it silently failed,
and 5 is what turns the residue into a question for the user. Fixing only the
message leaves the latency; fixing only the latency leaves the message inviting
undo offers on the paths where triage legitimately cannot run.

## Explicitly out of scope

The justfile's `verify` recipe runs main's Python, not the worktree's, so a
Python-side change is verified against landed code while a Go-side change is
verified against candidate. Real asymmetry, but Mike has ruled it WONTFIX: the
fix is complex and Python is slated for a port to Go, so fixing it in Python
only delays the port.
