# Evidence: why automatic triage never fires where tasks are filed

Gathered 2026-08-13 during the E-1958 brainstorm. The prescription lives in this
task's plan text; this is only the trace behind it.

## The suppression's premise does not hold on this path

`triage.inline_suppressed()` returns a suppression reason for "self-dev worktree
pinned to the real ledger", mirroring `internal/jobs`'s `suppressedWithReason`.
The mirrored rationale is that candidate code must not write the real ledger.

Traced under `--db main` from inside a worktree:

- `triage.spawn_detached` launches `sys.argv[0]` — the `endless` shim. `just
  install` runs `uv tool install -e .` from the MAIN checkout, so the shim
  resolves to main's source. CLAUDE.md forbids installing editable from a
  worktree.
- The child writes via `event_bridge._resolve_endless_go()`, whose documented
  behavior is: prefer `<worktree>/bin/endless-go` under `--db sandbox`,
  otherwise fall back to the PATH-resolved global.

So under `--db main` both the Python and the Go halves are landed code. The DB
router had already closed the door the suppression guards.

Corroborating: the justfile's `verify` recipe invokes `endless --db sandbox task
verify`, i.e. the global shim; only the `test` recipe's `uv run pytest` resolves
worktree Python. Nothing in normal use runs candidate Python via the `endless`
command.

Where the same rule IS correct: the Claude hooks written into a worktree's
`.claude/settings.json` invoke `<worktree>/bin/endless-go`, which is genuinely
candidate. `internal/jobs`'s suppression protects that; triage copied it without
re-deriving it.

## What is and is not already race-safe

Safe — sweep vs. sweep across processes. `internal/jobs` claims with a CAS lease
(one conditional UPDATE whose WHERE clause is the precondition) and takes every
due/expiry comparison from SQLite's clock, so N processes share one clock. The N
`session monitor` instances that each call `jobs.RunDue` contend and one wins.
`triagejob`'s Schedule sets `LeaseTTL` explicitly from `batchLimit *
perTaskTimeout + leaseHeadroom`, not from Interval, so shortening the interval
does not shrink the lease.

NOT safe — inline vs. sweep. `spawn_detached` invokes `endless triage run --task
N` directly, bypassing the jobs runner entirely, so it holds no lease. A sweep
firing during an inline child's model call re-selects the same still-`untriaged`
row and pays for a second model call. Python's post-call re-read guards the
write but not the spend.

Latent today only because the suppression means the inline path never runs in a
worktree. Fixing the suppression makes it live.

## Errors are unobservable

`spawn_detached` routes all three stdio streams to DEVNULL, on top of a
`triage.run` that is fail-open by design — timeout, missing `claude`, non-zero
exit and unparseable verdict all leave the task `untriaged` without a sound. A
crashed child and a considered no-verdict are indistinguishable, and neither is
recorded anywhere.

## Scale of the symptom

137 live worktrees under `.endless/worktrees/`. Agents file the large majority of
tasks, from worktrees, with `--db main`. So the suppressed path is the normal
path, and the 15-minute sweep is the effective triage latency for nearly every
task filed.

# Sandbox tooling rot — inventory

Found while brainstorming E-1958. Mike believed the ephemeral sandbox feature had
been removed from Endless entirely ("we realized YAGNI so we eliminated them from
the Endless feature set") and that `sandbox run`/`enter`/`prune` did not exist.
They do — just not where he looked.

## 1. Error strings name a binary that does not exist

Every error and usage string in `internal/sandboxcmd/` is prefixed
`endless-sandbox <cmd>:` — init.go, bind.go, run.go, prune.go, destroy.go,
list.go. There is no such binary:

```
$ which endless-sandbox
endless-sandbox not found
$ ls cmd/
endless-go
```

The real surface is `endless-go sandbox <cmd>`. `endless sandbox` (the Python
CLI) also does not exist, which is what made the whole feature look absent.
So a user hitting any sandbox error is handed a command they cannot run.

## 2. The ephemeral, non-worktree sandbox path is still live code

`endless-go sandbox --help` lists:

```
  run     [--clone] [--name N] [--keep] -- <cmd> [args]
  enter   [--clone] <name>
  init    [--mode empty|worktree|seed|clone] [--force] <name>
  bind    <worktree-path> [<sandbox-name>]
  list
  prune   [--older-than DURATION]
  destroy [--force] [--if-exists] <name>
```

`run` provisions `modeEphemeral` with a random hex name and auto-destroys on
exit; `enter` forks a subshell; `prune` exists solely to reap orphaned
ephemerals (minimum `--older-than 24h`). None of this is reachable from the
worktree lifecycle, which is 1-to-1 with a task.

Falls out if run/enter/prune go: `modeEphemeral`/`modeKeep`, orphan.go,
supervisor.go, livewriters.go, and the `--clone` flags that only warn about
unimplemented E-1087.

Related: `init --mode seed` and `--mode clone` both hard-exit "not yet
implemented". Dead flags on a live command.

## 3. CLAUDE.md documents the nonexistent binary

The "Self-dev DB sandbox — E-1281" section ends with: "manually
`endless-sandbox destroy e-NNN` if the cache needs reclaiming." Cannot be run.

This item may be moot depending on E-1958: if sandboxes move inside the
worktree they die with it, so manual destroy stops being a thing to document
at all.

## 4. `ENDLESS_SANDBOX` semantics are worth a look while in here

`Sandbox.Env()`  injects `ENDLESS_SANDBOX=<dir>` alongside
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, but only on the run/enter paths — never via `bind`. Its
only consumer is the E-1162 refusal gate in the Python CLI: when set,
project-bound endless subcommands refuse. If run/enter are deleted, nothing
sets the variable and the gate becomes unreachable. Decide whether the gate
goes too, or gets re-keyed onto something that still exists.

## Decision needed

Whether to delete the ephemeral path or keep it deliberately. If deleted, the
`endless-sandbox` → `endless-go sandbox` string fix shrinks to the files that
survive.

payload.title: Make per-worktree sandboxes universal by moving them into the worktree
payload.description: Implements the design settled in the E-1958 brainstorm. Sandboxes move from `~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/<name>` to `<worktree>/.endless/sandbox/`, are created for EVERY project rather than only `self_dev` ones, self-ignore via a `.gitignore` containing `*` written at worktree-create time, and live and die with their worktree. Contents are the project's business, filled by its own post-worktree-create hook — endless creates an empty dir and seeds nothing. Path resolution is composition behind a single resolver function, with a project-level override for trees that cannot take extra files. `self_dev` is removed from sandbox provisioning and retained only for endless's own DB routing; the `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` injection and `sandbox bind` are deleted. 126 existing sandboxes migrate by rename.
payload.analysis:
# Implementation notes: universal per-worktree sandboxes

Design settled in the E-1958 brainstorm; read that task's outcome for the
reasoning. This file carries only what an implementing session needs that the
outcome does not spell out.

## Order of work

1. Move the resolver. One function returns the sandbox path; every caller goes
   through it. Go's `monitor.SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox` stops mapping a worktree
   to `~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/<name>` and appends a fixed relative segment
   instead. Python's `config.sandbox_config_dir()` does the same. `_cache_root()`
   drops out of sandbox resolution entirely.
2. Ungate provisioning. `worktree_cmd._maybe_auto_sandbox_bind` stops consulting
   `config.project_is_self_dev`. Creating the dir, writing its self-ignoring
   `.gitignore`, and running the project's `post-worktree-create` hook happen for
   every project.
3. Migrate. Rename each `~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/e-NNN` whose worktree still
   exists into that worktree. Same filesystem, so a rename, not a copy. Add
   provision-on-miss to the resolver as the backstop for pre-change worktrees and
   for sandboxes already gone.
4. Delete the XDG injection and `sandbox bind` with it — AFTER the check below.
5. Documentation. CLAUDE.md's "Self-dev DB sandbox" section describes the cache
   location, the `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` injection and a manual `endless-sandbox
   destroy` that will all be gone.

## The one thing to verify before deleting the injection

`bind`'s own comment gives two justifications. The first — "the Python CLI
resolves its default config dir from XDG_CONFIG_HOME" — appears already
unreachable: `config.apply_db_choice("sandbox")` computes the dir directly and
reads `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, never `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, and E-1429's gate refuses to run
in a self-dev worktree without an explicit `--db`, so the XDG-derived default is
never consulted there.

The second justification is the live one: it "keeps Go config.json/log reads on
the sandbox even when a binary is invoked with a cwd outside the worktree."
`--config-dir` threading covers deliberate callers. Find out whether anything
relies on ambient inheritance instead, and cover those explicitly before the
injection goes. If something does, that is a finding worth reporting, not a
reason to keep the injection by default.

## Scale, as of 2026-08-13

137 worktrees under `.endless/worktrees/`; 126 sandboxes under
`~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/` totalling 102 MB. Roughly two dozen of those
sandboxes have no surviving worktree — orphans from worktrees already reaped,
including one `worktree-e-1449` from a superseded naming scheme. In-worktree
placement makes that class of orphan structurally impossible, which is a
secondary win worth stating in the commit.

## Interaction with E-1963

E-1963 removes the sandbox tooling rot. Its item 3 (CLAUDE.md documenting
`endless-sandbox destroy`) is subsumed by this task's step 5 if this lands first.
Its decision about deleting the ephemeral `run`/`enter`/`prune` path is
independent and should not be folded in here.

payload.title: Per-worktree sandboxes live inside the worktree and die with it
payload.description: A worktree's sandbox lives at `<worktree>/.endless/sandbox/`, gitignored, with a lifetime exactly equal to the worktree's — not under the XDG cache root. In-tree because the sandbox holds files a task is exercised against (throwaway DB, fixture spreadsheet, OpenAPI doc) that get opened and edited in the IDE already holding the worktree; the cache root was also wrong on XDG's own terms, which define cache as deletable without loss. Worktree-lifetime because it makes orphans structurally impossible rather than managed: 126 sandboxes, 102 MB, roughly two dozen already orphaned when this was decided. Anything that must outlive the worktree does not belong in a sandbox — commit it. Consequences: provisioning becomes universal, `self_dev` is retained only for endless's own DB routing, resolution becomes composition with no new env var, and the `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` injection and `sandbox bind` are deleted.

# Sandboxes for every project — brainstorm synthesis

## The reframing that did the work

The seed described one word doing two jobs: per-worktree storage (universal) and
`endless.db` routing (endless-only), conflated because the second was implemented
as the delivery mechanism for the first and the first inherited its `self_dev`
gate. That framing is right about the defect but understates the fix.

Mike's correction: the split is not universal-storage vs. endless-only-routing.
It is that a sandbox's *contents* are the project's business. Endless declares it
needs `endless.db`; a hypothetical WhackyWidgets declares it needs `ww.duckdb`.
There is then no Job A and Job B — there is one job, isolated per-worktree state,
and endless is simply one of its clients.

That dissolves the gate rather than relocating it. A downstream project's endless
commands reach the real ledger not because a flag permits it, but because that
project never asked for `endless.db` to be sandboxed. `self_dev` does not gate
sandbox provisioning and does not need a replacement meaning: it keeps the jobs
it already had (pinning the land's binary, applying endless's own schema changes,
suppressing the Go jobs runner, validating `--db`) and stops being consulted in
one place.

## What was decided

Recorded as ED-1554; implementation is E-1964.

**Location.** `<worktree>/.endless/sandbox/`. The XDG cache root was wrong on its
own terms — cache is defined as deletable at any moment without loss, which is
false of files a task needs in order to be verified and hostile if a project puts
credentials there. In-tree wins over any other out-of-tree location because these
files get opened and edited in the IDE that already has the worktree open.

**Lifetime equals the worktree's.** Deliberately accepted, not a side effect. It
makes orphans structurally impossible instead of managed: worktrees are already
reaped after a grace period, so no prune, no orphan scan, no manual destroy.
Anything that must outlive the worktree does not belong in a sandbox — commit it.

**Contents: empty dir, project's hook fills it, no seeding.** Endless cannot know
which of a main checkout's files a task needs, and copying is the exact failure
sandboxes exist to prevent — a worktree quietly pointed at the real database or a
live account. The `post-worktree-create` hook is the declaration; no config
manifest in this increment.

**Resolution by composition, not injection.** In-tree placement makes the path a
fixed relative segment from the worktree root, so no environment variable is
needed and none is introduced. Behind one resolver function, so a project-declared
override can be added later as a branch inside it rather than a new mechanism.
That seam earns its keep on day one for the rare project whose task-exercising
files are themselves a git repo.

**The `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` injection is deleted**, and `sandbox bind` with it.

**Out-of-tree override, per project.** For strict build hermeticity, `git clean`
in CI, or monorepo tooling that walks everything. Project level, never worktree
level.

**Migration by rename.** 126 existing sandboxes, 102 MB, attached to 137 live
worktrees. Both paths under `$HOME`, so this is a rename per worktree, plus
provision-on-miss in the resolver as backstop.

## Corrections made during the discussion, worth preserving

**"Hijack" was imprecise, then earned.** `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is a standardized
affordance used as intended — per-process, a process finds its own config. What
endless does is write it into Claude Code's session-wide `env` block, so every
child of the session inherits it for the session's life. The affordance is
per-invocation configuration; it was used as ambient policy. Defensible while
endless owned the only repo it applied to; short-sighted as a design that would
have to generalize, and chosen because Python already read that variable.

**The injection may already be vestigial.** `apply_db_choice("sandbox")` computes
the config dir directly and never reads `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, and E-1429's gate
refuses to run in a self-dev worktree without an explicit `--db`, so the
XDG-derived default is unreachable there. If that holds, this task deletes the
injection rather than teaching Python anything new. One case still needs checking
before deletion: a binary invoked with a cwd outside the worktree.

**"Don't migrate" was wrong.** Proposed on the grounds that sandbox contents are
throwaway. They are throwaway relative to the real ledger, not to a session
mid-task, and skipping migration would have knee-capped 126 sandboxes at once.

**A rejected framing: naming.** Argued "sandbox" describes isolation-from-real and
therefore misdescribes the storage job. Wrong — isolation-from-real describes all
of it. The distinction did not exist.

**Two lines of speculation abandoned.** Sandboxes holding throwaway git checkouts
(over-read from an agreement that "sandbox" meant more than config); and seeding a
new sandbox from the main checkout.

## Deliberately out of scope

- **No sandbox for the main checkout.** Sandboxes stay 1-to-1 with worktrees and
  worktrees 1-to-1 with tasks. Collapsing the two is what keeps this simple, and
  the complexity of separating them was already judged YAGNI.
- **No declaration manifest.** The hook is the declaration.
- **The `just verify` asymmetry.** The recipe runs main's Python against the
  worktree's sandbox, so a Python-side change is verified against landed code
  while a Go-side change is verified against candidate. Real, and ruled WONTFIX:
  the fix is complex and Python is slated for a port to Go, so fixing it in
  Python only delays the port.
- **The E-1958 blocks E-1957 relation.** Left in place; determining whether it is
  real costs more than waiting for this to land.

## Follow-ups spawned

- **E-1964** — the implementation, with ordering, the pre-deletion check, and
  migration scale in its analysis.
- **ED-1554** — the placement and lifetime decision.
- **E-1963** — sandbox tooling rot found while looking: every error string names
  an `endless-sandbox` binary that does not exist, the ephemeral non-worktree
  sandbox path (`run`, `enter`, `prune`) is live code despite having been judged
  YAGNI and dropped from the documented surface, and CLAUDE.md instructs a
  command that cannot be run. Includes the observation that deleting `run`/`enter`
  strands the E-1162 refusal gate, since nothing else sets `ENDLESS_SANDBOX`.
- **E-1859, reopened to `revisit`** — surfaced by a tangent that turned out to be
  a real defect. Automatic triage never fires from a self-dev worktree, which is
  where nearly every task is filed; the inline path takes no lease and races the
  sweep once that is fixed; child failures go to DEVNULL; the 15-minute interval
  was never specified; and the reset message offers `--keep-status` as an undo
  rather than naming the model call it would skip. Five fixes, ordered, in its
  plan.

# Plan: remove the sandbox tooling rot

Decision taken 2026-08-13 (Mike): **delete the ephemeral-sandbox commands.**
Not "decide whether to" — the analysis framed it as an open question and it is
not one. Nothing in code, tests, the justfile or docs invokes `run`, `enter` or
`prune`; every reference found is in historical plan documents. Mike believed the
feature had already been removed. E-1114's plan records it actively biting: a
leaked `enter` subshell survived for hours writing into an already-destroyed
sandbox, leaving him in a destroy/enter loop until he killed the Go parent by
hand.

A note on the word, since it caused confusion: the *sandboxes* `run` creates are
ephemeral (auto-destroyed on exit). The code producing them is not. Everything
below is about deleting that code.

## 1. Delete the ephemeral-sandbox commands

Remove the `run`, `enter` and `prune` cases from the dispatcher and their usage
lines, then the files behind them: `run.go`, `enter.go`, `enter_inject.go`,
`prune.go`, `orphan.go`, `supervisor.go`, `livewriters.go`, with their tests
(`enter_inject_test.go`, `livewriters_test.go`, and the run/enter/prune portions
of `sandbox_test.go`).

Falling out of `sandbox.go`: `modeEphemeral` and `modeKeep` become unreferenced
once `list.go` no longer distinguishes them. So does `Sandbox.Env()` — its only
callers are `run.go` and `enter.go`. Delete it; see item 2 for what that implies.

`list.go` keeps `stateOrphaned` only if orphan detection still means something
after `prune` is gone. It should not: every surviving sandbox is persistent and
bound to a worktree, so the state collapses. Simplify `list` accordingly rather
than leaving a state nothing can produce.

Also remove `init`'s `--mode seed` and `--mode clone`. Both hard-exit "not yet
implemented"; a flag that only ever errors is not an affordance. Note in the
commit that this closes out the E-1087 deep-clone idea as unbuilt.

## 2. Decide the fate of the E-1162 refusal gate

`Sandbox.Env()` is the only thing that sets `ENDLESS_SANDBOX`, and `bind` never
writes it. Its sole consumer is the E-1162 refusal gate in the Python CLI, which
makes project-bound subcommands refuse when the variable is set. Delete `Env()`
and nothing can ever set it, so the gate becomes unreachable code guarding a
situation that can no longer arise — you can no longer be inside an ephemeral
sandbox subshell.

**Recommendation: delete the gate and `test_sandbox_gate.py` with it.** The
alternative — re-keying it onto something that still exists — is only worth doing
if the hazard survives the deletion, and it does not.

Flag to Mike if implementation turns up any other consumer.

## 3. Fix the binary name in everything that survives

Every error and usage string in the package is prefixed `endless-sandbox <cmd>:`.
No such binary exists; the surface is `endless-go sandbox <cmd>`. Fix in the
survivors — `init.go`, `bind.go`, `list.go`, `destroy.go`, `sandbox.go` — after
the deletions, so the edit is not spent on files about to be removed.

## 4. Documentation

CLAUDE.md's "Self-dev DB sandbox" section instructs `endless-sandbox destroy
e-NNN`, which cannot be run.

Check E-1964 first. It rewrites that whole section (sandboxes move into the
worktree, die with it, and manual destroy stops existing). If E-1964 has landed,
this item is already handled — do not write a correction that E-1964 deletes. If
it has not, fix the command name only and leave the surrounding prose alone.

## Sequencing against E-1964

Both touch `internal/sandboxcmd`. E-1964 deletes `bind` outright and rewrites
path resolution. This task is the cheaper and less contentious of the two, so
landing it first shrinks E-1964's surface. If E-1964 lands first instead, skip
`bind.go` in item 3 — it will not exist.

## Verification

`just build` and `just test` both clean. `endless-go sandbox --help` lists only
the surviving commands. A deliberate error from each survivor names `endless-go
sandbox`, not `endless-sandbox`. Grep the repo for `endless-sandbox` and for
`ENDLESS_SANDBOX` — outside `.endless/` historical documents, both should be
gone.

# E-1962 — implementation record

## The empirical finding that decided the design

Claude Code Desktop told Mike `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` "does not exist". It does.
Both surfaces were dumped on 2026-08-13:

| var | terminal (CC 2.1.222) | Desktop app |
|---|---|---|
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` | `cli` | *absent* |
| `CLAUDECODE` | `1` | *absent* |
| `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_VERSION` | *absent* | `0.3.222` |
| `__CFBundleIdentifier` | `com.apple.Terminal` | `com.anthropic.claudefordesktop` |

Desktop hosts the agent through the **Agent SDK**, not the CLI, so none of the
CLI's own variables reach a hook subprocess there. That gap is the discriminator.

## What shipped

`internal/hookcmd/surface.go` — new. `terminalSurface()` returns
`os.Getenv("CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT") == "cli"`.

**Allow-list, not deny-list.** A deny-list must name every surface that exists,
and the cost of missing one is that a brand-new Claude Code host silently starts
enforcing a contract nobody chose for it. The allow-list's failure direction is
the opposite — an unrecognized surface lands ungated, which is where everything
except the terminal is meant to be.

**One variable only.** `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_VERSION` was rejected as a second
signal: it says "an SDK hosts this agent," not "this is not a terminal," and a
terminal-launched SDK/background session could plausibly carry it. Treating it as
disqualifying would switch the channel off for terminal sessions that should
have it.

`internal/hookcmd/claude.go` — `reportChannelOn` gained the check. Placement is
the whole point: that one function feeds the SessionStart rule, the PostToolUse
reinforcement, AND the Stop gate, so E-1953's told-iff-gated invariant holds
automatically. Gating a single call site would have satisfied "Desktop isn't
blocked" while still telling Desktop to report.

Surface and `report_gate` are **independent vetoes** — the product's decision and
the project's, both must say yes. Never an override: a terminal session in a
`"report_gate": false` project (Endless's own checkout) stays off.

`internal/hookcmd/claim_handoff.go` — the handoff's `report_gate` var is now
`terminalSurface() && ReportGateEnabledForCwd(...)`. This renders in the
*claiming session's own hook*, so the environment read is that session's.

## Deliberately NOT changed

`src/endless/task_cmd.py:_handoff_report_gate()` (the **spawn** handoff).
`endless task spawn` opens a tmux window, so the session it describes is a
terminal by construction whatever surface ran the command. Gating it on the
caller's environment would strip the contract from terminal sessions spawned
from Desktop. `tests/tasks/e-1962-verify.sh` asserts `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`
never appears in `task_cmd.py` so this stays deliberate rather than drifting.

## Regression caught and fixed

`tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh` drives the real hook from a **bare shell**
(`esu && ./tests/tasks/...`), where `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` is absent — 12 of
its assertions started failing. The script impersonates a terminal Claude
session, so it now `export`s the environment it is impersonating. Verified: 69/69
from a bare shell.

## Verification

`./tests/tasks/e-1962-verify.sh` — 17 checks, all passing. Both surfaces are
simulated by environment alone (`env CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=cli` vs `env -u`),
which is not a stub of Desktop but a reproduction of the exact condition.

- Part 0: build, vet, `go test ./internal/hookcmd/...` (fail-fast).
- Part 1: all three consumers, real hook binary → sandbox DB. Terminal injects
  the rule / blocks an unreported reply / fires the reinforcement; Desktop is
  silent on every one.
- Part 2: terminal + `report_gate:false` → still off (veto, not override).
- Part 3: claim handoff gated; Python spawn handoff provably left alone.
- Part 4: E-1953's suite re-run end-to-end from a bare shell.

Project-wide: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` clean;
`just test` 1357 passed.

## Found along the way — filed as E-1965

Two verify suites fail on **baseline main**, unrelated to this change:
`e-1901-verify.sh` (17 failures, asserts contracts E-1953 retired) and
`e-1822-verify.sh` (1 failure, fixture payload never gained E-1953's
`report_gate` var). Shared root cause: E-1953's rewrite left them stale.

## Open question for later

The terminal-only rule is hardcoded, matching Mike's "currently" framing — a
product policy that may widen, not a per-project knob. If a second consumer ever
wants a different set, promote it to a `report_gate_surfaces` config key rather
than growing conditionals in `terminalSurface`.

payload.title: Gate the Python wind-down report nudge on report_gate
payload.description: task_cmd.py's _is_report_wind_down nudge (~line 2944) prints 'Route this handoff ... through endless task report' whenever _running_under_agent() is true, without ever consulting project_report_gate(). It fires in Endless's own checkout, which ships "report_gate": false — observed on E-1962's own 'task update --status unverified'. Same class as the PostToolUse defect E-1953 fixed on the Go side (TestReportReinforcement_RespectsTheSwitch): an instruction pointing at a channel that will not gate this session. The Python emitter was missed. Surface is already covered incidentally — _running_under_agent keys on CLAUDECODE=1, which the Desktop app does not set — so this is the config-key half only.

# Plan: remove the sandbox tooling rot

Decision taken 2026-08-13 (Mike): **delete the ephemeral-sandbox commands.**
Not "decide whether to" — the analysis framed it as an open question and it is
not one. Nothing in code, tests, the justfile or docs invokes `run`, `enter` or
`prune`; every reference found is in historical plan documents. Mike believed the
feature had already been removed. E-1114's plan records it actively biting: a
leaked `enter` subshell survived for hours writing into an already-destroyed
sandbox, leaving him in a destroy/enter loop until he killed the Go parent by
hand.

A note on the word, since it caused confusion: the *sandboxes* `run` creates are
ephemeral (auto-destroyed on exit). The code producing them is not. Everything
below is about deleting that code.

## 1. Delete the ephemeral-sandbox commands

Remove the `run`, `enter` and `prune` cases from the dispatcher and their usage
lines, then the files behind them: `run.go`, `enter.go`, `enter_inject.go`,
`prune.go`, `orphan.go`, `supervisor.go`, `livewriters.go`, with their tests
(`enter_inject_test.go`, `livewriters_test.go`, and the run/enter/prune portions
of `sandbox_test.go`).

Falling out of `sandbox.go`: `modeEphemeral` and `modeKeep` become unreferenced
once `list.go` no longer distinguishes them. So does `Sandbox.Env()` — its only
callers are `run.go` and `enter.go`. Delete it; see item 2 for what that implies.

`list.go` keeps `stateOrphaned` only if orphan detection still means something
after `prune` is gone. It should not: every surviving sandbox is persistent and
bound to a worktree, so the state collapses. Simplify `list` accordingly rather
than leaving a state nothing can produce.

Also remove `init`'s `--mode seed` and `--mode clone`. Both hard-exit "not yet
implemented"; a flag that only ever errors is not an affordance. Note in the
commit that this closes out the E-1087 deep-clone idea as unbuilt.

## 2. Delete the E-1162 refusal gate

`Sandbox.Env()` is the only thing that sets `ENDLESS_SANDBOX`, and `bind` never
writes it. Its sole consumer is the E-1162 refusal gate in the Python CLI, which
makes project-bound subcommands refuse when the variable is set. Delete `Env()`
and nothing can ever set it, so the gate becomes unreachable code guarding a
situation that can no longer arise — you can no longer be inside an ephemeral
sandbox subshell.

**Decided by Mike, 2026-08-13: delete the gate and `test_sandbox_gate.py` with
it.** Do not re-key it onto something that still exists; the hazard does not
survive the deletion, so there is nothing left to guard.

If implementation turns up another consumer of `ENDLESS_SANDBOX`, that is a
finding to report before proceeding — not grounds to keep the gate on your own
judgment.

## 3. Fix the binary name in everything that survives

Every error and usage string in the package is prefixed `endless-sandbox <cmd>:`.
No such binary exists; the surface is `endless-go sandbox <cmd>`. Fix in the
survivors — `init.go`, `bind.go`, `list.go`, `destroy.go`, `sandbox.go` — after
the deletions, so the edit is not spent on files about to be removed.

## 4. Documentation

CLAUDE.md's "Self-dev DB sandbox" section instructs `endless-sandbox destroy
e-NNN`, which cannot be run.

Check E-1964 first. It rewrites that whole section (sandboxes move into the
worktree, die with it, and manual destroy stops existing). If E-1964 has landed,
this item is already handled — do not write a correction that E-1964 deletes. If
it has not, fix the command name only and leave the surrounding prose alone.

## Sequencing against E-1964

Both touch `internal/sandboxcmd`. E-1964 deletes `bind` outright and rewrites
path resolution. This task is the cheaper and less contentious of the two, so
landing it first shrinks E-1964's surface. If E-1964 lands first instead, skip
`bind.go` in item 3 — it will not exist.

## Verification

`just build` and `just test` both clean. `endless-go sandbox --help` lists only
the surviving commands. A deliberate error from each survivor names `endless-go
sandbox`, not `endless-sandbox`. Grep the repo for `endless-sandbox` and for
`ENDLESS_SANDBOX` — outside `.endless/` historical documents, both should be
gone.

# E-1966 — plan

## The defect

`src/endless/task_cmd.py`, the wind-down nudge (the function guarded by
`_is_report_wind_down`, ~line 2944). It prints:

```
▸ Report through the command, not prose. Route this handoff — and all
  further status reporting for the rest of this session — through:
      endless task report E-NNNN --draft-file <path>
```

Its only guard is `_running_under_agent() or agent_view_requested()`. It never
consults `project_report_gate()`, so it fires in projects that have switched the
channel off — observed firing at E-1962's own `task update --status unverified`
inside Endless's own checkout, which ships `"report_gate": false`.

## Why it matters, precisely

This is the defect E-1953 already fixed once on the Go side. See
`TestReportReinforcement_RespectsTheSwitch` in
`internal/hookcmd/claude_report_test.go`, whose comment states the distinction
this must preserve:

> An instruction may outlive its enforcement harmlessly ("send it verbatim" is
> still reasonable advice with no gate behind it). A factual assertion about
> enforcement may not: a session told it is being checked when it is not learns
> that Endless's statements about its own behavior cannot be relied on.

The Python emitter was missed in that sweep. Its wording is squarely an
instruction *plus* a claim about scope ("all further status reporting for the
rest of this session"), directed at a session no Stop hook will check.

## Scope

**Config-key half only.** The agent-harness half (E-1962) is already covered
here incidentally: `_running_under_agent()` keys on `CLAUDECODE == "1"`, which
Claude Code Desktop does not set (verified 2026-08-13 — Desktop exports
`CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_VERSION` and no `CLAUDECODE`). So this nudge cannot reach an
unsupported harness today.

Whether to *also* route it through `agent_env.supported()` is a judgment call
worth making deliberately rather than by omission. Argument for: `CLAUDECODE` is
a proxy, `agent_env` is the deliberate answer, and the proxy will drift. Argument
against: `_running_under_agent`'s docstring says it is "used only to surface a
stronger anti-rationalization variant of the verb-gate error — never to gate
behavior", and this call site already violates that; widening it further compounds
a layering mistake instead of fixing it.

Recommendation: fix the config-key half now, and if the harness half is wanted,
do it by having this call site ask `agent_env` directly rather than by teaching
`_running_under_agent` a second job.

## Implementation sketch

1. In the nudge, after the existing guards, add the project-gate check —
   the same resolution `_handoff_report_gate()` already performs:

   ```python
   from endless import config
   root = config.enclosing_project_root()
   if root is not None and not config.project_report_gate(root):
       return
   ```

   Note the `root is None` direction: **fail open**, matching
   `_handoff_report_gate`'s documented reasoning — the channel ships on, and an
   unresolvable root is ignorance rather than an opt-out.

2. Consider extracting that three-line resolution into a shared helper rather
   than a second copy; `_handoff_report_gate()` is already exactly it. Reusing it
   verbatim is probably right, and its name would want widening.

## Verification

- New pytest: the nudge is silent when the enclosing project sets
  `"report_gate": false`, and still fires when it is unset or true. Model on
  the existing report-gate config tests.
- Manual, from this repo (which ships the gate off):
  `endless task update E-NNNN --status unverified` prints no report nudge.

## Do not

Do not fix this by softening the wording so the claim becomes true-ish. The
sentence is correct where the gate is on; the bug is that it is emitted where the
gate is off.

payload.title: Refuse spawn on a task a prior session already worked, and make that history durable
payload.description: `endless task spawn` creates a second session on a task a prior session already worked, because its multi-owner refusal is scoped to LIVE sessions and the prior session is usually `ended`. Keying the guard on `sessions.active_task_id` would not fix it either — that column is NULL once the binding is released. The only durable record is `session_tasks`, and it cannot answer 'who owned this' today: `relation_id` is written once at first touch and never revised, so a session that revisits a task and then claims it stays `revisited` forever. Fix both halves together: key `session_tasks` on `(session_id, task_id, relation_id)` so ownership history is append-only rather than overwritten, then refuse a spawn whose target already has a `goal` row, with an error naming `endless session resume <id>` as the intended path.
payload.analysis:
# Evidence

Gathered 2026-08-13 after Mike accidentally spawned a second session on E-1859
instead of resuming the one that had worked it.

## Session→task binding is treated as 1-to-1 in practice, enforced nowhere

Writers create duplicates freely. `task claim` checks the task's status and
resolves a session; it never asks whether another session already holds the
task. `task bind` sets `active_task_id` with no ownership check at all.

Readers all assume exactly one and silently pick when there is more. Three
places resolve task → session, each ending `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`:

- `monitor.resumeByTask` — `WHERE active_task_id = ? AND session_id IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY last_activity DESC LIMIT 1`
- `monitor`'s session_focus query — `JOIN sessions bg ON bg.active_task_id =
  coord.active_task_id ... LIMIT 1`
- `monitor`'s tmux_lookup query — same shape

So `endless session resume E-NNNN` takes the most recently active session and
gives no signal that it discarded another.

The only place the invariant is named is `release_item`'s refusal when a
different LIVE session owns the task. One guard, on the release path, protecting
an invariant nothing else maintains.

## Why the existing spawn guard did not fire

`task spawn` already refuses when another session owns the task — but the check
is scoped to LIVE sessions. ES-1046 was `ended`, so there was no live owner and
the spawn proceeded.

Keying the guard on `sessions.active_task_id` would not fix this either: by the
time the spawn ran, that column was already NULL for E-1859 (an earlier
`task reopen` had released it). The only durable record that ES-1046 had ever
worked the task was `session_tasks`.

## Why session_tasks cannot answer "who owned this" today

`session_tasks` has `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id)` and a `relation_id` FK to
`session_task_relations` (1 goal, 2 surfaced, 3 revisited). Per the schema
comment the relation is "set once at capture time by the task-mutation
executors (claim→goal, create/import→surfaced, else→revisited) and never
changed on a later touch."

So a session that first revisits a task and later claims it keeps `revisited`
forever. Observed on E-1859:

    996 → surfaced;  1029, 1043, 1046, 1070 → revisited

ES-1046 held `active_task_id = 1859` and is nevertheless recorded as
`revisited`. The table can say who saw a task; it cannot say who owned it.

## Mike's design call

Put `relation_id` in the key — `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id, relation_id)` —
rather than making the existing row's relation upgradeable. Upgrading would
overwrite "saw it" with "owned it"; the composite key keeps both, so the history
reads "saw it, then owned it."

This also serves the deliberate fresh-context case: when a task is
intentionally moved to a new session for a clean context, null the old session's
`active_task_id` and write a `goal` row for the new session. The old session's
`goal` row survives, so "which sessions ever owned E-NNNN" stays answerable.

Open question for implementation: with the relation in the key, does a `goal`
row mean "owned it at some point" or "owns it now"? Append-only ("at some
point") is what recovery needs.

payload.title: Make task reopen stop silently destroying a session's task binding
payload.description: `endless task reopen` releases the session→task binding as a deliberate side effect, but announces nothing — it prints only the status change, while its own help says 'Metadata-only: no worktree creation, no session binding'. The only record is the user-machine log and a `task.released` ledger event. Consequences: `session resume E-NNNN` resolves through `active_task_id`, so clearing it makes the prior session unfindable by task; and the move to `revisit` takes the task out of spawn's done-ish gate, so a later plain `spawn` proceeds with no prompt. Per Mike: keep the release but require `--force`, and announce it either way. Also reconsider spawn's error message, which offers 'run task reopen first' as one of two recovery routes — the one that leads here.
payload.analysis:
# Evidence

Observed 2026-08-13. `endless task reopen E-1859` destroyed ES-1046's
session→task binding without saying so, and neither the user nor the agent that
ran it knew until the loss was investigated hours later.

## What it does

`_reopen_task_core`'s own docstring: "Validates eligibility, releases any
lingering session→task binding, and emits `task.status_changed`."

So the release is intentional. What is not intentional is that it is invisible.
The command printed only:

    Updated E-1859 (Implement the triage job that evaluat...) (text: present):
    • Status: assumed -> revisit

No mention of the released binding. The only record is
`~/.config/endless/log/user-machine.jsonl`:

    ts 2026-08-13T10:05:20Z  session 6b6413b7-...  old_active_task_id 1859
    reason "release"  caller "events.execTaskReleased"

plus a `task.released` event in the ledger.

## The help text says the opposite

`task reopen --help`: "Metadata-only: no worktree creation, no session
binding." That reads as "does not create a binding." It also destroys one.

## Why it matters beyond the surprise

Two consequences, both realised in the incident:

1. `session resume E-NNNN` (the task-keyed form, `monitor.resumeByTask`)
   resolves through `active_task_id`. Clearing it makes the prior session
   unfindable by task. Resume by session id still works, but only if you
   already know the id.

2. Reopen moves the task to `revisit`, which is NOT in
   `_CLAIM_REQUIRES_FORCE`. On `assumed`, `task spawn` refuses with:

       E-NNNN is 'assumed'; pass --reopen to reopen-and-spawn, or run
       `endless task reopen E-NNNN` first.

   `--reopen` inherits the most-applicable prior ended session by default —
   the correct outcome. The other branch that same message offers, running
   `task reopen` first, drops the binding AND moves the status out of the
   guarded set, so a subsequent plain `spawn` proceeds silently. The error
   message routes the user into the trap.

## Mike's design call

Keep the ability to release, but require `--force` for it.

Whatever the gate, the release must be announced — one line naming the session
and task released. A silent destructive side effect on a command documented as
"metadata-only" is the core defect; the flag is the secondary fix.

Consider also whether that error message should stop offering the bare
`task reopen` branch, given where it leads.

fields.text:
# E-1962 — implementation record

## The empirical finding

Claude Code Desktop told Mike `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` "does not exist". It does.
Both harnesses were dumped on 2026-08-13:

| var | Claude Code, terminal (2.1.222) | Claude Code Desktop |
|---|---|---|
| `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` | `cli` | *absent* |
| `CLAUDECODE` | `1` | *absent* |
| `AI_AGENT` | `claude-code_2-1-222_agent` | *absent* |
| `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_VERSION` | *absent* | `0.3.222` |
| `__CFBundleIdentifier` | `com.apple.Terminal` | `com.anthropic.claudefordesktop` |

Desktop hosts the agent through the **Agent SDK**, not the CLI, so none of the
CLI's own variables reach a subprocess there. That gap is the discriminator.

Directly useful to **E-1505**, which already guessed at this: it calls for
`platform='claude-desktop'` on the session row and names `AI_AGENT` as the
signal. `AI_AGENT` turns out to be absent on Desktop, so it cannot carry that;
`agentenv.Detect()` now can.

## What shipped

### `internal/agentenv` (new package)

Answers "which agent harness is running Endless, and do we support it?" — an
identity plus a support flag, not a boolean, because the shape has to hold for
Codex CLI and whatever comes next.

- `Detect() ID` → `claude_cli` | `claude_desktop` | `unknown`
- `Supported() bool` → allow-list; today `{claude_cli}`
- `Label(ID) string` → human phrasing for the guide banner
- `DetectWith`/`SupportedWith` take a `Lookup` so detectors are testable without
  mutating the process environment.

Named `agentenv`, not `agent`: Endless already calls the background workers under
an epic "agents".

**Detector table is the extension point** — a new harness is one row plus an ID
constant. Deliberately **no Codex CLI row yet**: a detector never checked against
a real `env` dump of that harness is a guess, and a guess fails silently (the
harness is misidentified and the support flag lands wrong either way). The
missing input is a dump, not code.

**Ordering matters** and is pinned by a test: `claude_cli`'s positive match runs
first, because `claude_desktop` is detected partly by ABSENCE. A terminal session
that happens to carry an SDK version stays `claude_cli`.

`claude_desktop` uses two signals with honest limits — the bundle id is proof but
macOS-only; the SDK version is portable but really means "an Agent SDK hosts
this". Neither is load-bearing while everything except `claude_cli` is
unsupported; both should be re-derived from a fresh dump under E-1505.

`src/endless/agent_env.py` mirrors it, thin, for `endless guide`. The Go side is
the one that enforces; a test asserts the two tables have not drifted.

### What is gated

**The Claude hooks** — `reportChannelOn` in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` gained
`supportedAgent()`. Placement is the point: that one function feeds the
SessionStart rule, the PostToolUse reinforcement, AND the Stop gate, so E-1953's
told-iff-gated invariant holds automatically. Harness and `report_gate` are
**independent vetoes** — the product's decision and the project's — never an
override: a terminal session in a `"report_gate": false` project stays off.

`internal/hookcmd/claim_handoff.go` — same AND. It renders in the *claiming
session's own hook*, so the environment read is that session's.

**`endless guide`** — an unsupported harness gets a banner telling it to ignore
Endless (naming E-1505), and the guide body is withheld: printing it would
contradict the banner in the same breath, since the guide's entire content is
instructions.

Nothing else. A hook fires inside the session and speaks to the agent, which is
where an unsupported harness gets mis-instructed. A user running `endless task
add` from Desktop is a person using a tool.

### The one deliberate asymmetry

The guide banner fails **open** on `unknown`; the hooks fail **closed**. `unknown`
is overwhelmingly a human at a shell prompt — the docs tell you to run `endless
guide` — and refusing them breaks a real workflow to defend against a harness
that may not exist. Getting it wrong here costs an unrecognized agent one guide
it should have ignored; the other way costs every human the guide.

## Deliberately NOT changed

`src/endless/task_cmd.py:_handoff_report_gate()` (the **spawn** handoff).
`endless task spawn` opens a tmux window, so the session it describes is a
terminal Claude Code one by construction whatever harness ran the command.
Gating it on the caller's environment would strip the contract from terminal
sessions spawned from Desktop. The verify script asserts `task_cmd.py` contains
no harness detection, so this stays deliberate rather than drifting.

## Deferred

Project-configurable harness support (`report_gate_surfaces` or similar) waits on
**E-1505** — there is no second supported harness to configure until then. Linked
`relates_to`.

## Verification

`./tests/tasks/e-1962-verify.sh` — 23 checks, all passing. Both harnesses are
simulated by environment alone, which is not a stub but a reproduction of the
observed conditions.

- Part 0: build, vet, `go test ./internal/agentenv/...` + `./internal/hookcmd/...`,
  `pytest tests/test_agent_env.py` (fail-fast).
- Part 1: all three hook consumers, real binary → sandbox DB. Terminal injects
  the rule / blocks an unreported reply / fires the reinforcement; Desktop silent
  on every one.
- Part 2: terminal + `report_gate:false` → still off (veto, not override).
- Part 3: claim handoff gated; Python spawn handoff provably left alone.
- Part 4: guide banner on Desktop; guide body withheld; terminal and bare-shell
  both still print.

# Plan: refuse spawn on an already-worked task, and make ownership durable

Two halves that ship together: the guard needs a durable record of who owned a
task, and that record has no consumer without the guard.

## Decision 1 — `goal` is append-only and means "owned it at some point"

Not "owns it now." Current ownership already has a representation
(`sessions.active_task_id`); a second one would drift from it, and the first
thing that drifts is the thing recovery depends on. A `goal` row is written when
a session claims and is never removed — not on release, not on reopen, not when
the session ends.

This is the decision the earlier analysis left open. Overturn it only if you
want `session_tasks` to answer "who owns this right now," which nothing needs.

## Decision 2 — backfill from the ledger

Existing `session_tasks` rows keep whatever relation they carry; the composite
key alone would leave every historical claim invisible to the guard, so the
guard would only protect tasks worked after this lands. That is the wrong way
round — the tasks most likely to be spawned-instead-of-resumed are old ones.

So: one-time backfill inserting a `goal` row for every `task.claimed` event in
the ledger. The ledger is authoritative for this and the events are already
there. If a claim predates the event kind and cannot be reconstructed, skip it
rather than guess; the guard degrades to "no record" for that task, which is
today's behavior, not a regression.

## Work

**Schema.** Replace `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id)` on `session_tasks` with
`UNIQUE(session_id, task_id, relation_id)`. The existing
`idx_session_tasks_task` index stays. Note the widened key means a session can
now hold several rows per task; every reader that assumed one row per
(session, task) must be checked — `session_tasks` is read by the task-detail
"Touched by" render and by session-scoped task listing, and both will need to
collapse duplicates or pick a display relation.

**Write path.** The task-mutation executors currently set the relation once at
capture time and never revise it. Change the claim path to additionally insert a
`goal` row (INSERT OR IGNORE, so re-claiming is idempotent) while leaving any
existing `surfaced`/`revisited` row untouched. The other two relations keep
their present write-once behavior.

**Guard.** `task spawn` refuses when the target has a `goal` row belonging to a
any session other than the one spawning. The message names the most recent such
session and the command to use:

    E-1859 was worked by session ES-1046. Resume it:
        endless session resume 1046
    To start a fresh session on this task anyway, pass --new-session.

List additional prior owners beneath when there is more than one. Refuse — do
not prompt, and do not silently inherit.

**Escape hatch.** `--new-session` already exists and already means "start a
fresh session instead of inheriting the prior ended session's restore context."
Extend it to plain `spawn` rather than inventing a second flag; per Mike, no new
`--force`.

## Sequencing

`task spawn`'s existing multi-owner refusal is scoped to LIVE sessions and stays
as-is — it covers a different case (someone is working this right now) and is
not superseded.

E-1968 (reopen's silent release) is independent and can land in either order.
Note only that reopen moves a task to `revisit`, which takes it out of spawn's
done-ish gate; this guard does not depend on that gate, so it holds either way.

## Verification

- A task with a prior `goal` row refuses a plain spawn and names the session.
- The same spawn with `--new-session` proceeds.
- A task never claimed by anyone spawns unchanged.
- Re-claiming a task the same session already owns inserts no duplicate row.
- A session that revisited a task and then claimed it shows BOTH relations.
- Post-backfill, E-1859 refuses a plain spawn and names ES-1046.

# Plan: stop `task reopen` silently destroying a session's task binding

`_reopen_task_core` releases the session→task binding on purpose and says
nothing about it. The command prints only the status change, while `task
reopen --help` says "Metadata-only: no worktree creation, no session binding" —
which reads as "does not create one" and is silent about destroying one.

## Decision 1 — gate the release behind `--force`, announce it either way

Mike's call: keep the ability to release, require `--force`.

Without the flag, refuse when a binding exists, naming what would be lost:

    E-1859 is bound to session ES-1046. Reopening would release that binding,
    and `endless session resume E-1859` would no longer find it.
    Pass --force to reopen and release, or run `endless session resume 1046`
    to pick the work back up in its original session.

With the flag, proceed AND print one line recording what was released. The
announcement is not conditional on the flag — a `--force` that still hides the
effect is the same defect with an extra keystroke.

Reopening a task with no binding is unaffected: no gate, no message.

## Decision 2 — remove the `task reopen` branch from spawn's done-ish error

This is the question the analysis left open. Decided: remove it.

`task spawn` on an `assumed`/`confirmed`/`completed` task currently refuses with

    E-NNNN is '<status>'; pass --reopen to reopen-and-spawn, or run
    `endless task reopen E-NNNN` first.

The two branches are not equivalent. `--reopen` inherits the most-applicable
prior ended session, which is the outcome the user wants. Running `task reopen`
first releases the binding and moves the task to `revisit`, which is outside
`_CLAIM_REQUIRES_FORCE`, so the subsequent plain `spawn` proceeds with no prompt
at all. The message offers, as equal alternatives, the safe path and the one
that dismantles the guard that produced the message.

So the error keeps `--reopen` only. `task reopen` remains a first-class verb for
reopening WITHOUT spawning — it is simply no longer advertised as a way to get
past this particular refusal.

## Work

- `_reopen_task_core` takes a `force` parameter; refuse-with-message when a
  binding exists and force is false.
- Thread `--force` through the `task reopen` verb. `task spawn --reopen` already
  releases as part of its own flow; decide there whether it passes force
  implicitly (it should — the user has already asked for reopen-and-spawn, and
  its own liveness guard runs first) rather than making the composite command
  demand two flags.
- Emit the release announcement from the same place that emits the release, so
  it cannot be bypassed by a caller that forgets.
- Fix `task reopen --help` to say what it does to an existing binding.
- Edit spawn's done-ish refusal message per Decision 2.

## Verification

- `task reopen` on a bound task refuses and names the session.
- `task reopen --force` on a bound task succeeds and prints the release.
- `task reopen` on an unbound task is unchanged, no message.
- `task spawn --reopen` still works in one step without demanding `--force`.
- Spawn's done-ish refusal no longer mentions `task reopen`.
- `task reopen --help` describes the release.

# E-1966 — plan

Scope decided by Mike 2026-08-13: reimplement `_running_under_agent` on
`agent_env`, and add the missing `report_gate` check to the wind-down nudge.

## Two defects, one root

### 1. `_running_under_agent()` is a crude precursor of `agent_env`

`src/endless/task_cmd.py:228`:

```python
def _running_under_agent() -> bool:
    """True if invoked from an LLM agent harness.

    Today: Claude Code (sets CLAUDECODE=1). Extend as other harnesses are
    encountered. Used only to surface a stronger anti-rationalization variant
    of the verb-gate error — never to gate behavior.
    """
    import os
    return os.environ.get("CLAUDECODE") == "1"
```

Harness detection is its *only* job — and it is exactly the job
`src/endless/agent_env.py` now does properly (E-1962). Keeping both means two
answers to one question, and the `CLAUDECODE` one is the worse answer: it says
"some Claude Code", not which, and it misses every non-Claude harness the
docstring's own "extend as other harnesses are encountered" anticipates.

**The docstring is stale, not a constraint.** Written in E-1106 (2026-05-02),
when the function had exactly one caller: the verb-gate error message. E-1772
later added the wind-down nudge, which *does* gate behavior, and the docstring
was never updated. Do not treat "never to gate behavior" as a rule to preserve —
it is a description that stopped being true and should be rewritten.

Fix:

```python
def _running_under_agent() -> bool:
    """True if invoked from an LLM agent harness (any recognized one)."""
    from endless import agent_env
    return agent_env.detect() != agent_env.UNKNOWN
```

Note this is `detect() != UNKNOWN`, **not** `supported()`. The two callers want
"am I talking to an agent at all" — a verb-gate error phrased for an agent, and a
nudge aimed at an agent — not "is this harness supported". Since E-1962 the CLI
refuses unsupported harnesses at the group callback anyway, so by the time either
caller runs, a recognized harness is a supported one.

Check whether `agent_view_requested()` (`endless/agent_help.py`) overlaps; if it
is a second spelling of the same question, fold it in rather than leaving three.

### 2. The wind-down nudge ignores `report_gate`

Same file, the function guarded by `_is_report_wind_down` (~line 2944). It
prints:

```
▸ Report through the command, not prose. Route this handoff — and all
  further status reporting for the rest of this session — through:
      endless task report E-NNNN --draft-file <path>
```

Guarded only on `_running_under_agent() or agent_view_requested()`. It never
consults `project_report_gate()`, so it fires in projects that switched the
channel off — observed firing during E-1962's own `task update --status
unverified` inside Endless's own checkout, which ships `"report_gate": false`.

"The `report_gate` check" means exactly this: the per-project
`.endless/config.json` key, resolved nearest-first, that says whether the report
channel is live for this project. `config.project_report_gate(root)` is the
existing reader; `_handoff_report_gate()` in the same file is already a working
call site to copy.

This is the defect E-1953 fixed once on the Go side —
`TestReportReinforcement_RespectsTheSwitch` in
`internal/hookcmd/claude_report_test.go` — whose comment names what is at stake:

> An instruction may outlive its enforcement harmlessly ("send it verbatim" is
> still reasonable advice with no gate behind it). A factual assertion about
> enforcement may not: a session told it is being checked when it is not learns
> that Endless's statements about its own behavior cannot be relied on.

The Python emitter was missed in that sweep.

Fix — after the existing guards:

```python
from endless import config
root = config.enclosing_project_root()
if root is not None and not config.project_report_gate(root):
    return
```

`root is None` **fails open**, matching `_handoff_report_gate()`'s documented
reasoning: the channel ships on, and an unresolvable root is ignorance rather
than an opt-out.

`_handoff_report_gate()` already is those three lines. Reuse it rather than
writing a second copy; its name wants widening (it is no longer handoff-specific).

## Verification

- pytest: the nudge is silent when the enclosing project sets
  `"report_gate": false`, still fires when unset or true.
- pytest: `_running_under_agent()` is true for the Claude CLI environment and
  false for a bare shell, driven through `agent_env`'s detection rather than
  `CLAUDECODE` directly.
- Manual, from this repo (ships the gate off):
  `endless task update E-NNNN --status unverified` prints no report nudge.

## Do not

Do not fix the nudge by softening its wording so the claim becomes true-ish. The
sentence is correct where the gate is on; the bug is that it is emitted where the
gate is off.

# Plan: record who claimed a task, and refuse spawn when someone already did

Two halves that ship together: the guard needs a durable record of who claimed a
task, and that record has no consumer without the guard.

All decisions below are Mike's, taken 2026-08-13, except the three message
strings marked DRAFT — those are mine to propose and his to edit.

## Background: the relation labels

`session_tasks.relation_id` FKs to `session_task_relations`, whose rows render
as the labels in `task show`'s "Touched by:" block. Today: `Goal`, `Surfaced`,
`Revisited` — set once at capture time (claim→goal, create/import→surfaced,
else→revisited) and never revised.

The defect: a session that revisits a task and LATER claims it keeps
`Revisited` forever. Observed on E-1859, where ES-1046 held
`sessions.active_task_id = 1859` and still renders as `Revisited`. So nothing
can answer "which sessions ever claimed this task."

## Decision 1 — rename the relation `goal` → `claimed`

Per Mike: `Goal:` is a bad label because it cannot be reasoned about; `Claimed:`
says what actually happened. Rename the slug and the label together, in this
task rather than a follow-up.

Touches the `session_task_relations` seed rows, every reader that matches on the
slug, and the "Touched by:" render. Historical rows keep their id, so this is a
label change, not a data migration.

## Decision 2 — `claim` ADDS a row, it does not overwrite

Replace `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id)` on `session_tasks` with
`UNIQUE(session_id, task_id, relation_id)`. On claim, INSERT OR IGNORE a
`claimed` row while leaving any existing `surfaced`/`revisited` row untouched,
so the history reads "saw it, then claimed it" rather than replacing one fact
with the other. Re-claiming is idempotent.

`surfaced` and `revisited` keep their present write-once behavior.

Consequence to handle: a session may now hold several rows per task, so every
reader that assumed one row per (session, task) must collapse or pick a display
relation — the "Touched by:" render and session-scoped task listing at minimum.
Find them before changing the key, not after.

## Decision 3 — backfill, most expansive form

Without a backfill the guard protects only tasks claimed after this lands, which
is backwards: old tasks are the ones most likely to be spawned-instead-of-
resumed. So insert a `claimed` row for:

1. every `task.claimed` event in the ledger, and
2. every session whose `sessions.active_task_id` is currently set — catching
   claims the ledger may have missed.

Skip anything that cannot be reconstructed rather than guessing; that task falls
back to today's behavior, which is not a regression.

## The guard

`task spawn` refuses when the target has a `claimed` row belonging to any
session other than the one spawning. Refuse — do not prompt, do not silently
inherit. `task spawn`'s existing multi-owner refusal is scoped to LIVE sessions
and covers a different case ("someone is working this right now"); it stays.

Escape hatch is the existing `--new-session`, not a new `--force`.

**DRAFT wording, pending Mike's edit and pending the navigation-verb decision
(see below):**

    E-1859 was claimed by session ES-1046. Pick the work back up:
        endless session goto E-1859 --resume
    To start a fresh session on this task anyway, pass --new-session.

List additional prior claimants beneath when there is more than one.

## Open dependency

The message above recommends `session goto --resume`, which today resolves a
task id only to a LIVE session — so it would not find ES-1046. This task's
`claimed` rows are what make that resolution work against an ended session, so
`session goto`'s task→session lookup must move onto them as part of this work.

Whether the message should instead mention `--revisit`/`--no-revisit`, and
whether `task spawn --reopen` survives at all, is being decided separately. Do
not finalize this string before that lands.

## Verification

- A task with a prior `claimed` row refuses a plain spawn and names the session.
- The same spawn with `--new-session` proceeds.
- A task never claimed by anyone spawns unchanged.
- Re-claiming a task the same session already claimed inserts no duplicate row.
- A session that revisited a task and then claimed it shows BOTH relations.
- `task show` renders `Claimed:` where it previously rendered `Goal:`.
- Post-backfill, E-1859 refuses a plain spawn and names ES-1046, and
  `session goto E-1859 --resume` finds ES-1046 despite it being ended.

## Relationship to `session goto --resume`

fields.title: Make the session and task movement verbs account for task state
fields.description: One root behind four defects: the verbs that move between sessions and tasks act on task state without making it explicit. `task reopen` releases a session's binding silently (its help says 'no session binding', which reads as 'does not create one'). `session resume` clobbers the current pane even when that pane holds live work. `session goto --resume` cannot express intent about a task needing revisit. And `task spawn --reopen` exists only because none of the navigation verbs could change status. Fix together: `--force` plus an unsuppressible announcement on reopen's release; `--force` on resume when the current pane holds a task; `--revisit`/`--no-revisit` on `session goto --resume`; retire `task spawn --reopen`; and rewrite spawn's done-ish refusal, which currently offers 'run task reopen first' as one of two routes — the one that dismantles the guard that produced the message.

# Plan: make the session/task movement verbs account for task state

One root: the verbs that move you between sessions and tasks act on task state
without making it explicit. `task reopen` destroys a binding silently,
`session resume` clobbers a pane that may hold live work, `session goto
--resume` cannot express intent about a task needing revisit, and `task spawn
--reopen` exists only because none of the others could change status.

All decisions are Mike's, 2026-08-13, except strings marked DRAFT — mine to
propose, his to edit.

## 1. `task reopen` gates its release behind `--force`, and announces it

`_reopen_task_core` releases the session→task binding — sets
`sessions.active_task_id` to NULL for whichever session held the task — as a
deliberate side effect, and prints nothing. Its `--help` says "Metadata-only:
no worktree creation, no session binding," which reads as "does not create
one" and is silent about destroying one.

Without `--force`, refuse when a binding exists. DRAFT:

    E-1859 is bound to session ES-1046. Reopening would release that binding,
    and `endless session goto E-1859 --resume` would no longer find it.
    Pass --force to reopen and release, or run
    `endless session goto E-1859 --resume` to pick the work back up.

With `--force`, proceed AND print one line naming what was released. The
announcement is not suppressible and is not verbose-only; a `--force` that
still hides the effect is the same defect with an extra keystroke. Reopening a
task with no binding is unaffected — no gate, no message.

Fix `task reopen --help` to state what it does to an existing binding.

## 2. `session resume` requires `--force` when the current pane holds a task

`session resume` relaunches into the CURRENT pane, clobbering it. When that
pane's session has a task bound, that is destroying live context. Require
`--force`, and name the task in the refusal. DRAFT:

    This pane is working E-1958. `session resume` would replace it.
    Use `endless session goto <ref> --resume` to open the target in a new
    window instead, or pass --force to replace this pane.

Note `session goto --resume` already exists precisely to avoid the clobber, so
the refusal has a good answer to point at.

## 3. `session goto --resume` gains `--revisit` / `--no-revisit`

When the target task is in a state needing revisit, require one of the two and
error explaining both:

- `--revisit` — flip the task to `revisit` and open the session to continue work.
- `--no-revisit` — open the session read-only, to page back through it with no
  intent to change anything. Task status untouched.

DRAFT:

    E-1859 is 'assumed'. Say what you intend:
      --revisit      reopen it and continue work
      --no-revisit   just read the session; leave the status alone

Neither flag is required when the task is in a state that needs no revisit.

## 4. Retire `task spawn --reopen`

Its only unique capability is changing task status, which item 3 now provides
on the navigation verb. Retiring it removes the composite verb and leaves three
single-purpose ones — which is also what makes a future top-level `endless
goto` / `endless resume` / `endless reopen` map cleanly, with no composite to
place.

Decide during implementation whether to delete outright or deprecate with a
message pointing at `session goto --resume --revisit`, given there are no
external users.

`--new-session` is currently documented as "with `--reopen`". It must survive
retirement, since E-1967's spawn guard uses it as its escape hatch — re-home it
onto plain `spawn`.

## 5. Rewrite `task spawn`'s done-ish refusal

Raised when `--force` was not passed and status is in `_CLAIM_REQUIRES_FORCE`
(`unverified`, `confirmed`, `declined`, `obsolete`, `assumed`, `completed`).
For the subset also in `_REOPENABLE_TERMINAL_STATUSES` (`assumed`, `confirmed`,
`completed`) it currently reads:

    E-NNNN is '<status>'; pass --reopen to reopen-and-spawn, or run
    `endless task reopen E-NNNN` first.

Both branches are wrong once item 4 lands, and the second was always the worse
of the two: running `task reopen` first releases the binding AND moves the task
to `revisit`, outside `_CLAIM_REQUIRES_FORCE`, so the follow-up plain `spawn`
proceeds with no prompt at all. The message routed the user into the trap.

DRAFT replacement:

    E-1859 is 'assumed' and was claimed by session ES-1046. Pick it back up:
        endless session goto E-1859 --resume --revisit

The other branch — force-set statuses that are NOT reopenable — keeps its
existing "pass --force to confirm the demotion" wording.

## Sequencing

Item 5's message names the prior claimant, which comes from E-1967's `claimed`
rows. Land E-1967 first, or land item 5's message without the claimant clause
and add it after.

Items 1-4 are independent of E-1967.

  succeeds and prints the release; an unbound task is unchanged.
- `session resume` from a pane with a bound task refuses and names it;
  `--force` proceeds; from a pane with no bound task, unchanged.

  flags; `--revisit` flips status and opens; `--no-revisit` opens without
  touching status.
- `task spawn --reopen` is gone (or deprecated with the pointer).
- `task spawn --new-session` still works without `--reopen`.
- Spawn's done-ish refusal no longer mentions `task reopen`.
- `task reopen --help` describes the release.

# Evidence

Mike's call, 2026-08-13, during the E-1958 session: rename
`sessions.active_task_id` to `sessions.task_id`. Rationale — "active_" was
meaningful when a session might hold several tasks and one of them was the
active one. That is no longer the model: a session holds at most one task, so
the qualifier describes a distinction that no longer exists. Endless has no
external users yet, so there is no reason to carry the legacy name.

## Scope is wider than one column

The name appears across both languages and in a second table:

- Go: the monitor package's session, resume, session_focus, tmux_lookup and db
  paths all name the column in SQL and in struct fields (`ActiveTaskID`);
  `internal/events`'s task-removal executor clears it; `internal/hookcmd`
  reads it.
- Python: session and task command paths read and write it; the pytest suite
  asserts on it directly.
- `session_statuses` carries its own `active_task_id` column with the same
  meaning, and the events executor clears both together. Renaming one without
  the other trades a legacy name for an inconsistent pair.
- `internal/schema/changes/` contains a historical change that recreates the
  sessions table with the old column name. Historical changes must keep
  reproducing the schema as it was at that point — the rename is a NEW change,
  not an edit to an old one.
- `monitor.SessionSnapshot` and `monitor.SessionTxn` both carry
  `ActiveTaskID` / `OldActiveTaskID` / `NewActiveTaskID`, and the latter two are
  serialized into `user-machine.jsonl` as `old_active_task_id` /
  `new_active_task_id`. Renaming the JSON keys breaks readers of existing log
  files; decide explicitly whether the log keeps its current key names.

## Not to be confused with

`sessions.active_epic_id` is a genuinely different thing — the epic a session is
working under while `active_task_id` holds a child. Decide whether it renames
too, or whether "active_" remains correct there because a session's epic and
task are simultaneously active.

# Plan: record who claimed a task, and refuse spawn when someone already did

Two halves that ship together: the guard needs a durable record of who claimed a
task, and that record has no consumer without the guard.

All decisions below are Mike's, taken 2026-08-13, except the three message
strings marked DRAFT — those are mine to propose and his to edit.

## Background: the relation labels

`session_tasks.relation_id` FKs to `session_task_relations`, whose rows render
as the labels in `task show`'s "Touched by:" block. Today: `Goal`, `Surfaced`,
`Revisited` — set once at capture time (claim→goal, create/import→surfaced,
else→revisited) and never revised.

The defect: a session that revisits a task and LATER claims it keeps
`Revisited` forever. Observed on E-1859, where ES-1046 held
`sessions.active_task_id = 1859` and still renders as `Revisited`. So nothing
can answer "which sessions ever claimed this task."

## Decision 1 — rename the relation `goal` → `claimed`

Per Mike: `Goal:` is a bad label because it cannot be reasoned about; `Claimed:`
says what actually happened. Rename the slug and the label together, in this
task rather than a follow-up.

Touches the `session_task_relations` seed rows, every reader that matches on the
slug, and the "Touched by:" render. Historical rows keep their id, so this is a
label change, not a data migration.

## Decision 2 — `claim` ADDS a row, it does not overwrite

Replace `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id)` on `session_tasks` with
`UNIQUE(session_id, task_id, relation_id)`. On claim, INSERT OR IGNORE a
`claimed` row while leaving any existing `surfaced`/`revisited` row untouched,
so the history reads "saw it, then claimed it" rather than replacing one fact
with the other. Re-claiming is idempotent.

`surfaced` and `revisited` keep their present write-once behavior.

Consequence to handle: a session may now hold several rows per task, so every
reader that assumed one row per (session, task) must collapse or pick a display
relation — the "Touched by:" render and session-scoped task listing at minimum.
Find them before changing the key, not after.

## Decision 3 — backfill, most expansive form

Without a backfill the guard protects only tasks claimed after this lands, which
is backwards: old tasks are the ones most likely to be spawned-instead-of-
resumed. So insert a `claimed` row for:

1. every `task.claimed` event in the ledger, and
2. every session whose `sessions.active_task_id` is currently set — catching
   claims the ledger may have missed.

Skip anything that cannot be reconstructed rather than guessing; that task falls
back to today's behavior, which is not a regression.

## The guard

`task spawn` refuses when the target has a `claimed` row belonging to any
session other than the one spawning. Refuse — do not prompt, do not silently
inherit. `task spawn`'s existing multi-owner refusal is scoped to LIVE sessions
and covers a different case ("someone is working this right now"); it stays.

OPEN — the escape hatch has no name. `--new-session` was the candidate, but it
moves to `session goto --resume` / `session resume` under E-1968 (on `spawn` it
is tautological: spawning always starts a new session). Mike has ruled out a new

his deliberate fresh-context handoff — currently has no expression. Resolve
before implementing the guard; a refusal with no stated way through is worse
than no refusal.

**DRAFT wording, pending Mike's edit and pending the navigation-verb decision

        endless session goto E-1859 --resume
    To start a fresh session on this task anyway, pass --new-session.
